mapped.summary: Every item has a row: 514 rows (DeepSeek 107, Kimi 110, ChatGPT 150, Claude 140 = 110 + 30 regional, owner 7: three lines split into seven requests). Not items: the source lines (leads for the research step), ChatGPT's value-per-$1 note (the engine already computes value/cost as the same gross ratio) and Claude's displacement caveat (all 81 types carry displacement text). Decisions: 234 existing (67 of 81 keys), 176 new (70 types), 8 owner-level, 38 quality-of-life only, 58 not modelled. Rules used: new_type = a costed project or program that a local data condition can switch on, even if its value effect turns out unmeasured; quality_of_life_only = events and small community services with no costed row; not_modelled = civic process, plans, funding tools, programs for people rather than places, owner advice and page features. New types by group: flood/hurricane 6, cold/snow 4, wildfire/heat/drought 4, tornado 2, shrinking city 4, rural 5, suburban 3, stabilize/schools/safety 10, other 32 (6 of them regional: new_freeway, high_speed_rail, transmission_line, planned_transit_line, water_recycling, anchor_employer). Proposed kinds, pending sources: 34 value, 24 qol, 5 policy, 6 regional, 1 owner (weatherization). Compound items map to one key; the other part is listed in that type's from_items (e.g. Claude's gravel roads plus water and sewer). Gaps found: 9 existing types that receive items have no trigger in the national engine (national/pipeline/engine.py), so outside Los Angeles they never appear: vacant_lot_green, skate_park, road_diet, litter, graffiti, speed_cameras, roundabout, murals, alley_gating. fiber_5g needs a rural trigger (FCC broadband map). speed_cameras and upzone_transit are named for California laws (AB 645, SB 79) and need state-law conditions elsewhere. The 8 owner-level items belong in the lot checks, not block-group rows. Numbers quoted inside the lists (200% door return, 89% sidewalks, 14.5-19.5% crime drop) are leads only.

types.name: Buy out repeatedly flooded homes and return the land to open space
types.trigger: A block group has at least one unmitigated NFIP Severe Repetitive Loss home (nfipSrl = true) or two or more Repetitive Loss homes (nfipRl = true), with mitigatedIndicator = false, a residential occupancyType (1-3, 11-16) and a rated floodZone of A* or V*. Optional extra condition: the block group intersects the NFHL Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA_TF = 'T'). Floodway areas (ZONE_SUBTY = 'FLOODWAY') rank first.
types.trigger_data:
Main dataset: OpenFEMA 'NFIP Multiple Loss Properties' v1 (FEMA).
- Contents: one record per NFIP repetitive-loss structure, with censusBlockGroup (12-digit 2020 block group, geocoded), fipsCountyCode, communityIdNumber, floodZone, nfipRl, nfipSrl, mitigatedIndicator, insuredIndicator, totalLosses and occupancyType. FEMA describes it as: 'This dataset provides information on structures that have had multiple National Flood Insurance (NFIP) claims across the history of the program.'
- API: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v1/NfipMultipleLossProperties (CSV and JSON). Metadata: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v1/DataSets?$filter=name%20eq%20%27NfipMultipleLossProperties%27
- Updated: metadata 'modified' 2025-12-05.
- Terms: OpenFEMA Terms and Conditions, https://www.fema.gov/about/openfema/terms-conditions. The metadata points to this page, but it returned HTTP 403 and I could not read it.
- Caveats: latitude and longitude are cut to 1 decimal place, and FEMA warns that block-group assignment is geocoded and has error.

Flood zone layer: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (NFHL), layer 28 'Flood Hazard Zones' (FLD_ZONE, ZONE_SUBTY, SFHA_TF), https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28. It is a live service covering every area FEMA has digitized. The data.gov NFHL record (https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/national-flood-hazard-layer-nfhl, a HIFLD copy last updated 2022-10-24) lists the license https://www.usa.gov/government-works.
types.effect:
Effect on nearby home values: negative for adjacent homes in the short run.
- New York coastal counties, post-Sandy NY Rising program: homes sold within 100 m of a buyout or acquisition sold for 10-20% less.
- For buyouts the drop fades after 100 m. The effect approaches zero about 4 years after the program starts and may turn positive after 5 years (Hashida & Dundas 2023).
- Other studies disagree, so treat the sign as uncertain (see notes).
- Safety benefit: the bought-out home is permanently removed from future flood losses.
types.effect_quote: Both a repeat sales difference-in-differences approach and an event study addressing treatment effect heterogeneity suggest that buyouts and acquisitions have sizable negative effects on prices (−20 to −10 percent) for homes sold adjacent (≤100 m) to participating properties. The spatial scale of the impacts differs across policy types, with negative effects attenuating after 100 m for buyouts but persisting for acquisitions up to 1200 m.
types.effect_source: Hashida, Yukiko & Dundas, Steven J. (2023). The effects of a voluntary property buyout and acquisition program on coastal housing markets: Evidence from New York. Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 121, DOI 10.1016/j.jeem.2023.102873. I read the publisher abstract on IDEAS/RePEc because ScienceDirect blocked automated access.
types.cost:
Unit cost: the pre-flood fair market value of the home, plus about $23,000 per property in local and state government activity costs (about 18% of the purchase price).
- Source: median buyout project in a 2020 survey of North Carolina local officials and state hazard mitigation officers nationwide (Curran-Groome et al. 2022, Land Use Policy 118:106128).
- Map formula: local median home value × about 1.18.
- Example from a high-cost market: New York's post-Sandy direct buyout cost was $274.86 million for 723 buyouts, about $380,000 each (my calculation; see notes).
types.cost_quote: Respondents reported that activity costs at the local and state government levels account for approximately $23,000 per property for the median buyout project, or roughly 18% of property purchase costs.
types.notes:
Other neighbor-effect estimates (they conflict):
- Guo, Liao & Miao (2023), RFF Working Paper 23-44, https://media.rff.org/documents/WP_23-44.pdf. It studies the same NY program: 'Our baseline specification in column (1) indicates that a home acquisition or buyout significantly increases property values within a 1 km radius by 3.66 percent.' However, for buyouts alone: 'In contrast, the effects of buyouts are much smaller and become negligible after 100 m.' RFF has also posted an updated version, which I did not read.
- Lee et al. (2023), Lincoln Institute WP23RJL1, Harris County, TX, https://storage.pardot.com/153411/1693934548kDKfVk8S/Lee_WP23RJL1.pdf: 'Specifically, it shows that an increase in buyout properties within any range of a buffer would decrease property values by a range of 0.12 to 0.60% per buyout.'
- Hashida & Dundas, same abstract: 'These impacts are shown to approach zero four years after policy initiation, and the effect of buyouts may turn positive after five years.'

Purchase price: CRS Insight IN11911, https://www.everycrsreport.com/files/2025-04-22_IN11911_86c088b43111aba7e95b4fc73d2c6f71a79a91a3.html: 'Homeowners are generally offered the pre-disaster fair market value of the property.' The same Insight says the local government must maintain the bought-out lots.

NY example, from the RFF paper: 'the direct cost of buyouts was $274.86 million' and 'Participating properties totaled 1,289, of which 566 were acquisitions and 723 buyouts.'

FEMA benchmark: FEMA's September 2021 pre-calculated benefits memo, https://www.fema.gov/sites/default/files/documents/fema_acquisition-elevation-precalculated-benefits-memo_092021.pdf, lists 'Acquisitions: $323,000 per structure'. Acquisitions in the 1% flood zone whose total project cost is at or below this are treated as cost-effective. This is an average-benefit (avoided loss) ceiling, not a price. I read the memo earlier in this run, but later re-fetches got HTTP 403. https://floodready.vermont.gov/node/832 restates: 'The 2021 pre-calculated values are $323,000 and $205,000 respectively.'

Scale (Mach et al. 2019, Science Advances, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6785245/): 'From 1989 to 2017, FEMA funded 43,633 voluntary buyouts of flood-prone properties for which data are publicly available'.

Policy note: Lee et al. find tree canopy offsets part of the loss. Pair buyouts with maintained green space so the lots do not become a vacant-lot discount.

types.name: Elevate flood-prone homes and roads
types.trigger:
Residential buildings inside the NFHL Special Flood Hazard Area (SFHA_TF = 'T'; FLD_ZONE A, AE, AH, AO or VE) built before the community's first flood map (pre-FIRM).
- Rule: FEMA counts a building as post-FIRM if construction or substantial improvement started after 31 Dec 1974 or on/after the community's initial FIRM date, whichever is later.
- Block-group measure: count NFIP policies with postFIRMConstructionIndicator = false (or preFIRMConstructionIndicator = true) and floodZoneCurrent in the SFHA, grouped by censusGeoid.
- Exclude homes already flagged for buyout (Severe Repetitive Loss).
types.trigger_data:
1) FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28. Live service, nationwide where digitized. License: https://www.usa.gov/government-works, per https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/national-flood-hazard-layer-nfhl.

2) OpenFEMA 'NFIP Community Status Book' v1, https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v1/NfipCommunityStatusBook. One row per NFIP community. Its field initialFloodInsuranceRateMap is, in FEMA's words, the 'dividing line between two building categories called Pre-FIRM and Post-FIRM'. Metadata modified 2026-07-28.

3) OpenFEMA 'NFIP Redacted Policies' v3, https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v3/NfipPolicies. Includes postFIRMConstructionIndicator and floodZoneCurrent, with censusGeoid 'presented at the Census Block Group level'. Metadata modified 2026-10-14.

Terms for 2 and 3: OpenFEMA Terms and Conditions, https://www.fema.gov/about/openfema/terms-conditions. The page returned HTTP 403 and I did not read it.
types.effect:
Effect on home values: no resale premium measured.
- Charleston, SC: repeated floods slowed appreciation, and elevated homes lost more appreciation than non-elevated homes. The market did not value elevation (Blackwell, Mothorpe & Wright 2024). The abstract gives no percentage.
- Safety and cost (Jefferson Parish, LA): raising existing homes 3 ft above ground or to the base flood elevation, whichever is higher, cut median average annual flood loss by 98%. Benefit-cost ratio: 1.5 over 30 years, 1.7 over 70 years (Al Assi et al. 2023; see notes).
types.effect_quote: We find flooding significantly reduces the rate of appreciation, and home elevation increases the rate of lost appreciation. Our results suggest home elevation is not a flood risk adaptation and mitigation strategy valued by the market.
types.effect_source: Blackwell, Calvin; Mothorpe, Chris; Wright, Julie (2024). Flooding and Elevation: An Examination of Differential Price Responses to Flood Events. Journal of Sustainable Real Estate 16(1), 2372133, DOI 10.1080/19498276.2024.2372133. I read the abstract on IDEAS/RePEc; tandfonline.com returned HTTP 403.
types.cost: About $120,000 per single-family home: the average elevation cost set by Louisiana GOHSEP for Jefferson Parish, LA, after the 2005 storms. FEMA's HMGP grant paid about $90,000 and Louisiana's Road Home grant about $30,000.
types.cost_quote: The cost of elevating homes in the selected study area (i.e., $120,000) was determined by GOHSEP. Because the HMGP grants typically cover 75% of the cost, while The Road Home Program grants cover the remaining 25%, the HMGP and Road Home Program grants typically provide $90,000 and $30,000 per home, respectively.
types.notes:
Cost source: Al Assi, Mostafiz, Friedland, Rohli, Taghinezhad & Rahim (2023), Cost-effectiveness of federal CDBG-DR Road Home Program mitigation assistance in Jefferson Parish, Louisiana. Natural Hazards 117:1291-1319, DOI 10.1007/s11069-023-05904-3, open access. Springer served a bot-check page when I re-fetched it; I had read the full article earlier in this run.

Safety and cost quotes from the same paper:
- 'The analysis reveals that elevating existing homes by either 3 feet above the ground or to the base flood elevation (BFE; 100-year flood elevation), whichever is higher, reduces the median AAL by 98%.'
- 'This elevation generates a BCR of 1.5 and 1.7 over a 30-year mortgage and a 70-year building lifetime, respectively, if the benefit is allocated proportionately.'

Other cost benchmarks:
- Reguero et al. (2018), PLoS ONE, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5894966/. Their Gulf-wide model prices raising homes 10 ft at '$83,300 / house' and finds a benefit-cost ratio of only 0.41-0.73 for home elevation across the Gulf.
- FEMA 2021 pre-calculated benefits memo: 'Elevations (and Mitigation Reconstruction3): $205,000 per structure'. This is a benefit ceiling for cost-effectiveness, not a price.

Roads: I found no cost or effect source for road elevation in this pass.

types.name: Living shoreline, dune or wetland restoration
types.trigger:
A block group touches a shoreline inside FEMA coastal flood zones: NFHL FLD_ZONE 'V' or 'VE', or seaward of the Limit of Moderate Wave Action line (Coastal A zone). Which project to suggest:
- Sheltered estuary, bay, river, sound or Great Lakes shore: living shoreline or marsh.
- Open-ocean beach (V/VE, or where the Primary Frontal Dunes layer is mapped): dune.
- Rank by FEMA National Risk Index coastal-flooding expected annual loss (CFLD_EALB).
types.trigger_data:
FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer MapServer, https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer. Layers used:
- 28 Flood Hazard Zones (FLD_ZONE V/VE)
- 19 Limit of Moderate Wave Action (landward edge of Coastal A)
- 25 Primary Frontal Dunes
- 0 NFHL Availability (coverage)
Live service, nationwide where digitized. License: https://www.usa.gov/government-works, per https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/national-flood-hazard-layer-nfhl (HIFLD copy last updated 2022-10-24).

Ranking: FEMA National Risk Index Census Tracts, https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Census_Tracts/FeatureServer. Fields CFLD_EALB and CFLD_RISKR. 'National Risk Index Data Version: December 2025 (1.20.0)'. Terms are in the item's licenseInfo, https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/9da4eeb936544335a6db0cd7a8448a51?f=json: planning use only, and a citation statement is required.
types.effect:
Dunes, home values: building dunes raised New Jersey coastal home prices by about 3.6% net. Lost ocean views and privacy partly offset the protection benefit (Dundas 2017).

Wetlands and marshes: no home-value estimate found. Measured damage reduction: wetlands avoided about $625 million of direct flood damage in Hurricane Sandy across 12 states. Homes behind a salt marsh in Barnegat Bay, NJ had 16% lower annual flood losses (Narayan et al. 2017).
types.effect_quote: I identify the net effect of treatment utilizing the doubly robust Oaxaca-Blinder estimator and show that coastal housing price increases attributable to constructed dunes are approximately 3.6%.
types.effect_source: Dundas, Steven J. (2017). Benefits and ancillary costs of natural infrastructure: Evidence from the New Jersey coast. Journal of Environmental Economics and Management 85: 62-80, DOI 10.1016/j.jeem.2017.04.008. I read the abstract on IDEAS/RePEc; ScienceDirect blocked automated access.
types.cost: $300 to more than $1,500 per linear foot of living shoreline, depending on wave energy and technique (Maryland Department of Natural Resources, May 2026).
types.cost_quote: A living shoreline can range from $300 to over $1,500 per linear foot, depending on the wave energy environment and technique utilized.
types.notes:
Siting rule (NOAA Fisheries, https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/insight/understanding-living-shorelines): 'Estuaries, bays, rivers, and other sheltered shorelines are good candidates for living shorelines. Typically, living shorelines are not found on beaches along the open ocean.' NOAA also says living shorelines 'tend to cost less than hardened shorelines, for both installation and maintenance.'

Dundas also finds a cost to views: 'A decomposition of the average impact suggests that the policy intervention generates ancillary costs related to impaired ocean views and privacy concerns that partially offset large protection benefits.'

Narayan et al. (2017), Scientific Reports 7:9463, https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-017-09269-z:
- 'Using an extensive database of property exposure, the regional study shows that wetlands avoided $625 Million in direct flood damages during Hurricane Sandy.'
- 'Properties behind a marsh, on average, save 16% in flood losses every year compared to properties where marshes have been lost.'

Other cost figures (they vary widely):
- Maryland DNR FAQ for local governments (2013 PDF), https://dnr.maryland.gov/ccs/Documents/ls/FAQs_LocalGovernments.pdf: 'a living shoreline project generally costs between $200 and $400 per linear foot'.
- Delaware DNREC I-ADAPT sheet (2022 dollars), https://documents.dnrec.delaware.gov/I-ADAPT/AdaptationStrategies/Living%20Shorelines.pdf: contractor design plus construction at $1,000-$5,000 per linear foot (from a table).
- Reguero et al. (2018), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5894966/: $25 M/mile for salt-marsh restoration and $1.5 M/mile for oyster reefs. They conclude: 'Nature-based adaptation options could avert more than $50 billion of these costs, and do so cost effectively with average benefit to cost ratios above 3.5.'

types.name: Stronger wind code and fortified-roof grants
types.trigger:
The county is in the hurricane-prone region per FEMA's Building Code Adoption Tracking (BCAT) data (Hurricane_Risk = 'T').
- Suggest a building-code upgrade where Hurricane_Resistance is 'Not Resistant' or 'Partially Resistant'.
- Suggest FORTIFIED Roof grants in tracts with National Risk Index hurricane rating HRCN_RISKR of 'Very High' or 'Relatively High'.
- The mapping step's ASCE 7 design wind speed of 130 mph or more cannot be applied from open data (ASCE 7 maps are not an open national dataset). The Alabama report supports 130 mph as the line above which the 2021+ residential code nearly matches FORTIFIED (see notes).
types.trigger_data:
1) FEMA Building Code Adoption Tracking (BCAT) Counties, ArcGIS feature service https://services.arcgis.com/DN2fPfpggEPlLhP6/arcgis/rest/services/FEMA_Building_Code_Adoptions_Tracking_Counties/FeatureServer/0. Item metadata: https://www.arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/dcd25a0db911410cbbb07d4c984ff54e?f=json.
- Geography: county, all 50 states, DC and 5 territories. Fields include Hurricane_Risk (T/F), Hurricane_Resistance and Wind_Risk. Description: 'Tracked hazards include: flood, seismic, damaging wind, hurricane wind, and tornado.'
- Updated: Data_Currency 2025-12-31; item modified 2026-02-03.
- License: 'This work is marked with CC0 1.0'.

2) FEMA National Risk Index Census Tracts, https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Census_Tracts/FeatureServer. Fields HRCN_RISKR, HRCN_EALB and HRCN_AFREQ. Data Version December 2025 (1.20.0). Terms (item licenseInfo): 'The National Risk Index data are meant for planning purposes only.' A citation statement is required.
types.effect:
Effect on home values (coastal Alabama):
- FORTIFIED-designated homes sold for about 2-4% more, from sales 2011-2021 (Petrolia et al. 2023).
- A second peer-reviewed study finds a 6-7% premium at median distance to the coast, highest nearest the coast (Awondo et al. 2023; see notes).

Losses:
- Hurricane Sally (2020, Alabama): FORTIFIED homes had 55-74% fewer claims and 14-40% smaller claims (ALDOI/UA CRIR 2025).
- Florida's 2001 statewide code cut windstorm losses by up to 72%, returning $6 of avoided loss per $1 of added cost (Simmons et al. 2018).
types.effect_quote: The results of our full- and nearest-neighbor-matched sample design suggest a likely price premium significance on the order of 2-4% for FORTIFIED homes.
types.effect_source: Petrolia, Daniel; Ishee, Shea; Yun, Seong; Cummings, Reid; Maples, Josh (2023). Do Wind Hazard Mitigation Programs Affect Home Sales Values? Journal of Real Estate Research 45(2): 137-159, DOI 10.1080/08965803.2022.2066249. I read the abstract on EconPapers.
types.cost: About $13,000 average per FORTIFIED Roof retrofit in Alabama's Strengthen Alabama Homes program, which pays up to $10,000 per roof (figures as of 12 Nov 2024; about 8,700 homes retrofitted with about $86 million paid).
types.cost_quote: SAH pays up to $10,000 per roof. The average cost of retrofitting a house in the SAH program is about $13,000.
types.notes:
Second resale study: Awondo, Hollans, Powell & Wade (2023), Estimating the effects of wind loss mitigation on home value. Southern Economic Journal 90(1): 71-89. Abstract: https://ideas.repec.org/a/wly/soecon/v90y2023i1p71-89.html. Quote: 'We find that on average homebuyers located at median distance to the coast pay a 6%–7% premium for Fortified homes, which exceeds the typical cost of building or retrofitting houses to the Fortified standard.'

From the ALDOI and UA Center for Risk and Insurance Research report (May 2025, same PDF as the cost):
- Claims: 'Depending on the selected designation, sample, and measure, Fortified construction reduced loss frequency by 55% to 74%, loss severity by 14% to 40%, and loss ratio by 51% to 72%.'
- Insurance: Alabama's required wind-premium discounts 'range from 50% for new Fortified Gold houses to 20% for Fortified Roof designations earned more than five years earlier.'
- 130 mph line: 'In areas which have adopted the latest IRC (2021 and soon 2024) with a design wind speed above 130 mph, the code now closely mirrors the IBHS Fortified standard.'
- Extra cost, cited second-hand (I did not open Ghosh et al.): 'Estimates of the increased cost range from 0.5% to 3% for new construction to the Fortified Gold level, and 6% to 16% for retrofitting an existing home to the Fortified Roof standard (Ghosh et al. 2023).'

Building code: Simmons, Czajkowski & Done (2018), Land Economics 94(2): 155-174, https://le.uwpress.org/content/94/2/155. Quote: 'We use 10 years of paid insured loss data to show that the FBC reduced windstorm losses by up to 72%, then use our results to conduct a benefit-cost analysis (BCA). The FBC passes the BCA by a margin of $6 in full reduced loss to $1 of added cost, with a payback period of approximately 8 years.'

Grant terms (https://strengthenalabamahomes.com/): 'Grants will pay 100% of the cost of mitigation up to $10,000'.

types.name: Join or move up in FEMA's Community Rating System (flood-insurance discount)
types.trigger: The NFIP community (participatingInNFIP = true) is not in the CRS (classRating blank or 10) or sits at a low class (8 or 9), and it contains NFHL Special Flood Hazard Area or NFIP policies. Rank block groups in those communities by NFIP policy count and premium (NFIP Redacted Policies, grouped by censusGeoid). Household savings: about 5% of the full-risk premium per class step.
types.trigger_data:
1) OpenFEMA 'NFIP Community Status Book' v1, https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v1/NfipCommunityStatusBook (CSV: https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v1/NfipCommunityStatusBook.csv).
- One row per NFIP community: communityIdNumber, participatingInNFIP, classRating, sfhaDiscount, nonSfhaDiscount and classRatingEffectiveDate.
- FEMA: 'In addition, this dataset provides the available insurance discount rates for communities that participate in the Community Rating System (CRS).'
- Metadata modified 2026-07-28.

2) OpenFEMA 'NFIP Redacted Policies' v3, https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v3/NfipPolicies. Fields crsClassCode, floodZoneCurrent, totalInsurancePremiumOfThePolicy and fullRiskPremium, with censusGeoid at block-group level. Metadata modified 2026-10-14.

Community boundaries are in the OpenFEMA 'NFIP Community Layer' datasets. Terms: OpenFEMA Terms and Conditions, https://www.fema.gov/about/openfema/terms-conditions (HTTP 403; not read).
types.effect:
Effect on home values: no peer-reviewed estimate found.
- Losses (nationwide, 1998-2020): CRS participation is linked to fewer NFIP claims, roughly in proportion to the premium discount. 'Flood Damage Reduction' activities are linked to 20-30% fewer claims. Cumulative damage reductions were $11.4 billion against $12.1 billion in premium discounts (Gourevitch & Pinter 2023).
- Premiums: each CRS class step adds a 5% discount, from 0% at Class 10 to 45% at Class 1, on all NFIP policies in the community (FEMA CRS Discount Guide; see notes).
types.effect_quote: We find that participation in CRS is associated with reduced flood damage, with the percent reduction in claims roughly proportional to NFIP premium discounts. Among CRS activities, those related to ‘Flood Damage Reduction’ are most effective in reducing flood losses and are associated with a 20%–30% decrease in NFIP claims.
types.effect_source: Gourevitch, Jesse D. & Pinter, Nicholas (2023). Federal incentives for community-level climate adaptation: an evaluation of FEMA's Community Rating System. Environmental Research Letters 18(3): 034037, DOI 10.1088/1748-9326/acbaae.
types.cost: About $4.17 million a year across 2,170 communities for CRS paperwork: application, annual recertification, environmental and historic preservation certification, and repetitive-loss updates. That is about $1,900 and 24 staff hours per community per year (my calculation), from FEMA's estimate in the Federal Register of May 31, 2023. It does not include the cost of the flood-reduction activities themselves.
types.cost_quote: Estimated Number of Respondents: 2,170. Estimated Number of Responses: 4,170. Estimated Total Annual Burden Hours: 52,292. Estimated Total Annual Respondent Cost: $4,173,947.
types.notes:
Discount schedule: FEMA CRS Discount Guide (July 2023), https://agents.floodsmart.gov/sites/default/files/media/document/2025-07/fema-nfip-crs-guide-2023.pdf. Class 9 = 5%, rising 5% per class to Class 1 = 45%.
- 'A Class 10 community is not participating in CRS and receives no discount.'
- The discount 'is applied to the full-risk premium for all NFIP policies in the Regular Program in a participating community, including policies outside of the Special Flood Hazard Area.'

Funding caveat (Gourevitch & Pinter): 'This means that all policyholders pay 15.3% more in premiums', which pays for the CRS discounts.

Cost of joining: New Hampshire Office of Planning and Development, https://www.nheconomy.com/getmedia/6a45abc9-11a8-4139-b469-f8632778e7c6/crs-resp-cost-ben.pdf: 'No fee is charged for a community to apply for CRS'. The real costs are staff time and carrying out creditable activities.

Home values: the only property-value evidence I saw was a Florida State University student poster, which I did not use.

types.name: Storm-drain and drainage upgrade on flood-prone streets
types.trigger: A block group whose streets lie inside an NFHL 1% flood zone (SFHA_TF = 'T') or 0.2% flood zone (FLD_ZONE = 'X' with ZONE_SUBTY = '0.2 PCT ANNUAL CHANCE FLOOD HAZARD'). Also: a block group with repeated NFIP claims outside mapped flood zones (floodZoneCurrent X, B or C, grouped by censusGeoid). FEMA's code definition for those zones includes 'Pockets of areas subject to drainage problems'.
types.trigger_data:
1) FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28 Flood Hazard Zones, https://hazards.fema.gov/arcgis/rest/services/public/NFHL/MapServer/28. Values seen in queries: FLD_ZONE 'AE', 'VE' and 'X'; ZONE_SUBTY '0.2 PCT ANNUAL CHANCE FLOOD HAZARD' and 'FLOODWAY'; SFHA_TF 'T'/'F'. Live service; license https://www.usa.gov/government-works per https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/national-flood-hazard-layer-nfhl.

2) OpenFEMA 'NFIP Redacted Claims' v3, https://www.fema.gov/api/open/v3/NfipClaims. Fields floodZoneCurrent, ratedFloodZone, yearOfLoss, amountPaidOnBuildingClaim and censusGeoid (block group). FEMA: 'This dataset provides details on flood insurance claims transactions.' Metadata modified 2026-07-20.

Terms: OpenFEMA Terms and Conditions, https://www.fema.gov/about/openfema/terms-conditions (HTTP 403; not read).
types.effect:
Grey storm-drain upgrades: no home-value effect measured; I found no study.

Green stormwater infrastructure (bioswales, rain gardens, tree trenches), Philadelphia: houses within 25 m of a completed site sold for about 10% more per square foot than houses near planned sites. The premium falls to 5-6% at 40 m and 3% at 50 m (Cohen, Huang & McMillen 2024, working paper).

New Haven, CT: nearby bioswales are linked to about 8.8% higher prices (Cohen, Dietz & Huang 2023, working paper).
types.effect_quote: Houses that are within 25m of a completed GSI sell at a premium of about 10 percent in price per-square foot compared with houses that are within a planned GSI location.
types.effect_source: Cohen, Jeffrey P.; Huang, Yuchen; McMillen, Daniel (2024). Can Fairness Flow in Philly? Real Estate Assessment Equity for Green Stormwater Infrastructure Finance. Lincoln Institute of Land Policy Working Paper WP24JC1, May 2024. Landing page: https://www.lincolninst.edu/publications/working-papers/can-fairness-flow-in-philly/
types.cost: Grey: about $500 per linear foot of storm sewer replacement or capital project, about $2.64 million per mile (City of Laramie, WY, consultant memo of 1 Dec 2023). Green: about $14,000 per curbside bioswale, installed (New Haven, CT, about 2023; see notes).
types.cost_quote: Improvements that require pipe replacement as well as implementation of the capital projects identified in the Master Plan have an average cost of approximately $500 per linear foot for storm sewers. If for example, the City provided a dedicated capital investment for one (1) mile of storm sewer replacement annually, the investment, at today’s prices, would be $2,640,000.
types.notes:
Philadelphia distance decay (same working paper): 'If we enlarge the treatment zone to 40m, the effect is at 5-6 percent of per square meter price; at 50 meters it goes further down to 3 percent.' The abstract says 'the causal impacts of GSI on single family residential sales prices per square foot of living area are in the range of 10 to 15 percent, on average.'

New Haven: Cohen, Dietz & Huang (2023), Lincoln Institute WP23JC1, https://storage.pardot.com/153411/16902983932kC1Snmu/Cohen_WP23JC1.pdf.
- Cost: 'Second, the New Haven Engineering Office has informed us that the full cost of a new bioswale similar to those currently installed in these neighborhoods, including installation costs and materials, is approximately $14,000.'
- Effect (executive summary): 'approximately an 8.8percent increase in residential property prices due to the presence of nearby bioswales in New Haven.'

Both Lincoln papers are working papers, not peer-reviewed.

The Laramie figure comes from a WSP consultant memo to the city's stormwater focus group. It is a local planning average, not a national one; the same memo gives lining costs of $109-$664 per linear foot. Use the green-infrastructure effect only for green projects. NFIP claims outside the 1% zone are the best open signal of drainage (not river) flooding.

result.summary:
I researched six flood and hurricane project types, each with a trigger, FEMA trigger data (with URLs, update dates and terms), a measured effect and a unit cost. I re-checked every main quote word for word against the downloaded page or PDF.

| Type | Effect | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Buyouts | Homes within 100 m sell 10-20% lower at first; the effect fades within about 4-5 years (Hashida & Dundas 2023, peer-reviewed). Two working papers disagree on the sign. | Pre-flood market value plus about $23,000 per property in activity costs, about 18% (Curran-Groome et al. 2022) |
| Elevation | No resale premium (Blackwell et al. 2024). It does cut median annual flood loss by 98%, benefit-cost ratio 1.5-1.7 (Al Assi et al. 2023). | About $120,000 per home in Jefferson Parish, LA |
| Dunes and living shorelines | Constructed dunes raised New Jersey coastal prices about 3.6% (Dundas 2017). For wetlands only damage avoided is measured. | $300 to more than $1,500 per linear foot (Maryland DNR, 2026) |
| FORTIFIED roofs and wind codes | Resale premium about 2-4% (Petrolia et al. 2023) to 6-7% (Awondo et al. 2023) in coastal Alabama. Claims fell 55-74% in Hurricane Sally. Florida's 2001 code cut windstorm losses by up to 72%. | About $13,000 average roof retrofit; Alabama's grant covers up to $10,000 |
| Community Rating System | No home-value estimate found. Claims fall roughly in line with the discount of 5% per class (Gourevitch & Pinter 2023). | Paperwork about $4.17 million a year across 2,170 communities |
| Drainage | Grey storm drains: nothing measured. Green stormwater infrastructure: about +10% within 25 m in Philadelphia (working paper). | About $500 per linear foot of storm sewer; about $14,000 per bioswale |

All trigger data is FEMA's: the OpenFEMA API (repetitive-loss properties, community status book with CRS class, policies and claims by block group), the flood hazard map service, the National Risk Index and the building-code tracking layer. The 130 mph wind-speed trigger can't be applied from open data, so I substituted FEMA's county hurricane-risk flag.

Some journal pages and fema.gov pages refused automated access, so several citations rest on publisher abstracts on IDEAS/EconPapers or on copies I read earlier in this run. The WebFetch tool could not reach any host this session, so all reading was done with direct downloads. Details are in open_questions.
open_questions: fema.gov returned HTTP 403 to automated downloads this session. I could not read the OpenFEMA Terms and Conditions page or the BCAT glossary that defines Hurricane_Risk. I read the September 2021 pre-calculated benefits memo earlier in this run, but re-fetches were refused. A person should confirm these pages in a browser.

Al Assi et al. 2023 (link.springer.com, used for the $120,000 elevation cost) served a bot-check page when I re-fetched it. I read the full open-access text earlier in this run, so a verifier may hit the same block.

Several journal pages blocked automated access: ScienceDirect (Hashida & Dundas 2023; Dundas 2017), Taylor & Francis (Blackwell et al. 2024; Petrolia et al. 2023) and Wiley (Awondo et al. 2023). I used the publisher abstracts on IDEAS/RePEc and EconPapers, so magnitudes not in an abstract (for example, how much appreciation elevated Charleston homes lost) were not read.

The 'ASCE 7 design wind speed of 130 mph or more' trigger has no open nationwide dataset; ASCE's Hazard Tool is licensed. I proposed FEMA's county hurricane-risk flag plus the National Risk Index hurricane rating instead. The 130 mph line is supported only by the Alabama report's statement that the 2021 and later residential code with design wind speed above 130 mph closely mirrors FORTIFIED.

Buyout effects on neighbours conflict for the same New York program: Hashida & Dundas (peer-reviewed) find negative effects next door; Guo, Liao & Miao (RFF working paper 23-44; an updated version exists that I did not read) find positive effects driven by acquisitions. Harris County, TX (Lee et al., working paper) finds negative effects. The map may need to show a range or a sign caveat.

I found no peer-reviewed estimate of how Community Rating System class affects home values; the only property-value evidence seen was an FSU student poster, not used. Should the map use claims reduction and premium savings for this type?

I found no study measuring the home-value effect of grey storm-drain upgrades. The green stormwater infrastructure evidence is two Lincoln Institute working papers (Philadelphia +10% within 25 m; New Haven +8.8%), not peer-reviewed.

Living-shoreline costs vary about tenfold: Maryland's 2026 news release ($300 to over $1,500 per linear foot), Maryland's 2013 FAQ ($200-$400), Delaware's 2022-dollar sheet ($1,000-$5,000 for design and construction) and Gulf planning costs ($25 M per mile for marsh). A regional cost table may be needed.

The original Awondo et al. FORTIFIED resale report at aei.culverhouse.ua.edu failed TLS verification even with the proxy CA bundle, so I used their 2023 Southern Economic Journal abstract. Ghosh et al. 2023 (HUD Cityscape, FORTIFIED retrofit costs) returned an empty HTTP 202 and is cited only second-hand through the Alabama report.

www.journals.uchicago.edu did not resolve in this session (Hashida & Dundas' New Jersey Blue Acres paper, DOI 10.1086/729868), and the WebFetch tool could not resolve any host (ideas.repec.org, media.rff.org). All reading was done by direct HTTPS download through the session proxy.
No cost or effect source was found for elevating roads, part of the flood_elevation type name.

Buyout cost is given as a formula (local home value × about 1.18). The only all-in example is New York's post-Sandy cost of about $380,000 per buyout (my calculation from the RFF paper). FEMA's $323,000 per structure is a benefit ceiling for cost-effectiveness, not a price.

checks.item: flood_buyout effect_url: Hashida & Dundas 2023, JEEM 121 (IDEAS/RePEc abstract)
checks.note: HTTP 200. The quote appears word for word in the abstract. The abstract also says 'These impacts are shown to approach zero four years after policy initiation, and the effect of buyouts may turn positive after five years', so the 4-year and 5-year claims hold. Volume 121(C) and DOI 10.1016/j.jeem.2023.102873 match. Minor: the abstract calls it 'a voluntary buyout and acquisition program in the U.S. state of New York' covering the state's coastal counties. It does not name NY Rising or Sandy; that context comes from the RFF paper on the same 1,289-property program.

checks.item: flood_buyout cost_url: Curran-Groome, Hino, BenDor & Salvesen 2022, Land Use Policy (NSF PAR accepted manuscript)
checks.note: PDF, HTTP 200. The quote appears word for word in the conclusions. The survey matches the description: 'staff in local governments (in the State of North Carolina) and state governments (all state hazard mitigation officers in the US)', sent at the end of August 2020 and closed at the start of December 2020. Land Use Policy 118:106128 (DOI 10.1016/j.landusepol.2022.106128) is confirmed on https://par.nsf.gov/biblio/10334742. Caveats: (1) The ~$23,000 is the sum of a local median ($14,428) and a state median ($8,161) taken from different projects: $22,589, n=14, a median 18.3% of purchase costs. Table 1 itself warns 'Combined costs are not equivalent to the total activity cost per project.' (2) This PDF does not contain the 'pre-flood fair market value' part; that comes from CRS IN11911, checked separately and verified. (3) The NC-heavy sample implies a purchase price of about $123k. In RFF's New York data the total buyout cost ($359.72M) is about 31% above the direct cost ($274.86M), so the x1.18 formula may understate overhead in high-cost programs.

checks.item: flood_elevation effect_url: Blackwell, Mothorpe & Wright 2024, J. Sustainable Real Estate 16(1) (IDEAS abstract)
checks.note: HTTP 200. The quote appears word for word in the abstract. The abstract names Charleston, SC and 'multiple flood events' and gives no percentage, as the research says. Vol. 16(1), article 2372133, DOI 10.1080/19498276.2024.2372133 match. The Jefferson Parish 98% / BCR part of the effect text comes from Al Assi et al. (next row).

checks.item: flood_elevation cost_url: Al Assi et al. 2023, Natural Hazards 117 (Springer article page)
checks.corrected: Verifiable alternative wording (Research Square preprint v1, 12 Oct 2022, https://www.researchsquare.com/article/rs-2126597/latest.pdf): 'The total elevation cost per existing home in the presented case study area is approximately $120,000, with around 25% ($30,000) being the Road Home Program share.'
checks.note: Springer returned a 3 KB 'Client Challenge' bot-check page (HTTP 200) instead of the article. I did not try to get past it; the session's permission check refused a further attempt on other Springer URLs. The LSU repository copy (repository.lsu.edu/bio_engineering_pubs/458) returned a Cloudflare 'Just a moment...' challenge (403). Corroboration only: Crossref metadata confirms the title, six authors, Natural Hazards 117(2):1291-1319, 2023 and the CC BY 4.0 license. The published abstract in Crossref contains the '98%' median AAL sentence and the 'BCR of 1.5 and 1.7' sentence word for word. The preprint had 96% and BCRs 6.13/7.01, so the research correctly used the published figures. The exact cost sentence ('(i.e., $120,000) was determined by GOHSEP ... $90,000 and $30,000 per home') is not in the preprint and could not be checked in the published version. The $120,000 total and $30,000 Road Home share are consistent with the preprint. The GOHSEP attribution and the word 'average' remain unverified.

checks.item: living_shoreline effect_url: Dundas 2017, JEEM 85:62-80 (IDEAS abstract)
checks.note: HTTP 200. The quote appears word for word in the abstract. New Jersey comes from the title ('Evidence from the New Jersey coast'), and the abstract's last sentence supports the offset from ocean views and privacy. Vol. 85(C), pp. 62-80, DOI 10.1016/j.jeem.2017.04.008 match. This source covers constructed dunes only; the wetland figures rest on Narayan et al., checked separately and verified.

checks.item: living_shoreline cost_url: Maryland DNR news release, 22 May 2026
checks.note: HTTP 200, dated May 22, 2026. The quote appears word for word. The figure covers living shorelines only. It gives no dune or marsh cost, yet the type's effect evidence is for dunes, so the cost and the effect refer to different measures. Consistency check on the same page: the Pickering Creek project ran 600 linear feet for $225,595 in loans plus $527,647 in other funding, about $1,255 per linear foot, inside the stated range.

checks.item: wind_retrofit effect_url: Petrolia et al. 2023, J. Real Estate Research 45(2) (EconPapers abstract)
checks.note: HTTP 200 after a redirect to econpapers.repec.org/article/tafrjerxx/v_3a45_3ay_3a2023_3ai_3a2_3ap_3a137-159.htm. The quote appears word for word. The abstract confirms coastal Alabama, ZTRAX sales 2011-2021, pages 137-159 and DOI 10.1080/08965803.2022.2066249. The source's wording is hedged: 'likely price premium significance on the order of 2-4%'.

checks.item: wind_retrofit cost_url: ALDOI & UA Center for Risk and Insurance Research, Performance of IBHS FORTIFIED Home Construction in Hurricane Sally (May 2025)
checks.note: PDF (5.1 MB), HTTP 200, redirected to aldoi.gov; the report is dated May 5, 2025. The quote is footnote 11, which begins 'SAH numbers are correct as of November 12, 2024.' The body says SAH 'has paid nearly $86 million to retrofit 8,700 houses to the Fortified Roof standard'; the foreword says 'more than $86 million' and 'more than 8,700 homes'. $86M / 8,700 is about $9,900 per grant, consistent with the $10,000 cap. Also present word for word in this PDF: the 55-74% frequency / 14-40% severity / 51-72% loss-ratio sentence, the 50%-to-20% premium discount sentence, the 130 mph IRC sentence, and the Ghosh et al. 0.5-3% / 6-16% sentence.

checks.item: flood_crs effect_url: Gourevitch & Pinter 2023, Environ. Res. Lett. 18(3):034037
checks.note: HTTP 200, full article HTML. The quote appears word for word in the abstract. The abstract also confirms national data for 1998-2020, cumulative damage reductions of $11.4 billion against $12.1 billion in discounts, and discounts 'ranging from 5% to 45%'. The body contains 'This means that all policyholders pay 15.3% more in premiums'. Volume 18, number 3, 034037 match.

checks.item: flood_crs cost_url: Federal Register 88 FR 34873, 31 May 2023 (Docket FEMA-2023-0013, CRS information collection)
checks.note: PDF, HTTP 200. The quote appears word for word. The collection covers the CRS Application Letter & Quick Check, Community Annual Recertification, Environmental & Historic Preservation Certifications and the NFIP Repetitive Loss Update Form, matching the four components the research lists. Arithmetic checks out: $4,173,947 / 2,170 = $1,923 and 52,292 h / 2,170 = 24.1 h. Respondents are 'State, Local, or Tribal government'. Respondent O&M and capital costs are listed as $0, consistent with the caveat that mitigation work itself is excluded. The research does not mention 'Estimated Total Annual Cost to the Federal Government: $12,992,290'.

checks.item: flood_drainage effect_url: Cohen, Huang & McMillen 2024, Lincoln Institute WP24JC1 (Philadelphia GSI)
checks.note: PDF (35 pages), HTTP 200, dated May 2024 and labeled Working Paper WP24JC1; not peer-reviewed, as the research says. The quote appears word for word. Also word for word: the 40 m (5-6 percent) / 50 m (3 percent) sentence and the abstract's '10 to 15 percent'. The GSI types include rain garden, tree trench, swale, planter and basin. The estimate is for green infrastructure, not grey storm drains, and the research says so.

checks.note: Page shows 'Updated April 22, 2025'. checks.note: HTTP 200 (nature.com added a cookie query string; the full article loaded). Both quotes appear word for word. verify.summary:
I checked 30 citations: all 12 effect and cost URLs, plus 18 URLs from the notes that back numbers in the effect and cost text. WebFetch could not resolve any host (getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND), so I downloaded every page with curl through the session proxy. I matched each quote ignoring case, spaces and punctuation, then read the surrounding text and the bibliographic details. The search budget was already used up, so I ran no web searches.

Main citations: 11 of the 12 effect and cost URLs could be read, contain their quotes word for word, and support the stated effect or cost. The journal, volume and DOI also match for each of those 11.

The one failure is the flood_elevation cost_url (Al Assi et al. 2023 on link.springer.com). Springer served a 'Client Challenge' bot-check page, and I did not try to get past it. The LSU repository copy returned a Cloudflare challenge.
- Crossref metadata confirms the paper itself (Natural Hazards 117(2):1291-1319, CC BY 4.0).
- The published abstract contains the 98% loss-reduction sentence and the benefit-cost 1.5/1.7 sentence word for word.
- The October 2022 preprint gives 'approximately $120,000' per home, with a $30,000 Road Home share.
- The exact quoted sentence crediting GOHSEP for the $120,000 could not be found, so this citation is marked unverified.

Notes citations: 16 of 18 check out fully.
- Cohen, Dietz & Huang 2023: the PDF sentence ends '...nearby bioswales.' without the quote's 'in New Haven'. The 8.8% figure is correct, and the exact text is in corrected.
- FEMA September 2021 memo: fema.gov returned 403. Its $323,000 / $205,000 figures are confirmed only through the Vermont Flood Ready page.

No number needed correcting. Caveats a reader of the result should know:
1. The roughly $23,000 (18%) buyout activity cost is the sum of a local median and a state median from different projects (14 projects). The paper itself warns it is not a per-project total. RFF's New York data put the total buyout cost at $359.72M against $274.86M direct, about 31% more, so the x1.18 formula may understate costs in expensive programs.
2. Lee et al. and the New Haven 8.8% estimate use tax-assessed values, not sale prices.
3. The CRS discount is computed after expense constants and mitigation discounts are taken off, so 'about 5% of the full-risk premium per class step' is slightly generous.
4. The living-shoreline cost does not cover dunes, which is the measure behind that type's 3.6% effect.
5. The Hashida & Dundas abstract does not name NY Rising or Hurricane Sandy.

Downloaded pages and extracted text are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/dl. The scripts used are /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/scripts/totext.py and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/scripts/findq.py.

types.name: Snow plowing and sidewalk clearing
types.trigger: The block group's nearest NOAA 1991-2020 normals station has ANN-SNOW-NORMAL (mean annual snowfall, inches) above 20. A sharper option is ANN-SNOW-AVGNDS-GE010TI (days per year with at least 1.0 in of snowfall) of 10 or more. Minneapolis-St Paul airport (USW00014922) shows 51.2 in and 14.6 such days, which matches Minneapolis's own '10 to 15 snow events' per winter. For sidewalk clearing, rank block groups inside the trigger area by pedestrian destinations (schools, grocery stores), as SMTC did for Syracuse.
types.trigger_data:
NOAA NCEI U.S. Climate Normals 1991-2020, Annual/Seasonal (gov.noaa.ncdc:C01619, doi:10.25921/4ek7-fk11; published 2021-05-04, revised 2023-05-15).
- Per-station CSV: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/normals-annualseasonal/1991-2020/access/<STATION>.csv
- Bulk archive: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/normals-annualseasonal/1991-2020/archive/us-climate-normals_1991-2020_v1.0.1_annualseasonal_multivariate_by-station_c20230404.tar.gz (54 MB, last modified 2023-06-27)
- Geography: weather stations (lat/lon) in the U.S. and territories.
- Terms (NCEI metadata page https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/metadata/landing-page/bin/iso?id=gov.noaa.ncdc:C01619): 'In most cases, electronic downloads of the data are free.' Cite as Palecki et al. (2021). No warranty.
- My count from the archive: 5,661 U.S. stations have ANN-SNOW-NORMAL, and 2,545 of them exceed 20 in. 4,890 of the 5,661 are flagged 'P', which the documentation defines as 'Provisional - meets WMO standards for data availability for 10 or more years'.
types.effect:
Home values: none measured for snow clearing itself. The only related study (Dayton, Ohio hedonic regression) found that resident satisfaction with a bundle of city services that includes snow removal is positively related to sale prices; the abstract gives no size.

Safety: on Ontario highways during snowstorms, a 10% improvement in a road-surface condition index (the stand-in for plowing and salting) was associated with nearly an 11% reduction in expected collisions.

I found no study that measures how municipal sidewalk clearing changes pedestrian fall injuries.
types.effect_quote: Among the main results, it was found that the RSI was statistically significant influencing the accident occurrence. According to our proposed index, our results suggest that a 10% improvement in road surface condition would lead to nearly an 11% reduction in the expected number of accidents.
types.effect_source: Usman, T., Fu, L., Miranda-Moreno, L.F. (2010). Accident Prediction Models for Quantifying Safety Benefit of Winter Road Maintenance. Transportation Research Board 89th Annual Meeting, paper 10-0774 (TRID record 909632). The journal version in Accident Analysis & Prevention 42(6), 2010, was not opened.
types.cost:
Municipal sidewalk clearing costs $1,400 to $4,000 per mile of sidewalk per season (SMTC memo for the City of Syracuse, Sept 18, 2018):
- Rochester, NY: $1,400 per mile per season (2014 e-mail).
- University Hill pilot, Syracuse: about $2,100 per mile (winter 2009/10).
- SMTC's conservative planning assumption: $4,000 per mile per season.

Street plowing for comparison: MnDOT's statewide plowing and materials cost was $4,012 per lane mile in 2024-25 and $6,980 in 2025-26.
types.cost_quote: For planning purposes, a conservative cost estimate of $4,000 per mile of sidewalk per season was assumed. The City of Rochester’s cost is $1,400 per mile per season (according to e-mail correspondence from 2014).
types.notes:
Other sources I opened:

1. MnDOT Winter Maintenance Report table row (https://www.dot.state.mn.us/maintenance/winter-report.html): 'Total plowing and materials costs per lane mile, statewide average $4,012 $6,980'. The columns are 2024-25 and 2025-26.

2. Minneapolis bills owners who do not shovel (Special Assessments Guide PDF, created Feb 2026, https://www.minneapolismn.gov/media/-www-content-assets/documents/Sidewalk-snow-clearing.pdf): 'Single Family/Duplex: Midblock (40ft) $99.20; Corner lot (165ft) $229; Every additional foot over the standard amount $2.48/ft.' At $2.48/ft that is about $13,100 per mile of frontage per clearing (my arithmetic). It is an enforcement charge, not a program cost.

3. Toronto Public Health staff report, Oct 14, 2016 (Canadian government; https://www.toronto.ca/legdocs/mmis/2016/hl/bgrd/backgroundfile-97431.pdf): 'Between 2006 and 2015, there were almost 30,000 emergency department visits and 2,800 hospitalizations among Toronto residents from falls on snow or ice, and older adults were especially vulnerable.' It also says these rates 'closely mirror annual snowfall amounts'. It does not measure what clearing changes.

4. FHWA Road Weather (https://ops.fhwa.dot.gov/weather/weather_events/snow_ice.htm): 'Over 1,300 people are killed and more than 116,800 people are injured in vehicle crashes on snowy, slushy or icy pavement annually.' FHWA defines snowy regions as those receiving 'more than five inches (or 13 cm) average snowfall annually', a much lower bar than 20 in.

5. Home values: Larsen & Blair (2010), Int. J. Housing Markets and Analysis 3(4):278-289 (abstract at https://ideas.repec.org/a/eme/ijhmap/v3y2010i4p278-289.html): 'All three satisfaction variables are positively related to house price, providing evidence that intra‐jurisdictional differences in the nature of public services are capitalized through market processes.' Snow removal is grouped with other services.

6. Scope of the safety finding: Usman's 2011 Waterloo PhD thesis (https://uwspace.uwaterloo.ca/handle/10012/6400) uses 'six winter seasons (2000 to 2006) for a total of 31 highway routes across Ontario'. The finding is for highways, not city streets or sidewalks.

types.name: Heated or enclosed bus shelters
types.trigger:
A GTFS stop (or parent station) with at least 16 scheduled bus departures between 07:00 and 09:00 on a representative weekday (8 or more an hour, from stop_times), where the nearest NOAA monthly normals station has a January MLY-TAVG-NORMAL (month=01) below 32°F.

Where stop boardings are available, Metro Transit's rule is a better filter: heat goes at major transfer points with at least 70 average daily boardings, and shelters at 20 or more daily boardings.

Caution: the Salt Lake City study found the shelter effect is larger at lower-frequency stops, where waits are longer.
types.trigger_data:
GTFS schedules for U.S. agencies listed in the Mobility Database Catalogs (MobilityData):
- Catalog CSV: https://files.mobilitydatabase.org/feeds_v2.csv (last modified 2026-11-06).
- README: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MobilityData/mobility-database-catalogs/main/README.md
- Terms: the catalog code is Apache 2.0. Each feed has its own optional license_url, and licenses vary by agency.

Climate: NOAA NCEI U.S. Monthly Climate Normals 1991-2020 (gov.noaa.ncdc:C01620, doi:10.25921/wck8-er13; revised 2023-05-15).
- Per-station CSV: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/normals-monthly/1991-2020/access/<STATION>.csv, field MLY-TAVG-NORMAL (°F).
- Free download; cite Palecki et al. (2021).
- More than 7,300 stations have temperature normals.
types.effect:
Home values: none measured.

Ridership (Salt Lake City, UTA stop-level data): extreme cold, extreme heat and heavy rain reduce ridership, and shelters have a 'modest' mitigating effect. The effect is larger on weekdays and at lower-frequency stops.

The authors' 2016 draft report (USDOT ROSA P) gives the sizes. On weekdays, an extreme-cold day (daily mean at or below the 10th percentile, about 26°F) lowered ridership at unsheltered stops by about 1.5% (log coefficient -0.0146; 7,300 stops). Shelters offset +0.00336, about a quarter of that loss (my arithmetic). There was no effect on weekends.

No study isolates heaters.
types.effect_quote: Using bus ridership data from the Salt Lake City metropolitan area, we find that extreme weather such as very high and low temperatures, and heavy rainfall reduces public transport ridership, while bus stop shelters have a modest effect on mitigating ridership losses resulting from these adverse weather conditions. The moderating effect of shelters is more pronounced on weekdays, and for bus stops with lower service frequency and fewer transfers.
types.effect_source: Miao, Q., Welch, E.W., Sriraj, P.S. (2019). Extreme weather, public transport ridership and moderating effect of bus stop shelters. Journal of Transport Geography 74:125-133, doi:10.1016/j.jtrangeo.2018.11.007. I read the abstract on Arizona State University's research portal; ScienceDirect returned 403.
types.cost:
Heated, lit BRT-station shelters: not to exceed $2,060,000 for 67 shelters, about $30,700 each (my arithmetic). That covers fabrication and delivery only; installation is in a separate construction contract (Metropolitan Council/Metro Transit, Minneapolis-St Paul, approved April 10, 2024).

Standard unheated three-wall shelter: $523,700 for 120 shelters, about $4,360 each. That is goods only; Metro Transit staff install them (January 2021).
types.cost_quote: That the Council authorize the Regional Administrator to exercise an option on existing contract 19P385B with Duo-Gard Industries, Inc. for the fabrication and delivery of bus rapid transit shelters for installation on the METRO E Line project, in an amount not to exceed $2,060,000. This is a finished goods purchase for Duo-Gard Industries, Inc. to fabricate and deliver 67 shelters primarily for the E Line.
types.notes:
1. Heat is confirmed in the same item: the shelter 'includes additional amenities such as seating, heat, light, and security features'.

2. The 2021 standard-shelter item (https://metrocouncil.org/Council-Meetings/Committees/Metropolitan-Council/2021/1-27-21/0127_2021_7.aspx) reads: 'That the Metropolitan Council authorizes award and execution of contract 20P061 with Brasco International in the amount not to exceed $523,700.00.' and 'This contract would procure 120 shelters in the first year...'.

3. Metro Transit (https://metrotransit.org/better-bus-stops/bus-stop-improvement-guidelines/): 'Lighting and heating are not standard features in shelters due to the high costs of installing and maintaining them.' I found no source for the cost of adding a heater to an existing shelter, or for heater operating cost.

4. The 2016 report (Miao, Welch, Sriraj; draft funded by CUTR, Univ. of South Florida, Sept 2016; https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/31626/dot_31626_DS1.pdf): 'Findings from Part II demonstrate that bus stop shelter and bench installation in UTA service area can effectively reduce the ridership losses due to extreme hot and cold weather, and shelters provide additional benefits on heavy rain days.' On fare revenue alone, at UTA's $1.08 average fare: 'the daily baseline ridership justifying a bench is around 80 while the baseline ridership for a shelter is more than 1,000.' The report's text defines extreme cold as 'at or above 10th percentile (26 °F)', evidently a typo, since its tables use '<= 10th percentile'.

5. Wait-time perception (Fan, Guthrie & Levinson, CTS Report 16-01, Univ. of Minnesota, 2016; https://cts-d10resmod-prd.oit.umn.edu/pdf/cts-16-01.pdf): 'most waits at stops with no amenities are perceived at least 1.3 times as long as they actually are. Basic amenities including benches and shelters significantly reduce perceived waiting times.'

6. UDOT report UT-20.11 (2020; https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/54742/dot_54742_DS1.pdf): improved stops (pads, shelters, benches together) had 5.9% more boardings afterwards, against 1.7% at control stops. That is a mixed package, not shelters alone.

types.name: Outdoor ice rink or sledding hill
types.trigger:
The nearest NOAA normals station has a January MLY-TAVG-NORMAL below 32°F, and no OpenStreetMap leisure=ice_rink (node or area, indoor or outdoor) lies within 5 km of the block group.

A better cold test for natural ice is DJF-TMAX-AVGNDS-LSTH032 ('Winter number of days with maximum temperature <= 32F') of 30 or more, because rinks need runs of freezing days. My count from the archive: 1,119 U.S. stations have a December-February mean below 32°F but fewer than 30 such days.
types.trigger_data:
OpenStreetMap leisure=ice_rink features (planet or Geofabrik extracts; updated continuously).
- License (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright): 'OpenStreetMap is open data, licensed under the Open Data Commons Open Database License (ODbL)'. Credit 'OpenStreetMap contributors'; derived databases must be shared under the same license.
- Tagging (https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Tag:leisure%3Dice_rink): skating lakes are tagged piste:type=ice_skate instead, and 'seasonal=yes should be used when it is only open in the cold season.'

Climate: NOAA NCEI Monthly Normals 1991-2020 (C01620, field MLY-TAVG-NORMAL) and Annual/Seasonal Normals (C01619, field DJF-TMAX-AVGNDS-LSTH032). Free download; cite Palecki et al. (2021).
types.effect:
None measured, for home values, health or use.

There is feasibility evidence only. The Minneapolis Park Board needs at least ten consecutive days below freezing, day and night, to establish ice. Canadian outdoor skating seasons shortened significantly at many stations between 1951 and 2005 (Damyanov et al. 2012).
types.effect_quote: It takes a minimum of ten consecutive days of below freezing temperatures during the day and night for ice to establish properly.
types.effect_source: Minneapolis Park & Recreation Board, 'Update on Ice Rinks and Warming Rooms in Minneapolis Parks this winter', GovDelivery bulletin, Dec 18, 2020. This is an operational requirement, not a measured effect.
types.cost:
Dasher boards for a 120 x 80 ft outdoor rink cost $29,083.25 including shipping and supervised installation (Lake Elmo, MN, staff report dated 8/8/2018; council cap $35,000).
- The total is $24,865.25 for materials delivered (368 linear ft of wood-framed boards plus 208 ft of chain-link end fencing) and $4,218.00 for an installation supervisor. Both are before the 5% Sourcewell discount.
- The city supplies a three-person crew.
- It excludes the slab or curb, lighting, warming house, water and flooding labor.
types.cost_quote: FISCAL IMPACT: Cost of the Dasher Boards and supervised installation is anticipated to be $29,083.25. This cost includes shipping and a company representative to assist Public Works Staff with construction.
types.notes:
1. Damyanov, Matthews & Mysak (2012), Environ. Res. Lett. 7:014028 (https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1748-9326/7/1/014028/pdf), peer-reviewed. It defines the season start as 'the last day in a series of the first three consecutive fall/winter days with a maximum surface air temperature below −5 °C' and finds 'many locations have seen a statistically significant decrease in the OSS length, particularly in Southwest and Central Canada.'

2. My counts from the NOAA annual archive: 3,490 U.S. stations have a December-February mean below 32°F, and 2,372 have 30 or more winter days with a maximum of 32°F or less. These counts use December-February, not January alone.

3. Sledding hills: I researched no cost or effect source.

4. Not used:
- A Lake Elmo 'Tablyn Park Pricing' sheet (refrigerated rink $27/sf, boards $65 per linear ft, warming house $400,000). It is a compilation that re-cites a college feasibility study and a 2015 Hopkins plan.
- Minneapolis's 2024 warm-winter rink costs, which are reported only by the Star Tribune (blocked, HTTP 429).

types.name: Weatherize and insulate older homes (program)
types.trigger:
All three must hold:
- The nearest NOAA normals station has ANN-HTDD-NORMAL (base 65°F) above 5,000, or a high ANN-CLDD-NORMAL for the 'very hot' branch.
- ACS 5-year B25034 shows more than half of housing units built before 1980.
- ACS B19013 block-group median household income is below the county median.

WAP eligibility itself is set per household: income at or below 200% of federal poverty guidelines, or 60% of state median income at the state's option. ACS C17002 (ratio of income to poverty level) would match that rule more closely. My count: 7,246 U.S. stations have HDD normals, and 4,108 exceed 5,000.
types.trigger_data:
NOAA NCEI Annual/Seasonal Normals 1991-2020 (gov.noaa.ncdc:C01619, doi:10.25921/4ek7-fk11), field ANN-HTDD-NORMAL ('Long-term averages of annual heating degree days with base 65F'). Free download; cite Palecki et al. (2021).

U.S. Census Bureau ACS 5-year tables B25034 (year structure built) and B19013 (median household income) for block groups, via the Census Data API (https://api.census.gov), released each December.
- Terms (https://www.census.gov/data/developers/about/terms-of-service.html): apps must display 'This product uses the Census Bureau Data API but is not endorsed or certified by the Census Bureau.' and must not re-identify people.
- My test query from this session got a 'Missing Key' page, so plan on a free API key.
types.effect:
Energy: in a randomized encouragement trial with about 30,000 eligible Michigan households, WAP cut monthly energy use by 10-20%, but upfront costs were about twice the realized savings. The published QJE version adds that model-projected savings were more than three times actual savings.

The DOE/ORNL national evaluation (program year 2008) found single-family homes saved $283 a year (12%): gas use fell 18% and electricity 7%. DOE now cites '$372 or more every year' (2022 dollars).

Home values: none measured for WAP-type retrofits. In a related study, Energy Star-certified homes sold for about 2% more in the Research Triangle and Portland, with no significant effect in Austin (Walls et al. 2017).
types.effect_quote: We estimate that the WAP energy efficiency investments reduce monthly energy consumption by 10-20% on average. Although this surely provides a substantial assist to participating low-income households in the form of reduced energy bills, the upfront investment costs are about twice the realized energy savings.
types.effect_source: Fowlie, M., Greenstone, M., Wolfram, C. (2015). Do Energy Efficiency Investments Deliver? Evidence from the Weatherization Assistance Program. NBER Working Paper 21331. Published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics 133(3):1597-1644 (2018); I read that abstract on RePEc because OUP returned 403.
types.cost:
DOE's program-year 2026 limit on the average cost per weatherized home is $8,813, covering labor, materials and related costs. It is the statutory $6,500 base adjusted by CPI (WPN 26-1, issued July 9, 2026).

Measured averages (DOE/ORNL summary, Aug 2015, and the Michigan study):
- PY2008: $4,695 total per home, of which $2,301 was DOE's share.
- PY2010: $6,812 total, of which $5,926 was DOE's share.
- Michigan study: $5,150 per household.
types.cost_quote: The percentage increase in the CPI for the previous 12-month period (January 2024–December 2024) was 3%. Therefore, the adjusted average expenditure limit for PY 2026 is $8,813.
types.notes:
1. DOE/ORNL summary table rows (https://www.energy.gov/sites/prod/files/2015/08/f25/WAP_NationalEvaluation_WxWorks_v14_blue_8%205%2015.pdf), columns PY2008 and PY2010:
- 'Average Annual Energy Cost Savings $283 (12%) $223 (12%)'
- 'Average Cost per Weatherized Home Total Cost: $4,695/DOE Investment: $2,301 Total Cost: $6,812/DOE Investment: $5,926'
- 'Program Wide Benefit Cost Ratio Including Health and Safety Benefits 4.1'

2. DOE WAP page (https://www.energy.gov/cmei/scep/wap/weatherization-assistance-program): 'Through weatherization improvements and upgrades, these households save on average $372 or more every year according to a national evaluation of the program.' The 2023 fact sheet (https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2023-08/2023-WAP-Fact-Sheet.pdf) says this figure is in 2022 dollars and sources it to ORNL/TM-2014/338.

3. Published QJE abstract (https://ideas.repec.org/a/oup/qjecon/v133y2018i3p1597-1644..html): 'The findings suggest that the upfront investment costs are about twice the actual energy savings. Furthermore, the model-projected savings are more than three times the actual savings.'

4. Eligibility (https://www.energy.gov/cmei/scep/wap/how-apply-weatherization-assistance): 'Households at or below 200% of the poverty income guidelines or that receive Supplemental Security Income are considered under DOE guidelines as eligible for weatherization services.'

5. Walls et al. (2017), JEEM 82:104-124, as summarised by RFF (https://rff.org/publications/journal-articles/is-energy-efficiency-capitalized-into-home-prices-evidence-from-three-us-cities): 'Our results show that Energy Star certification is associated with an increase in the sales prices of single-family homes in the Research Triangle and Portland markets of approximately 2 percent, but we find no statistically significant effect in Austin'. This covers certified homes, not low-income retrofits, so it is only indirect evidence for home values.

result.summary:
I researched the four cold_snow types the mapping step proposed. I downloaded every cited page or PDF with curl through the session proxy, because WebFetch could not resolve hosts, and checked each quote against the downloaded text. None of the four has a measured effect on home values.

Measured effects:
- **Snow clearing (safety):** on Ontario highways in snowstorms, a 10% better road-surface condition went with nearly 11% fewer crashes (TRB paper).
- **Heated shelters (ridership):** in Salt Lake City, shelters modestly reduce cold-day ridership losses (peer-reviewed, 2019), with sizes from the authors' 2016 USDOT-hosted report. No study isolates heaters.
- **Weatherization (energy):** a Michigan randomized trial found WAP cuts energy use 10-20%, with upfront costs about twice the savings. DOE's national evaluation found $283 a year (12%) for single-family homes.
- **Ice rinks:** none measured. There is only a feasibility rule: at least 10 consecutive days below freezing, day and night.

Unit costs:
- Sidewalk clearing: $1,400-$4,000 per mile of sidewalk per season (SMTC 2018). MnDOT street plowing: $4,012-$6,980 per lane mile.
- Heated BRT shelters: about $30,700 each for fabrication and delivery (Met Council 2024). Standard shelters: about $4,360 each.
- Rink dasher boards: $29,083 for a 120 x 80 ft rink (Lake Elmo 2018).
- Weatherization: DOE's PY2026 average cost limit is $8,813 per home. Measured averages were $4,695 (PY2008) and $6,812 (PY2010).

Trigger data:
- NOAA 1991-2020 normals: annual/seasonal set C01619 and monthly set C01620. Downloads are free with citation.
- My counts from the NOAA archive: 2,545 of 5,661 U.S. stations with snowfall normals exceed 20 in, and most snowfall normals are provisional. 4,108 of 7,246 stations with heating degree day normals exceed 5,000.
- Other sources: OpenStreetMap (ODbL), GTFS feeds listed in the Mobility Database (licenses vary by feed), and the Census ACS through the Census API, which returned 'Missing Key' to a test query.

Downloaded sources are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/cs/dl. The URL log is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/cs/urls.tsv.
open_questions: Minneapolis Public Works' 2023 estimate for citywide municipal sidewalk clearing (about $40M a year in news reports) and the 2018 Pedestrian and Bicycle Winter Maintenance Study are not cited. The www2.minneapolismn.gov PDFs now return 404, and web.archive.org is blocked from this session.
Syracuse's actual sidewalk-clearing contract cost per mile is unconfirmed, because syr.gov returned 403. Only the SMTC planning figures and the Rochester and University Hill figures are cited.

Journal full texts were not opened because publishers returned 403: Usman et al. 2010 (Accident Analysis & Prevention 42(6); cited through the TRB paper record), Miao et al. 2019 (Journal of Transport Geography; abstract only), Fowlie et al. 2018 (QJE; abstract only, with numbers from the NBER working paper), and Walls et al. 2017 (JEEM; abstract and RFF summary only).
I found no study measuring heated versus unheated shelters, or municipal sidewalk clearing's effect on pedestrian falls. None of the four types has a home-value study.
I found no source for the cost of adding a heater to an existing shelter, or for a heater's electricity and maintenance cost per season.
Per-rink operating cost (flooding labor, warming-house staff) is not sourced. The Minneapolis Park Board figures appear only in the Star Tribune (blocked, HTTP 429), and I found no agency document.
Sledding hills, part of the ice_rink type, have no cost or effect source.
Freeze-thaw resistant pavement is in the group brief but not among the mapping step's types, so I did not research it.

Snowfall normals are mostly provisional (4,890 of 5,661 U.S. stations). NOAA warns that normals 'are limited in their applicability at locations in between stations as distance from the station increases horizontally and vertically'. Nearest-station assignment may be poor in mountains.

The Census Data API returned a 'Missing Key' page for a block-group query from this session. Confirm the pipeline has a key. I did not check whether ACS C17002 (ratio of income to poverty, the closest match to WAP's 200%-of-poverty rule) is published for block groups.

checks.item: snow_clearing effect_url (Usman, Fu, Miranda-Moreno 2010, TRB paper 10-0774)
checks.note: HTTP 200. The quote is word for word in the abstract. The abstract covers accident frequency during snow-storm events, a road surface condition index (RSI) and a generalized negative binomial (GNB) model. It finds that a 10% better RSI leads to nearly 11% fewer expected accidents. The page shows the TRB 89th Annual Meeting (Jan 10-14, 2010), paper 10-0774, 23 pages and authors that match. The page does not say Ontario or highways; its only highway mention is the keyword 'Highway safety'. That scope is confirmed by Usman's 2011 thesis (checked below: 31 highway routes across Ontario, 2000-2006). Calling it a working paper fits a conference compendium paper.

checks.note:
17-page PDF dated September 18, 2018, from SMTC to Syracuse's Director of Operations. The quote is word for word. It also says the 'University Hill Partnership's sidewalk snow clearing pilot project cost roughly $2,100 per mile during the winter of 2009/2010'. Caveats:
- The $4,000 is a deliberately conservative worst-case planning assumption ('roughly double' University Hill), not an observed cost.
- The memo does not say whether Rochester's $1,400 is per sidewalk mile or per centerline mile. A footnote says mileage means centerline miles unless noted, and the budget math ($25k-$100k gives 6-25 miles) applies $4,000 to centerline miles.
- University Hill was a partnership pilot, not a city program.
The memo also confirms the trigger's ranking by schools and grocery stores.
