verify.summary:
I checked 30 URLs: the 8 effect and cost URLs, plus 22 URLs from the notes and trigger data whose numbers appear in the stated effects, costs and triggers. All 30 could be read.

How I fetched: WebFetch failed with getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND, so I downloaded each page with curl through the session proxy. Two hosts needed curl's default user agent: rosap.ntl.bts.gov (Akamai returns 403 to browser-like agents) and uwspace.uwaterloo.ca (Anubis bot challenge). Each quote was checked with whitespace and punctuation ignored. Downloads are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/vcs/dl and scripts in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/vcs/scripts.

Result: no quote is made up and no number differs from its source. Every cited figure matches. Checked figures include:
- -11% crashes per 10% better road surface (RSI)
- $1,400 / $2,100 / $4,000 per mile for sidewalk clearing
- $2,060,000 for 67 BRT shelters
- -0.0146 and +0.00336 for 7,300 stops
- $523,700 for 120 shelters
- $29,083.25 for rink boards
- 10-20% energy savings, about 2x cost, more than 3x projected savings (QJE)
- $8,813 cost limit for PY2026
- $283 (12%), 18% gas, 7% electric
- $4,695/$2,301 and $6,812/$5,926
- $372 in 2022 dollars
- $4,012 and $6,980 per lane mile
- 51.2 in and 14.6 days at MSP
- 5.9% vs 1.7% boardings
- 70 and 20 daily boardings

Fixes needed:
1. **Met Council 2024-70 quote (heated_shelter cost):** it joins two sentences from different paragraphs without an ellipsis, so quote_found=false. The page still supports the cost. The page is the committee report for the April 10, 2024 Council meeting and does not record the Council's vote.
2. **ROSA P report (heated_shelter effect):** 'There was no effect on weekends' is true only for the shelter offset. Extreme cold still cut weekend ridership (-0.00432). The UTA ridership measure is boardings per bus run.
3. **Met Council 2021-7 (heated_shelter cost):** the item itself does not say 'three-wall' or 'unheated'. That description comes from Metro Transit's guidelines page.
4. **Lake Elmo (ice_rink cost):** the $35,000 is the staff-recommended not-to-exceed amount, not a recorded council cap.
5. **2023 WAP fact sheet (weatherization notes):** it does not footnote the $372 figure to ORNL/TM-2014/338 directly.
6. **Minor scope notes:**
   - The 'Ontario highways' scope of the snow-plowing safety finding comes from Usman's thesis, not from the TRID page.
   - SMTC's $4,000 is a worst-case planning assumption, and the memo leaves unclear whether Rochester's figure is per sidewalk mile or per centerline mile.

types.name: Defensible space and home hardening (neighborhood program)
types.trigger: Block groups with homes that meet either test. (a) Nationwide: the share of the block group's land (suggested: block group plus a ~1 km buffer) in USFS Wildfire Hazard Potential 2023 class 4 (high) or 5 (very high) is at or above an engine threshold (suggested 10%). The buffer is needed because WHP codes developed land as 6 (non-burnable). (b) California: the engine's existing 'fire' share (block-group area in CAL FIRE Very High Fire Hazard Severity Zones, SRA 2023 / LRA 2025) is above 0. Optional refinement: the housing-weighted mean of WRC 2nd-edition Risk to Potential Structures (RPS) is in the top national tercile. The program is offered to a whole neighborhood because of the measured spillovers between neighbors.
types.trigger_data: USDA Forest Service, Wildfire Hazard Potential for the United States (270-m), version 2023, 4th ed. (Dillon 2023, RDS-2015-0047-4). Published 12/21/2023 and updated 07/17/2024. Covers CONUS, Alaska and Hawaii. Classified raster: 1 = very low, 2 = low, 3 = moderate, 4 = high, 5 = very high, 6 = non-burnable, 7 = water. County and ZIP summary tables are included. The data zip is 368 MB and downloads from www.fs.usda.gov (HTTP 200 checked 10 Nov 2026): https://www.fs.usda.gov/rds/archive/products/RDS-2015-0047-4/RDS-2015-0047-4_Data.zip (catalog page https://www.fs.usda.gov/rds/archive/catalog/RDS-2015-0047-4). Terms: 'These data were collected using funding from the U.S. Government and can be used without additional permissions or fees' (citation requested). Companion: Wildfire Risk to Communities, 2nd ed. (Scott et al. 2024, RDS-2020-0016-2, https://www.fs.usda.gov/rds/archive/catalog/RDS-2020-0016-2). It has 30 m rasters (RPS, burn probability, WHP and others) under the same terms. It spreads burn probability into developed areas, so it is better inside towns. But the files are very large and hosted on usfs-public.box.com (CONUS RPS 33.7 GB; California zip 11.1 GB); a ranged GET worked here. California only: the CAL FIRE FHSZ layers already used by the pipeline.
types.effect: Home values (California, sales 2013–2020, event-study difference-in-differences on home vintages): homes built after California's wildfire building codes took effect in high-hazard areas sell for 1.4%–2.5% more than homes built before the codes. The effect is on the home itself; the paper reports no distance-based effect. The author's benefit–cost check finds the premium roughly equals the cost of a basic set of wildfire fortifications. Losses avoided (Baylis & Boomhower, see notes): a 2008-or-newer California home is ~16 percentage points (40%) less likely to be destroyed when exposed (working paper; the published JPE estimate as cited by RFF is 13 points, or 34%). A code-built neighbor within 10 m lowers a home's destruction risk by ~2.5 points (6%). Caveat: the evidence is for code-built homes. No study measures the price effect of retrofits or defensible-space programs on existing homes.
types.effect_quote: Using sales data from 2013–2020 in an event study difference-in-difference model of home vintages, we estimate that treated homes – those built after the codes went into effect – sell for 1.4%–2.5% more than homes built before the policies were enacted. Combining our estimates with home prices and estimates of costs to retrofit homes in a benefit–cost analysis reveals that premiums are roughly equal to the cost of meeting a basic set of wildfire fortifications.
types.effect_source: Wrenn, Douglas H. (2026). Wildfire risk and home prices: The case of California building codes. Journal of Housing Economics 72, article 102139 (June 2026), doi:10.1016/j.jhe.2026.102139. Crossref lists Wrenn as sole author. The abstract was read on Penn State's research portal because sciencedirect.com is not reachable from this session.
types.cost: $52,408 average per completed home/site (construction $41,231 + defensible space $11,177). Source: California Wildfire Mitigation Program (Cal OES/CAL FIRE joint powers authority) pilot, 190 sites completed 2024 to 10 Sep 2026 in Lake, San Diego, Shasta and Siskiyou counties. County averages run from $35,543 (Siskiyou, mostly defensible space) to $71,875 (San Diego). The program pays the full cost ('upwards of $40,000') for households up to 120% of area median income. Above that, owners pay a 10% or 25% cost share.
types.cost_quote: To encourage broad neighborhood participation, the program covers the full cost of retrofit and defensible space implementation, upwards of $40,000, for homeowners earning up to 120 percent of the area median income. | Table '12. Cost Average Totals per Site' (columns Construction Total, Defensible Space Total, Grand Total): 'Total $41,230.85 $11,176.66 $52,407.51' — 'Shows the average total cost per home/site by county.'
types.notes: Losses avoided: Baylis & Boomhower, NBER WP 29621 (Dec 2021), https://www.nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w29621/w29621.pdf, published as JPE 134(3):895–948 (Mar 2026), doi:10.1086/739331. Quotes: 'A 2008 or newer home is about 16 percentage points (40%) less likely to be destroyed than a 1990 home experiencing an identical wildfire exposure.' and 'Our results imply that, all else equal, code-induced mitigation by a neighbor located less than 10 meters away (within the distance fire experts refer to as the home ignition zone) reduces a home’s likelihood of destruction during a wildfire by about 2.5 percentage points (6%).' The same WP: 'the costs of retrofitting existing homes to meet current wildfire building standards are substantial and our analysis suggest full retrofits are only economic in areas with extreme wildfire hazard.' RFF WP 25-30 (Ludington, Liao, Walls, Dec 2025; https://media.rff.org/documents/WP_25-30.pdf) cites the published version as finding homes 'are 13 percentage points less likely to be destroyed than similar homes built before the code was in effect (a 34 percent reduction from the sample mean of 39 percent).' Insurance discounts under California's Safer from Wildfires rule, from the same RFF WP (working_paper): 'Being in a Firewise USA community is valuable, providing an average discount of between $32 and $46, which is more than any single property-level action.' Also: 'Insurers that use the IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home program to set discounts provide an average discount of approximately $60 for the standard certification and $94 for the “Plus-level” certification.' And doing every property-level action gives 'a maximum discount of 5.65 percent, or approximately $98 for an average policy'. RFF concludes 'the costs of property retrofits are orders of magnitude greater than the insurance savings.' The rule itself, from a CDI release of 17 Oct 2022 (government, https://www.insurance.ca.gov/0400-news/0100-press-releases/2022/release076-2022.cfm): 'The regulation requires insurance companies to submit new rates that recognize the benefit of safety measures such as upgraded roofs and windows, defensible space, and community-wide programs such as Firewise USA and the Fire Risk Reduction Community designation developed by the state’s Board of Forestry and Fire Protection'. Other states' rules were not researched. Alternative cost estimate from a nonprofit (Headwaters Economics 2024, funded by CAL FIRE and the USDA Forest Service; https://headwaterseconomics.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/Wildfire_Retrofit_Report_20240624.pdf): 'for a typical 2,000-square-foot home in California, retrofitting costs can be as low as $2,000 for minimal retrofits to upwards of $100,000 if all retrofits to the highest level of protection are needed'. A targeted ember package (vents, flashing, gutter guards, gravel mulch) costs 'between $10,000 and $15,000'. An earlier CWMP figure (Aug 2025 board item, 92 projects): 'Reported average cost per home is currently $38,634.39'.

types.name: Water-wise landscaping and smart irrigation (turf-replacement rebates)
types.trigger: Block group where either test holds. (a) The NOAA 1991–2020 gridded annual precipitation normal (annprcp_norm), averaged over the block group, is under 20 in (508 mm). (b) The county had at least 50% of its area in D1 or worse (USDM 'cumulative' statistics, D1 column; suggested cut) in more than 25% of the weekly maps over the last 5 years (about 65 of 261 weeks). In both cases the block group must also be 'mostly lawns'. No national lawn layer was assessed; suggested proxy: ≥50% single-family detached homes (ACS B25024) or a high share of NLCD developed open-space and low-intensity land.
types.trigger_data: Drought: U.S. Drought Monitor county statistics, weekly maps since 2000, % of area in D0–D4 (cumulative or categorical). Downloads from https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/DmData/DataDownload.aspx or the API, e.g. https://usdmdataservices.unl.edu/api/CountyStatistics/GetDroughtSeverityStatisticsByAreaPercent?aoi=06037&startdate=1/1/2021&enddate=12/31/2025&statisticsType=1 (tested 10 Nov 2026; statisticsType=1 is cumulative, 2 is categorical). Terms (https://droughtmonitor.unl.edu/About/Permission.aspx): 'The U.S. Drought Monitor map and associated data are available and authorized for use by third parties, including by commercial and non-commercial entities.' Credit must be given ('[Map / Data] courtesy of NDMC'). Rainfall: NOAA NCEI U.S. Monthly Gridded Climate Normals 1991–2020 (nClimGrid-based, 1/24° ≈ 4–5 km, contiguous U.S. only; annual normal variable annprcp_norm). File: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/data/oceans/archive/arc0196/0245564/1.1/data/0-data/prcp-1991_2020-monthly-normals-v1.0.nc (281 MB, Last-Modified 18 Jan 2022). Product page: https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/land-based-station/us-climate-normals. Terms: federal NOAA data; NCEI's normals metadata says 'In most cases, electronic downloads of the data are free', with a no-warranty disclaimer. Alaska and Hawaii need station normals.
types.effect: Home values (Las Vegas valley, SNWA lawn-to-desert 'Cash-for-Grass' rebate participants, event studies and panel fixed effects): the average conversion raises the converted home's value by about 1%. There is little evidence of value spillovers to neighboring homes. The same conversions cut the home's water use by 19%–21% and may raise its energy use by 3%.
types.effect_quote: Using event studies and panel fixed-effects models, I find that the average conversion reduces water use by 19%–21%, may increase energy use by 3%, and increases property values by about 1%. ... I find little evidence of property value spillovers to neighboring properties.
types.effect_source: Baker, Jonathan E. (2021). Subsidies for Succulents: Evaluating the Las Vegas Cash-for-Grass Rebate Program. Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists 8(3): 475–508, doi:10.1086/712429. The journal abstract was read on RePEc/IDEAS because journals.uchicago.edu is not reachable from this session.
types.cost: $2.00 per sq ft of lawn replaced, up to 5,000 sq ft per year (Metropolitan Water District of Southern California base rebate via SoCal Water$mart, residential, page read 10 Nov 2026). Local agencies add to it. LADWP (Los Angeles) pays $5/sq ft in total ($3 LADWP + $2 MWD). SNWA (Las Vegas) pays $5.00/sq ft for the first 10,000 sq ft and $2.50/sq ft after that for single-family applicants as of 18 Sep 2025, but that rate may have ended (see notes). These are rebate (program) costs, not the full installed cost.
types.cost_quote: Metropolitan Water District is offering a rebate of $2.00 per square foot up to 5,000 square feet of converted yard per year. Your water agency may offer an additional rebate incentive.
types.notes: LADWP (https://www.ladwp.com/who-we-are/water-system/water-conservation/turf-replacement-rebate): 'LADWP customers can get $5 per square foot (LADWP $3/sq ft + MWD $2/sq ft = $5/sq ft) to transform existing lawn into a sustainable, low water use landscape.' SNWA terms page (https://www.snwa.com/apps/watersmart-landscape-residential/?lang=en): 'As of September 18, 2025, new single family residential (SFR) applicants will be paid $5.00 per square foot for the first 10,000 square feet of Functional Turf conversions, as defined by the Authority, and $2.50 per square foot thereafter on a per-property, per-fiscal year (July 1 – June 30) basis.' Las Vegas Valley Water District customers can get $2/sq ft more. A KLAS news item (search snippet only, not opened) says the temporary $5 rate has ended, so confirm the current rate. Cost-effectiveness from Baker (2021) abstract: 'The program saves water at an annual rate of $2.65/kgal to $3.31/kgal and generates net benefits of between $2.35 and $2.88 per square foot of desert landscape converted.' The ~1% value effect belongs to the converted parcel only. With no spillover, the block-group effect is roughly 1% times the share of homes that convert. Not opened: Brelsford & Abbott, 'How smart are Water Smart Landscapes?', JEEM 2021, doi:10.1016/j.jeem.2020.102402 (ornl.gov returned 403). Smart-irrigation controllers were not researched separately.

types.name: Water recycling and secure water supply (regional project, local share)
types.trigger: Block groups whose HydroBASINS level-6 sub-basin(s), area-weighted, have a WRI Aqueduct 4.0 baseline annual water-stress category of 'High' (40–80%) or 'Extremely high' (>80%), or that are in a county meeting the USDM recurring-drought rule used for drought_landscaping. Model it as a utility/regional project: each block group carries a per-household local share of the regional cost (federal Title XVI grants can cover at most 25% in the 17 Western States).
types.trigger_data: WRI Aqueduct 4.0 Current and Future Global Maps Data, published 16 Aug 2023 (https://www.wri.org/data/aqueduct-global-maps-40-data). Global coverage by HydroBASINS level-6 sub-basin. Baseline water stress categories: Low <10%, Low-medium 10–20%, Medium-high 20–40%, High 40–80%, Extremely high >80%, plus 'Arid and low water use'. Zip of 261 MB with CSVs (Aqueduct40_baseline_annual_y2023m07d05.csv) and a file geodatabase: https://files.wri.org/aqueduct/aqueduct-4-0-water-risk-data.zip. License: the technical note (https://files.wri.org/d8/s3fs-public/2023-08/aqueduct-40-technical-note.pdf) says 'This work is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License'; the data page lists 'Creative Commons' without a version. Recurring drought: USDM county statistics (see drought_landscaping).
types.effect: Home values: none measured; searches found no U.S. hedonic study of recycled-water or supply-reliability projects. Losses avoided: across 53 California urban water utilities (more than 20 million customers), an annual supply disruption costs an average of $1,458 per acre-foot of shortage for a 10% shortage and $3,426 per acre-foot for a 30% shortage. Households would pay about $60–$600 a year to avoid an annual disruption, depending on shortage size and location.
types.effect_quote: Welfare losses for an annual disruption range from an average of $1,458 per acre-foot of shortage for a 10% supply disruption to an average of $3,426 per acre-foot of shortage for a 30% supply disruption. The results indicate a household-level willingness to pay to avoid an annual disruption of approximately $60–$600 depending on the shortage size and location.
types.effect_source: Buck, Steven; Auffhammer, Maximilian; Hamilton, Stephen; Sunding, David (2016). Measuring Welfare Losses from Urban Water Supply Disruptions. Journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists 3(3): 743–778, doi:10.1086/687761. Abstract read on EconPapers; the journal site is not reachable from this session.
types.cost: Indirect potable reuse in California, levelized, 2015 dollars: large projects (>12 million m3/yr) cost $0.91–$1.28 per m3, median $1.06/m3 (≈$1,120–$1,580 per acre-foot, median ≈$1,310/AF). Small projects cost $1.21–$1.80/m3, median $1.50/m3 (≈$1,850/AF). Small non-potable 'purple pipe' projects including distribution cost $1.21–$1.70/m3, median $1.25/m3 (≈$1,540/AF). The acre-foot figures are my conversions at 1,233.5 m3 per AF. The local share is the cost after federal and state grants, recovered through water rates.
types.cost_quote: The costs of small indirect potable reuse projects range from $1.21 to $1.80/m3, with a median cost of $1.50/m3. The cost of larger projects ranges from $0.91 to $1.28/m3, with a median cost of $1.06/m3.
types.notes: Cost source: Cooley, Phurisamban & Gleick (2019), 'The cost of alternative urban water supply and efficiency options in California', Environmental Research Communications 1: 042001 (open access, peer-reviewed topical review; authors at the Pacific Institute). Cost basis: 'The levelized cost of water is expressed as 2015 dollars per cubic meter of water.' Non-potable: 'Thus, the total cost for a small, non-potable reuse project would range from $1.21 to 1.70/m3, with a median cost of $1.25/m3.' The costs are California only. Federal share, from the Bureau of Reclamation FY2026 Title XVI webinar (https://www.usbr.gov/watersmart/title/docs/2026/FY26TitleXVI_Desalination_NOFOWebinar.pdf): 'Category A Applicants may request up to $20 million in Federal funds, unless specified otherwise in the project’s congressional authorization, not to exceed 25% of the total project cost.' and 'Category B Applicants may request up to $40 million in Federal funds, not to exceed 25% of the total project cost.' The webinar also states '75% non-Federal cost share required' and 'Applicants must be located in the 17 Western States, Hawaii, American Samoa, Guam, the Northern Mariana Islands, or the Virgin Islands'. Buck et al.'s losses are the value of avoided shortages. A recycling project avoids them only to the extent it reduces shortage frequency or size, which the engine would have to assume. Aqueduct is a prioritization screen ('Aqueduct remains primarily a prioritization tool and should be augmented by local and regional deep dives'), so county-level utility supply data would be better where available.

types.name: Cool or green roofs (rebates)
types.trigger: Block groups where the engine's heat measure ht is at least +1.1 °F, i.e. the Tree Equity Score block-group temp_diff (heat disparity) re-centred on the county's block-group mean (already computed by the pipeline). Optional extra condition: many low-rise roofs, e.g. a high single-family or low-rise share from ACS.
types.trigger_data: American Forests Tree Equity Score (block groups; per-state CSV zips used by the pipeline at https://tes-app-data-share.s3.amazonaws.com/<st>/<st>_csv.zip; e.g. az_csv.zip Last-Modified 27 Oct 2026; field temp_diff). Terms: no open data license found. The site copyright notice (https://www.treeequityscore.org/privacy) says American Forests 'expressly prohibits the copying of any protected or copyrighted materials' except fair use, and 'This prohibition includes the downloading of site content for commercial use or for use on personal websites'. Whether this covers the data downloads is unclear. Public-domain alternative for the same heat measure: USGS Landsat Collection 2 Level-2 Surface Temperature (Landsat 4–9, 1982–present; https://www.usgs.gov/landsat-missions/landsat-collection-2-surface-temperature). USGS policy: 'USGS-authored or produced data and information are considered to be in the U.S. Public Domain.'
types.effect: Home values: none measured. No hedonic study of cool (reflective) roofs was found, and a 2010 UC Berkeley literature review found none. Health (modelled, West Midlands, UK; summer 2006 and the 2003 and 2006 heatwaves): cool roofs across the whole city could offset 18% of seasonal heat deaths linked to the urban heat island (7% of all heat-related deaths), and about 25% of UHI-linked heat deaths during a heatwave. Energy (EPA summary of a modelling study): cool roofs can cut peak cooling demand 11–27% in air-conditioned homes.
types.effect_quote: Our results suggest that the UHI contributes up to 40% of heat related mortality over the summer period and that cool roofs implemented across the whole city could potentially offset 18% of seasonal heat-related mortality associated with the UHI (corresponding to 7% of total heat-related mortality).
types.effect_source: Macintyre, H.L.; Heaviside, C. (2019). Potential benefits of cool roofs in reducing heat-related mortality during heatwaves in a European city. Environment International 127: 430–441, doi:10.1016/j.envint.2019.02.065 (open-access copy on UCL Discovery).
types.cost: Rebate of up to $0.60 per sq ft of qualifying cool roof (LADWP Consumer Rebate Program, Los Angeles, 2024 fact sheet). Installed cost, from US EPA's 2008 compendium citing a 2006 report: cool coatings on low-slope roofs cost $0.75–$1.50/sq ft for materials and labor; single-ply membranes cost $1.50–$3.00/sq ft. For most products the premium over conventional roofing is $0 to $0.05–0.10/sq ft. Green roofs start at $10/sq ft for extensive roofs and $25/sq ft for intensive roofs (EPA, citing a 2001 report). The installed costs are old (see notes).
types.cost_quote: Cool Roofs: up to $0.60 per square feet
types.notes: EPA Compendium, Cool Roofs chapter (https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2017-05/documents/reducing_urban_heat_islands_ch_4.pdf): 'Cool roof coatings might cost between $0.75 and $1.50 per square foot for materials and labor, which includes routine surface preparation like pressure-washing, but which does not include repair of leaks, cracks, or bubbling of the existing roof surface.' and 'In terms of dollars per square foot, the premium ranges from zero to 5 or 10 cents for most products'. EPA Green Roofs chapter (https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2017-05/documents/reducing_urban_heat_islands_ch_3.pdf): 'A 2001 report estimated that initial costs start at $10 per square foot (0.09 m2) for the simpler, extensive roof and $25 per square foot for intensive roofs.' EPA cool roofs page (https://www.epa.gov/heatislands/using-cool-roofs-reduce-heat-islands): 'In air-conditioned residential buildings, solar reflectance from a cool roof can reduce peak cooling demand by 11–27%.' This rests on a modelling study (Synnefa et al. 2007). U.S. modelling for Los Angeles (Kalkstein et al. 2022, Int J Biometeorol 66:911–925, https://escholarship.org/content/qt08v664xk/qt08v664xk.pdf) combines more trees with higher-albedo roofs and pavement: 'We found that roughly one in four lives currently lost during heat waves could be saved.' That result is not roof-only. No measured home-value effect, per the CREC review (Kroll & Cray 2010, UC Berkeley, https://uc-ciee.org/ciee-old/downloads/CRECHedonicAnalysis.pdf): 'our queries identified no hedonic property valuation articles addressing roof characteristics and only seven articles addressing pavement, none of which focused on pavement attributes relevant to cool community design.' The often-cited green-roof rent premium (Ichihara & Cohen 2011, Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences 4(1):21–30, doi:10.1007/s12076-010-0046-4) could not be opened and is not used. The catalog already has cool_pavement and cooling_center types on the same ht ≥ 1.1 trigger.

result.summary:
I researched all four proposed types from primary sources that I opened and read. Every quote was checked word for word against the downloaded page or PDF.

Home-value effects were measured for two types. Homes built under California's wildfire codes in high-hazard areas sell for 1.4%–2.5% more (Wrenn 2026, Journal of Housing Economics). Las Vegas lawn-to-desert conversions raise the converted home's value about 1%, with no spillover to neighbors, and cut its water use 19–21% (Baker 2021, JAERE). For water recycling and cool roofs no home-value study was found, so the effects given are losses avoided instead. Urban water shortages cost $1,458–$3,426 per acre-foot of shortage, or $60–$600 per household a year (Buck et al. 2016, JAERE). Modelled city-wide cool roofs offset 18% of UHI-related seasonal heat deaths in the UK West Midlands (Macintyre & Heaviside 2019). Wildfire losses avoided: code-built homes are ~16 points (40%) less likely to be destroyed (NBER WP; 13 points per the published JPE version as cited by RFF). A code-built neighbor within 10 m cuts destruction risk ~2.5 points. California's Safer from Wildfires insurance discounts are small: Firewise USA $32–46 a year, IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home $60/$94, at most ~$98 for all property actions.

Unit costs:
- California Wildfire Mitigation Program: $52,408 average per completed home (190 sites, Cal OES report of Sep 2026).
- MWD turf rebate: $2.00 per sq ft (LADWP $5 in total; SNWA $5 as of Sep 2025, possibly ended).
- California indirect potable reuse: $0.91–$1.28 per m3 for large projects, about $1,120–$1,580 per acre-foot (2015$). Title XVI pays at most 25% federally.
- LADWP cool-roof rebate: up to $0.60 per sq ft. EPA installed costs are $0.75–$1.50 per sq ft but date from 2006 data.

Trigger data:
- USFS Wildfire Hazard Potential 2023 (270 m, classes 4–5 = high/very high, 368 MB on www.fs.usda.gov, free to use). It fills the pipeline's noted gap of no national high-hazard share layer. The 30 m Wildfire Risk to Communities data use the same terms but are very large files on Box.
- US Drought Monitor county weekly statistics: open API, free including commercial use, with credit.
- NOAA 1991–2020 gridded precipitation normals: free.
- WRI Aqueduct 4.0: CC BY 4.0.
- Tree Equity Score heat: no clear data license; USGS Landsat surface temperature is a public-domain fallback.

Working files: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/wf/dl
open_questions: Hosts not reachable from this session: sciencedirect.com, journals.uchicago.edu, link.springer.com (and ornl.gov returned 403). So Wrenn (2026), Baker (2021) and Buck et al. (2016) were read from abstracts on Penn State Pure, RePEc/IDEAS and EconPapers, not the full text. The published JPE version of Baylis & Boomhower (2026) was not opened. Its main estimate, 13 percentage points / 34% as cited by RFF WP 25-30, differs from the 2021 NBER working paper's 16 points / 40%, and its neighbor-spillover figure in the final version is unconfirmed.

Green-roof rent premium (Ichihara & Cohen 2011, Letters in Spatial and Resource Sciences 4(1):21–30, doi:10.1007/s12076-010-0046-4) could not be opened (Springer blocked; the IDEAS page has no abstract), so it is not cited.

SNWA's single-family turf rebate: the official terms page (read 10 Nov 2026) still shows $5.00/sq ft as of 18 Sep 2025. A KLAS news item seen only as a search snippet says the temporary $5 rate has ended. Confirm the current rate with SNWA.

Tree Equity Score license: no open data license was found. The site copyright notice prohibits downloading site content for commercial use or for personal websites without permission. Ask American Forests whether the CSV downloads are covered, or switch the heat measure to USGS Landsat Collection 2 surface temperature (public domain).

'Mostly lawns' has no national dataset assessed here. A proxy, such as the ACS single-family detached share or the NLCD developed open-space/low-intensity share, needs testing against known lawn areas.

Wildfire trigger design: WHP codes developed land as non-burnable (class 6), so a block group's own WHP 4–5 share understates risk inside towns. Choose a buffer distance and threshold, or use WRC 2nd-edition Risk to Potential Structures (30 m, spread into developed areas; CONUS RPS 33.7 GB, per-state zips 5–11 GB on usfs-public.box.com).

The wildfire home-value evidence is for code-built (new) homes in California. No study measures the price effect of retrofits, defensible space or Firewise USA status on existing homes. Applying the 1.4–2.5% premium to a retrofit program is an assumption.
Insurance-discount rules outside California (e.g., Oregon, Colorado) and NFPA's Firewise USA participation requirements were not researched or opened.
Cool-roof installed costs come from EPA's 2008 compendium citing 2006 data; no current agency cost survey was found. Green-roof costs cite a 2001 report.

Water-recycling costs are California only (2015 dollars). The per-household local share depends on each utility's rates and grants and was not computed. No U.S. hedonic study links recycled-water supply to home values.
Cooling centers and cool pavement were named in the group brief but are already catalog types (cooling_center, cool_pavement), so they were not re-researched.

checks.item: wildfire_hardening effect_url: Wrenn (2026), Journal of Housing Economics abstract on Penn State Pure
checks.note: HTTP 200. The quote appears word for word in the abstract (3 times: page text, BibTeX and RIS). The page lists Wrenn as the only author, JHE vol. 72, article 102139, published Jun 2026. The Crossref record for doi:10.1016/j.jhe.2026.102139 agrees: sole author Wrenn, June 2026. The page supports the 1.4%–2.5% premium for homes built after the codes and the benefit–cost sentence. One claim cannot be checked: 'the paper reports no distance-based effect'. The abstract says nothing about spillovers, and the full text is paywalled (ScienceDirect returned 403). Treat that sentence as unconfirmed.

checks.item: wildfire_hardening cost_url: CWMP Monthly Status Report, September 2026 (Cal OES)
checks.corrected: Table 12 'Total' row: Construction Total $41,230.85, Defensible Space Total $11,176.66, Grand Total $52,407.51 ('Shows the average total cost per home/site by county.'). These averages cover 157 sites with reported costs, not the 190 completed sites (derived: $8,227,979.44 ÷ $52,407.51 = 157; Lake 68, San Diego 28, Shasta 37, Siskiyou 24). The report also says: 'Cost figures reflect site work financial data submitted by Local Program Partner to date and do not represent all expenditures incurred by the communities.'
checks.note:
HTTP 200, 23-page PDF, 'Last Updated September 10, 2026'. Both quotes were found. The table row only matches in the layout extraction because the PDF lays it out as columns. Confirmed:
- 190 completed sites: Lake 73, San Diego 35, Shasta 38, Siskiyou 44 (11 in 2024, 107 in 2025, 72 in 2026).
- County averages run from $35,543.45 (Siskiyou, 'focused primarily on defensible space and Zone 0') to $71,875.11 (San Diego).
- Cal OES/CAL FIRE joint powers authority; 'upwards of $40,000' covered for owners at or below 120% AMI.
- Owner cost share is 10% at >120–200% AMI and 25% above 200% AMI.

The claim leaves out that these cost shares are capped at $3,000 and $6,000 (Resolution 2025-03). The phrase 'per completed home' is the researcher's: the report says average per home/site.

checks.item: drought_landscaping effect_url: Baker (2021) JAERE abstract on IDEAS/RePEc
checks.note: HTTP 200. Both quote fragments appear word for word in the abstract. The page cites JAERE 8(3):475–508, 2021, doi:10.1086/712429. It supports four results: about 1% higher value for the converting property, 19–21% water savings, a possible 3% energy increase, and little evidence of spillovers to neighbors. The cost-effectiveness quote in the notes ($2.65–$3.31/kgal; net benefits of $2.35–$2.88 per sq ft) is also in this abstract. The abstract says 'a Las Vegas area water conservation program' and does not name SNWA.

checks.item: drought_landscaping cost_url: SoCal Water$mart residential Turf Replacement Program page
checks.note: HTTP 200. The quote appears word for word on the residential page. The page also says 'Rebate amounts are subject to change at any time and are based on availability at the time of application approval'. It offers an optional $100 per tree (up to 5) since 4 Mar 2024. Supports MWD's base rebate of $2.00/sq ft, up to 5,000 sq ft per year. This is a rebate (program) cost, not the installed cost.

checks.item: water_recycling effect_url: Buck, Auffhammer, Hamilton & Sunding (2016) JAERE abstract on EconPapers
checks.note: HTTP 200. The quote appears word for word. The abstract also confirms 'a sample of 53 urban water utilities in California collectively providing service to over 20 million customers' (JAERE 2016, 3(3):743–778). It supports losses of $1,458/AF for a 10% shortage and $3,426/AF for a 30% shortage, and a household WTP of $60–$600. As the notes say, these are losses from shortages, not a measured effect of recycling projects.

checks.item: water_recycling cost_url: Cooley, Phurisamban & Gleick (2019), Environ. Res. Commun. 1:042001 (PDF)
checks.corrected: The paper continues right after the quoted sentences: 'If the water is used to recharge groundwater prior to use, there is an additional cost of $0.37/m3 to convey the water to a groundwater basin, extract it from the aquifer, and treat it to drinking water standards. Thus, the total cost for small indirect potable reuse projects range from $1.59 to $2.17/m3 with a median cost of $1.88/m3. The total cost for large indirect potable reuse projects ranges from $1.28 to $1.66/m3, with a median cost of $1.43/m3.' My conversions at 1,233.5 m3/AF: large ≈ $1,580–$2,050/AF (median ≈ $1,760); small ≈ $1,960–$2,680/AF (median ≈ $2,320).
checks.note:
Fetched with curl (HTTP 200); WebFetch could not resolve iopscience.iop.org. The quote is word for word, but it gives the treatment-facility cost only: Table 3 labels it 'Indirect potable reuse facility ($/m3)'. Table 3's 'Total cost of indirect potable reuse' column and the next sentences add $0.37/m3. So the stated IPR cost (large $0.91–$1.28, median $1.06/m3, ≈ $1,310/AF) is about a quarter to a third below the paper's own total. The low and high values are the 25th and 75th percentiles of only 3 small and 3 large projects.

Confirmed: levelized costs in 2015 dollars; the '>12 million m3' size class; non-potable total including purple-pipe distribution of $1.21–$1.70, median $1.25/m3; open-access topical review. Cooley and Gleick are at the Pacific Institute; Phurisamban is listed at the University of Zurich.

checks.item: cool_roofs effect_url: Macintyre & Heaviside (2019), Environment International 127:430–441 (UCL Discovery PDF)
cool_roofs cost_url: LADWP Consumer Rebate Program fact sheet (Rev 04 2024)
wildfire_hardening notes: Baylis & Boomhower, NBER Working Paper 29621 (Dec 2021)
checks.note: HTTP 200; 50-page PDF, NBER WP 29621, December 2021 (not peer reviewed). All three quotes appear word for word. The 16-point (40%) figure compares a 2008-or-newer home with 'a 1990 home experiencing an identical wildfire exposure'. The neighbor effect is 2.5 points (6%) in the introduction but 'about 2 percentage points or 6%' in the conclusion. Crossref confirms the published version: JPE 134(3):895–948, March 2026, doi:10.1086/739331 (the article itself was not opened).

checks.item: wildfire_hardening notes: RFF Working Paper 25-30 (Ludington, Liao, Walls, Dec 2025)
checks.note:
HTTP 200; 34-page PDF. Authors and 'Working Paper 25-30, December 2025' confirmed; not necessarily peer reviewed. All five quotes were found.

The 13-point (34%) figure is RFF's summary of 'Baylis and Boomhower (forthcoming)', JPE, with a link to the preprint. It refers to homes under Chapter 7A (in effect since 2008).

The claim omits a qualifier: the 5.65% (≈$98) maximum applies 'if they have an insurer that discounts based on the full premium'. For insurers that discount only the wildfire portion, 'the maximum discount averages only $54'.

verify.summary:
I opened 30 cited URLs: all 8 effect_url/cost_url pages, all 12 URLs in the notes that back effect or cost figures, and 10 trigger-data URLs. Each page was downloaded with curl through the session proxy and the quotes were matched against the downloaded text, ignoring case, whitespace and punctuation. WebFetch could not resolve iopscience.iop.org, so I stayed with curl. All 30 returned HTTP 200, or 206 for ranged GETs on the large data files. All 26 items with quoted text matched; the 4 data files have no quote, and their stated sizes and dates match.

One cited claim is not supported as stated:
- **water_recycling cost (Cooley et al. 2019):** the quoted indirect-potable-reuse figures are treatment-facility costs only. In the next sentences and in Table 3, the paper adds $0.37/m3 to convey water to a groundwater basin, extract it and treat it. Its total IPR cost is $1.28–$1.66/m3 for large projects (median $1.43, ≈ $1,760/AF) and $1.59–$2.17/m3 for small ones (median $1.88, ≈ $2,320/AF). The stated $0.91–$1.28 (median $1.06, ≈ $1,310/AF) is roughly 26% below the paper's own large-project total. Each range is the 25th–75th percentile of just 3 projects.

Caveats on claims that are otherwise supported:
- **CWMP ($52,407.51 per site):** the number is right, but it averages the 157 sites with reported costs ($8,227,979.44 ÷ $52,407.51), not the 190 completed sites. It covers site-work costs only. The owner cost shares of 10% and 25% are capped at $3,000 and $6,000.
- **Wrenn 2026:** the 1.4%–2.5% premium is confirmed (sole author, JHE 72:102139). 'The paper reports no distance-based effect' cannot be checked: the abstract is silent and ScienceDirect returned 403.
- **LADWP cool roofs:** 'up to $0.60/sq ft' is confirmed. The current CRP page pays $0.20–$0.60 depending on 3-year SRI and roof slope, and only for roof area over conditioned space.
- **RFF:** the 5.65% (≈ $98) maximum applies only to insurers that discount the full premium; for insurers that discount only the wildfire portion it is $54. The 13-point (34%) figure is RFF's citation of the 'forthcoming' JPE paper. Crossref confirms that paper is JPE 134(3):895–948, March 2026.
- **NBER WP:** its 16-point (40%) estimate compares 2008-or-newer homes with 1990 homes. Its neighbor effect is 2.5 points in the introduction but 'about 2 percentage points' in the conclusion.
- **SNWA:** the terms page still shows the $5.00/$2.50 rate from 18 Sep 2025, and the extra $2 for Las Vegas Valley Water District customers is confirmed. The claim that the rate ended could not be checked because the web-search budget was used up.
- **WHP 2023:** the county and ZIP summary files are in the separate Supplements zip, not the Data zip.

All other effects, costs, dates, licence terms, file sizes and the WHP class codes (1–7) match the sources.

types.name: Community storm shelter or safe rooms
types.trigger: The block group sits in a census tract whose FEMA National Risk Index tornado rating (TRND_RISKR) is 'Relatively High' or 'Very High'. In NRI v1.20 (Dec 2025) that is 21,559 of 85,154 tracts: 15,946 Relatively High plus 5,613 Very High (my count from the FEMA feature service). Rank block groups higher where mobile homes are common, measured as ACS 2020-2024 B25024_010E / B25024_001E. Nationally 5.6% of housing units are mobile homes. Of the 239,637 block groups that have housing, 17.9% are at or above 10% mobile homes and 10.5% are at or above 20% (my computation from the 2020-2024 table-based summary file). The reason for ranking this way: shelters cost about 11 times less per life saved in mobile homes than in permanent homes. FEMA P-361 says to site the shelter within a 1/4-mile walk or 1/2-mile drive of the homes it serves. For local display only, the SPC (E)F2+ tornado paths since 1950 can be shown: 13,404 of 73,458 tracks, which account for 6,061 of 6,341 deaths (my count from the SPC CSV).
types.trigger_data: (1) FEMA National Risk Index, 'National Risk Index Census Tracts' feature service, field TRND_RISKR (Tornado - Hazard Type Risk Index Rating). Its values are Very High, Relatively High, Relatively Moderate, Relatively Low, Very Low, No Rating and Insufficient Data. Version December 2025 (1.20.0); item modified 18 Dec 2025. Service: https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Census_Tracts/FeatureServer/0. Item page: https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=9da4eeb936544335a6db0cd7a8448a51. Covers all census tracts nationwide. FEMA NRI terms: use is free, but you must cite the dataset, its version and the access date, and state that the product 'uses the Federal Emergency Management Agency's National Risk Index dataset API or downloadable datasets but is not endorsed by FEMA'. Reverse engineering is not allowed; the data are for planning only. (2) ACS 2020-2024 5-year table B25024, Units in Structure (B25024_010E 'Mobile home'; B25024_001E total), at block-group level: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25024.dat. Variable list: https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs5/groups/B25024.json. The summary file needs no key. Census API terms require the notice 'This product uses the Census Bureau Data API but is not endorsed or certified by the Census Bureau.' (3) NOAA/NWS Storm Prediction Center SVRGIS tornado paths 1950-2025, page updated 23 April 2026: https://www.spc.noaa.gov/gis/svrgis/zipped/1950-2025-torn-aspath.zip. CSV of single tracks: https://www.spc.noaa.gov/wcm/data/1950-2025_actual_tornadoes.csv (fields include mag, fat, inj, slat, slon, elat, elon, len, wid). The data are lines and points, public domain per https://www.weather.gov/disclaimer.
types.effect: Home values: none measured. No study was found on how a community shelter affects nearby home values. The closest housing-market evidence is from Oklahoma manufactured-home parks: lot rents in parks with shelters were 5-8% higher, which is about enough to pay for the shelters. That estimate is statistically significant in only one specification (Simmons & Sutter 2007). Safety and cost-effectiveness: in Oklahoma, at a 3% real discount rate, a shelter costs about $6.0 million per life saved in mobile homes against $68 million in permanent homes. By that measure, shelters are cost-effective for mobile homes in the most tornado-prone states but not for permanent homes (Simmons & Sutter 2006, Risk Analysis).
types.effect_quote: We find that rents for lots in parks with shelters are 5–8% higher, which generates sufficient revenue to approximately pay for shelters, but the point estimate is statistically significant in only one specification.
types.effect_source: Kevin Simmons and Daniel Sutter (2007), 'Tornado shelters and the manufactured home parks market', Natural Hazards 43(3): 365-378, doi:10.1007/s11069-007-9123-4. The abstract was read on IDEAS/RePEc because the Springer page returned a bot check.
types.cost: One project: $1,657,000 total construction cost for a 10,000 sq ft, FEMA P-361 multi-purpose safe room for 1,592 people at Coahoma Community College in Clarksdale, Mississippi. FEMA HMGP paid 90% ($1,491,300); the award was announced in Sept 2016. That works out to about $166 per sq ft and about $1,040 per occupant (my arithmetic). A second check: three Missouri school safe rooms approved in March 2019 imply about $1,700-$2,000 per occupant, total cost. I derived this from the federal shares, match rates and capacities in the SEMA release.
types.cost_quote: Federal funding, which totals $1,491,300, represents 90 percent of the $1,657,000 total construction cost.
types.notes:
Size and capacity of the cost example, from the same page: "The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Hazard Mitigation Grant Program award will support construction of a 10,000-square-foot safe room built to FEMA-361 standards to protect people during hurricane or tornado-force winds." and "When completed, the safe room will be able to protect 1,592 students, faculty, staff, and residents within a half-mile radius of Coahoma Community College."

Missouri SEMA release, 7 Mar 2019 (https://sema.dps.mo.gov/news/newsitem/uuid/63c958e8-db88-4210-91d3-febc28703e32): "The federal share of the Sparta project is approximately $1.4 million. The federal share of the Neosho project is approximately $1.1 million, and the federal share for the Miller project is approximately $925,000." Capacities are 1,089 (Sparta), 660 (Goodman/Neosho) and 519 (Miller). The local match is 25% for Sparta and 10% for the other two. That gives totals of about $1.87M, $1.22M and $1.03M, or $1,714, $1,852 and $1,980 per occupant (my arithmetic). On funding, the same release says: "The FEMA Pre-Disaster Mitigation grant program provides 75 percent funding for approved safe room projects, which rises to 90 percent for communities meeting small size and low income levels."

FEMA P-361, 4th ed., April 2021, read on a Texas state mirror because fema.gov returned 403 (https://newtools.cira.state.tx.us/upload/page/12213/docs/SR/FEMA%20Publication%20P-361.pdf). On funding: "As of November 2020, FEMA has provided approximately $1.2 billion in FEMA funds towards the design and construction of over 40,000 residential and nearly 2,200 community safe rooms in 25 states and territories." On sizing: "Tornado safe rooms: ICC 500 Section 502.2 requires a minimum of 5 square feet per person for standing or seated occupants for community tornado safe rooms." On service area: "indicates a ¼-mile radius for occupants walking to the safe room; a ½-mile travel distance typically applies to occupants driving to a community safe room." P-361 (2021) describes cost increases only qualitatively. Its benefit-cost tool takes tornado probability from NOAA records.

Safety evidence. Simmons & Sutter 2006, Risk Analysis 26(4): 945-954 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/wly/riskan/v26y2006i4p945-954.html): "Despite the very different method used, the estimates are $68 million in permanent homes and $6.0 in mobile homes in Oklahoma using a 3% real discount rate, within about 10% of estimates based on historical fatalities. The findings suggest that shelters provide cost-effective protection for mobile homes in the most tornado-prone states but not for permanent homes." The Natural Hazards abstract (effect_url) says: "In the US over 40% of tornado fatalities occur in mobile homes even though they comprise about 8% of US housing units." Simmons & Sutter 2008, Weather and Forecasting 23(2): 246-258 (https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/wefo/23/2/2007waf2006027_1.xml): "If mobile homes compose an additional 1% of a county’s housing stock, expected fatalities increase by about 6.6%." The CDC study of the April 2011 Alabama tornadoes (PLOS ONE, see warning_sirens): "Mobile home residents showed the highest odds of injury (OR, 6.98; 95% CI: 2.10–23.20). No severe injuries occurred in tornado shelters."

NIBS, Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves 2019 (https://nibs.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/NIBS_MMC_MitigationSaves_2019-1.pdf), on a sample of FEMA-funded wind grants: "Large facilities with dual purposes, such as school gymnasia and cafeterias, exhibit an average BCR of 8.0."

I found no nationwide public list of existing community safe rooms, so 'no shelter nearby' cannot be tested. Keep kind 'qol', since no effect on nearby home values has been measured.

types.name: Outdoor warning sirens and alerts
types.trigger: The block group sits in a census tract with NRI TRND_RISKR 'Relatively High' or 'Very High', and no OpenStreetMap feature tagged emergency=siren lies within 1.5 km (0.93 mi) of the block group's populated area, such as its internal point or its populated blocks. Basis for 1.5 km: Clinton County (Ohio) EMA says a siren may be heard about a mile away on a calm day, but less than half a mile away upwind during storms. Texas TWDB defines a siren's coverage as the area that receives at least 70 dB. Show this as 'no siren mapped', not 'no siren', because OSM mapping is incomplete. In Nov 2026 Geofabrik extracts, St. Charles County, MO had 135 mapped sirens against the 143 the county reports. Sedgwick County, KS had only 87 against the 153 the county maintains (my count inside TIGERweb county polygons).
types.trigger_data: (1) OpenStreetMap features tagged emergency=siren. Tag definition: https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Tag:emergency%3Dsiren (optional siren:purpose=tornado, siren:range). Get them from Geofabrik state extracts or Overpass. Taginfo counts 26,178 tagged objects worldwide, data until 2026-11-09 (https://taginfo.openstreetmap.org/api/4/tag/stats?key=emergency&value=siren). The data are points and are updated continuously. License: ODbL (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright): free to copy and adapt with credit to OpenStreetMap and its contributors; share-alike. Coverage is uneven. My counts in the project's Nov 2026 state extracts: Iowa 2,262, Missouri 488, Oklahoma 369, Kansas 159, Alabama 74. (2) FEMA NRI tract field TRND_RISKR, v1.20 (Dec 2025): https://services.arcgis.com/XG15cJAlne2vxtgt/arcgis/rest/services/National_Risk_Index_Census_Tracts/FeatureServer/0. FEMA NRI terms require a citation and a non-endorsement statement. (3) NOAA SPC tornado paths 1950-2025, for display: https://www.spc.noaa.gov/gis/svrgis/ (public domain).
types.effect: Home values: none measured; I found no study of sirens and home prices. Safety: CDC ran a case-control study of the 27 April 2011 Alabama tornadoes with 98 injured cases and 200 uninjured controls. People who received the siren warning had half the odds of injury (adjusted odds ratio 0.50, 95% CI 0.30-0.85), and people who heard sirens more often had lower odds of injury. No study was found that links a community's siren coverage to tornado deaths. For warnings in general, Simmons & Sutter (2008) found injuries fell by over 40% at some lead times, while results for deaths were mixed.
types.effect_quote: Exposure to warnings via the Internet (aOR, 0.20; 95% CI: 0.09–0.49), television (aOR, 0.45; 95% CI: 0.24–0.83), and sirens (aOR, 0.50; 95% CI: 0.30–0.85) decreased the odds of injury, and residents frequently exposed to tornado sirens had lower odds of injury.
types.effect_source: Thomas Niederkrotenthaler, Erin M. Parker, Fernando Ovalle, Rebecca E. Noe, Jeneita Bell, Likang Xu, Melissa A. Morrison, Caitlin E. Mertzlufft and David E. Sugerman (2013), 'Injuries and Post-Traumatic Stress following Historic Tornados: Alabama, April 2011', PLOS ONE 8(12): e83038, doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0083038.
types.cost: $30,000-$50,000 to install one outdoor warning siren (St. Charles County, Missouri, county page current as of 2026). A Texas Water Development Board guide (Jan 2026, based on 2025 interviews) gives $24,000-$70,000 per siren for capital and installation. It puts maintenance at about 10% of installation cost per year. Ann Arbor expects about $17,000 a year to maintain its 22 sirens, about $770 per siren (my arithmetic).
types.cost_quote: The cost of installing a siren now ranges between $30,000 and $50,000.
types.notes:
Texas Water Development Board, Flash Flood Warning Siren Guide, January 2026 (https://www.twdb.texas.gov/about/sb3/doc/TWDB-Flash-Flood-Warning-Siren-Guide.pdf). On cost: "Capital and installation costs range from $24,000 to $70,000 per siren depending upon siren type and size." and "Maintenance costs also vary by system type; a common annual maintenance budget estimate is 10 percent of installation costs." On coverage: "The siren’s coverage area is defined as the area in which the audible alert is at least 70 dB." (the PDF text uses an 'fi' ligature). On funding, it names "FEMA Hazard Mitigation Grant Program Funding" as one route.

Clinton County (Ohio) EMA, 3 Apr 2025 (https://www.cc-ema.org/post/outdoor-warning-sirens). On cost: "The estimated cost of a single outdoor warning siren in today's dollars ranges from $25,000 to $35,000, depending on features, installation, and site requirements." It says installation can push this to $40-50K. On range: "On a calm day, you might hear a siren from a mile away." and "If you’re standing in an upwind direction, you may not hear the siren even from less than half a mile away."

Upkeep. Ann Arbor (https://engage.a2gov.org/siren-review): "There are 22 outdoor warning sirens in Ann Arbor." and "The city expects to spend $60,000 each of the next three years on repairs, then roughly $17,000 annually on maintenance." The council funded maintenance on 23 Sept 2026. Brighton, Colorado retired its system instead (2 Aug 2024, https://www.brightonco.gov/CivicAlerts.aspx?AID=2567): "The total estimated cost to repair and maintain the current system totaled roughly $131,000 for initial repairs and updates, plus ongoing maintenance costs."

OSM completeness check. St. Charles County page: "There are 143 warning sirens located within St Charles County." Sedgwick County, KS (https://www.sedgwick.gov/emergency-management/outdoor-warning-system/): "Emergency Management maintains 153 sirens throughout Sedgwick County and in 21 jurisdictions." OSM has 135 and 87 siren features inside those two counties (my count).

Warnings in general. Simmons & Sutter 2008 abstract (https://journals.ametsoc.org/view/journals/wefo/23/2/2007waf2006027_1.xml): "It is found that warnings have had a significant and consistent effect on tornado injuries, with a reduction of over 40% at some lead time intervals. The results for fatalities are mixed." NIST Technical Note 1950 (Kuligowski & Wakeman, Feb 2017, https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/TechnicalNotes/NIST.TN.1950.pdf), summarizing surveys in Ford County, KS: "The efficacy of the outdoor siren system was examined, with 40 % of people reporting that they took cover after receiving the siren alert."

Sirens are meant to be heard outdoors only, so pair them with outreach on Wireless Emergency Alerts and alert sign-up. Kind 'qol'.

types.effect: Oklahoma City homes with a tornado shelter sold for 3.5% to 4% more, about $4,200 at the 2005 mean sale price. At the time, shelters cost $2,500-$3,000 installed (Simmons & Sutter 2007). This premium applies only to the house that has the shelter; no effect on neighbors was measured. Safety per dollar is low in permanent homes: about $30 million per life saved without discounting (Merrell, Simmons & Sutter 2005), or $68 million at a 3% discount rate (Simmons & Sutter 2006).
types.effect_quote: We find that a shelter increases the sale price of a home by 3.5% to 4% or approximately $4200 given the mean price of homes sold in 2005. The magnitude of the premium is plausible given that shelters retail for $2500-$3000 installed.
types.effect_source: Kevin Simmons and Daniel Sutter (2007), 'Tornado shelters and the housing market', Construction Management and Economics 25(11): 1119-1126, doi:10.1080/01446190701618299. The abstract was read on IDEAS/RePEc because the Taylor & Francis page returned 403.
types.cost: For a safe room built during construction of a new home: $9,400-$13,100 for 8 x 8 ft and $18,900-$25,500 for 14 x 14 ft (FEMA P-320, 5th ed., March 2021; 2019 dollars, national RSMeans averages, 15% contingency). A tested door adds about $2,500-$3,200. Retrofits cost more. Small steel in-ground units cost $5,000-$6,000 before installation and delivery. As a rebate example, Michigan's FEMA-funded program pays 75% of the cost, up to $7,131.75.
types.cost_quote: During the construction of a new home, the estimated basic cost to construct a safe room using the design plans in this publication ranges from approximately $9,400 to $13,100 for an 8-foot × 8-foot safe room and from $18,900 to $25,500 for a 14-foot × 14-foot safe room
types.notes:
This type was added by the research step; it was not on the mapping list. The group brief names residential safe rooms, and the only measured home-value effect in this group is for a house with its own shelter. Fold it into storm_shelter if one type is preferred. Because a home-value effect is measured, it could be a 'value' type.

The P-320 PDF is FEMA's March 2021 edition, read on a Texas state mirror because fema.gov returned 403. FEMA's 6th edition (Dec 2024) could not be opened. From the same PDF: "Estimates of safe room designs for each construction type were developed using industry-accepted cost-estimating guides and are provided in 2019 dollars." On doors: "Market research shows that entry level prices for properly tested and labeled residential safe room door assemblies are between approximately $2,500 and $3,200 at the time of this publication." On retrofits: "Further, safe rooms installed in existing homes will be more expensive than those built as part of new construction." On prefabricated units: "Small steel in-ground units typically cost between $5,000 and $6,000 not including installation (excavation and ground anchors) and delivery fee." P-320 also repeats the roughly 3.5% / $4,200 price premium.

Rebate program example: the Michigan State Police EMHSD Safe Room Rebate Program FAQ (BRIC-funded; https://www.michigan.gov/msp/divisions/emhsd/response-recovery-responsive/michigan-safe-room-rebate-program/faqs): "Homeowners who are selected for the program are eligible for a rebate of 75% of the eligible cost to install/construct a safe room up to a maximum of $7,131.75. This amount is 75% of the predetermined benefit amount for safe rooms of $9,509."

Safety. Merrell, Simmons & Sutter 2005, Land Economics 81(1): 87-99 (https://le.uwpress.org/content/81/1/87): "The cost per life saved for shelters in permanent homes without discounting is around $30 million." NIBS 2019, which uses FEMA's benefit-cost method, finds instead: "In-home safe rooms generally appear to be cost effective, exhibiting an average BCR of 4.25." P-361 (2021) reports over 40,000 FEMA-funded residential safe rooms as of Nov 2020.

result.summary:
I covered three project types. The mapping step proposed two (storm_shelter, warning_sirens). I added a third, safe_room_rebate (residential safe rooms), because the group brief names it and it is the only type here with a measured effect on home values. All figures come from pages I opened and read with curl through the session proxy, because WebFetch could not resolve any host. fema.gov returned 403 Access Denied, so FEMA P-361 and P-320 (2021 editions) were read on a Texas state mirror, and the NRI was read from FEMA's ArcGIS service.

- **Trigger data:** the FEMA NRI tract tornado rating (TRND_RISKR, v1.20, Dec 2025). 21,559 of 85,154 tracts are rated Relatively High or Very High. To this I add the ACS 2020-2024 block-group mobile-home share and NOAA SPC tornado paths for 1950-2025 (SVRGIS page updated 23 April 2026, public domain).

- **Storm shelters (community):** no effect on nearby home values has been measured. The closest housing-market evidence: lot rents in Oklahoma mobile-home parks with shelters were 5-8% higher, significant in only one specification. Shelters cost about $6.0M per life saved in mobile homes against $68M in permanent homes. Unit cost: $1.657M for a 10,000 sq ft safe room for 1,592 people (Coahoma, MS, 2016), about $1,040 per occupant. Missouri school safe rooms in 2019 imply $1,700-$2,000 per occupant.

- **Residential safe rooms:** a home with a shelter sold for 3.5-4% more, about $4,200 (Oklahoma City, 2005). FEMA P-320 puts an 8x8 ft room at $9,400-$13,100 and a 14x14 ft room at $18,900-$25,500 in new construction (2019 dollars), plus $2,500-$3,200 for the door.

- **Sirens:** no effect on home values has been measured. In a CDC case-control study of the April 2011 Alabama tornadoes, receiving a siren warning halved the odds of injury (adjusted OR 0.50). One siren costs $30,000-$50,000 installed (St. Charles County, MO). A Texas state guide gives $24,000-$70,000, plus about 10% a year for maintenance. Siren locations come from OpenStreetMap (ODbL), but coverage is incomplete: 135 of 143 sirens are mapped in St. Charles County, MO and 87 of 153 in Sedgwick County, KS (my counts).
open_questions: fema.gov returned 403 'Access Denied' (Akamai) to this session, so FEMA's own pages could not be opened. These include: the Safe Room FAQ and Safe Room Funding pages; FEMA P-320 6th edition (Dec 2024); any P-361 edition newer than April 2021; the 2015 memo 'safe room project application using precalculated benefits'; the HMGP application overviews for community safe rooms and warning sirens; the HMGP 5% Initiative page; FEMA press releases (e.g. the Potosi, MO safe room, July 2026); and OpenFEMA HMA Projects, which would give a national sample of safe room and siren project costs. hazards.fema.gov (the NRI data page) redirected to fema.gov too; I used FEMA's ArcGIS item and service instead.

WebFetch could not resolve any host in this session (ENOTFOUND for ideas.repec.org, le.uwpress.org, journals.plos.org and www.spc.noaa.gov). I read every page with curl through the session proxy, and the verifier may need to do the same.

Bot checks blocked the publisher pages for three papers: Taylor & Francis (Simmons & Sutter 2007, Construction Management and Economics), Springer (2007, Natural Hazards), and PubMed/Wiley (2006, Risk Analysis); Mercatus was blocked too. I read their abstracts on IDEAS/RePEc and did not read the full texts. The Land Economics 2005 abstract was read on the journal's own page.

No study was found that measures any of these: a community shelter's effect on nearby home values; outdoor sirens' effect on home values; or the effect of a county's siren coverage on tornado deaths across many counties and years.

I found no nationwide public inventory of existing community safe rooms, so 'no shelter within 1/2 mile' cannot be computed. OSM siren mapping is uneven: 135 of 143 sirens mapped in St. Charles County, MO, and 87 of 153 in Sedgwick County, KS. Statewide OSM totals are low too: 74 in Alabama and 159 in Kansas.
The community safe room cost per occupant rests on four projects in two states (Mississippi 2016, Missouri 2019). The Missouri totals are my derivation from 'approximately' stated federal shares.

FEMA P-361 (2021) describes the cost of hardening part of a building as a safe room only qualitatively. I saw the 3rd edition's (2015) quantitative figure, a 5%-7% addition to building cost, only as quoted by NIBS (2019). The Georgia GEMA mirror of the 3rd edition returned a Cloudflare 429, and the UNT web-archive copy of FEMA's 2015 Community Safe Room Fact Sheet failed TLS verification.

I could not confirm on a FEMA page that outdoor warning sirens are eligible under the HMGP 5% Initiative. A Clare County, Michigan PDF that reportedly says FEMA removed sirens from grant-eligible items returned HTTP 429 and was not opened, so this is unresolved.

Two sources disagree on residential safe rooms. NIBS 2019 reports an average benefit-cost ratio of 4.25 for in-home safe rooms (FEMA BCA method, FAA casualty values). Simmons & Sutter estimate $30-68 million per life saved in Oklahoma permanent homes. Deciding which figure the page shows needs a call.

The tornado rating is published per census tract, so block groups inherit their tract's rating. ACS block-group mobile-home counts have large margins of error. Census API data queries now require a key; the table-based summary files on www2.census.gov do not.

checks.item: storm_shelter effect_url: Simmons & Sutter 2007, Natural Hazards 43(3):365-378 (IDEAS/RePEc abstract)
checks.note: HTTP 200 with curl. WebFetch failed with ENOTFOUND, as the research reported. The effect quote is verbatim in the abstract. Metadata matches: vol 43(3), pp 365-378, Dec 2007, doi 10.1007/s11069-007-9123-4. The page supports the lot-rent part: rents 5-8% higher in Oklahoma parks with shelters, roughly enough to pay for them, significant in only one specification. The notes' '40% of tornado fatalities ... about 8% of US housing units' sentence is also verbatim. The rent premium is for a shelter inside the park, not an effect on nearby home values, which matches how the research frames it. The '$6.0M vs $68M per life saved' part of the effect is not on this page. It comes from the Risk Analysis 2006 abstract, checked separately and supported.

checks.item: storm_shelter cost_url: Wicker/Cochran press release on the Coahoma Community College safe room
checks.note: Page dated September 16, 2016. The cost quote is verbatim. The notes' sentences on the 10,000 sq ft FEMA-361 room and on protecting 1,592 people within a half-mile radius are also verbatim. The page calls it an HMGP award for a multi-purpose room built for 250 mph winds. Arithmetic: 90% of $1,657,000 is $1,491,300; $1,657,000 / 10,000 sq ft = $165.70; $1,657,000 / 1,592 = $1,040.83 per occupant. All match the research.

checks.item: warning_sirens effect_url: Niederkrotenthaler et al. 2013, PLOS ONE 8(12): e83038
checks.note: The quote is verbatim in the abstract. Authors, volume/issue, doi and publication date (Dec 18, 2013) match. Confirmed on the page: a case-control survey of 98 injured cases and 200 uninjured controls; sirens aOR 0.50 (95% CI 0.30-0.85); siren exposure more than 5 times a year aOR 0.41 (95% CI 0.17-0.99), which supports 'heard sirens more often had lower odds'. Caveats from the paper itself: the warning-source models were adjusted only for age, sex, race and access to each warning source, not for distance to the tornado track, even though cases were closer to tracks than controls (0.46 vs 0.95 mi). The sample was a convenience sample and is not representative. The effect field's wording 'had half the odds' is fine. The summary's 'receiving a siren warning halved the odds of injury' sounds causal and should be worded as an association. The notes' mobile-home OR 6.98 and 'No severe injuries occurred in tornado shelters' sentences are also verbatim.

checks.item: warning_sirens cost_url: St. Charles County, MO Outdoor Warning Sirens page
checks.note: The quote is verbatim. The page is current: it describes the automated, zoned system that started in January 2026. The notes' 'There are 143 warning sirens located within St Charles County.' is also verbatim. The page adds that the county installed and maintains 72 units and municipalities run the rest, and that sirens are not designed to be heard indoors. It supports $30,000-$50,000 installed per siren. The TWDB and Ann Arbor parts of the cost come from other pages, checked separately and supported.

checks.item: safe_room_rebate effect_url: Simmons & Sutter 2007, Construction Management and Economics 25(11):1119-1126 (IDEAS/RePEc abstract)
checks.note: The quote is verbatim. Metadata matches (doi 10.1080/01446190701618299). The abstract is about Oklahoma City home sales after the 3 May 1999 tornadoes and the state's safe-room initiative. A shelter raises the sale price 3.5-4%, about $4,200 at the 2005 mean price, and shelters retail for $2,500-$3,000 installed. This supports the home-price part. The abstract says nothing about neighbors, which fits 'no effect on neighbors was measured'. The $30M figure (Land Economics 2005) and the $68M figure (Risk Analysis 2006) are on other pages, both checked and supported.

checks.item: safe_room_rebate cost_url: FEMA P-320, 5th ed., March 2021 (Texas state mirror PDF)
checks.note: PDF returned 200: 15.3 MB, 91 pages. Its metadata lists FEMA as author, created 2 Mar 2021, and the cover reads 'FEMA P-320, March 2021, Fifth Edition'. The cost quote is verbatim in Section 4.3. Its footnotes confirm 2019 dollars, a 15% contingency and RSMeans 2019 national averages, and the basic cost excludes the door. Also verbatim: the door at $2,500-$3,200, the line that retrofits cost more, and steel in-ground units at $5,000-$6,000 before installation and delivery. Elsewhere P-320 repeats the ~3.5% (~$4,200) price premium. The file is a mirror, not fema.gov, and fema.gov also returned 403 to me. A newer edition with updated costs (the research mentions a Dec 2024 6th edition) could not be ruled out.

checks.item: Notes/effect: Simmons & Sutter 2006, Risk Analysis 26(4):945-954 (source of $6.0M vs $68M)
checks.note: The quote is verbatim. The abstract literally says '$6.0 in mobile homes', without the word 'million', but it clearly means $6.0 million. Setting: Oklahoma, 3% real discount rate, a tornado-probability method that lands within about 10% of estimates from historical fatalities. It concludes shelters are cost-effective for mobile homes in the most tornado-prone states but not for permanent homes. This supports the storm_shelter safety sentence, the $68M in safe_room_rebate, and the trigger's 'about 11 times' (68 / 6.0 = 11.3).

checks.item: Notes/cost: Missouri SEMA release, 7 Mar 2019 (second check on community safe room cost)
checks.note: Both quotes are verbatim; the release is dated March 07, 2019. Capacities (Sparta 1,089, Miller 519, Goodman/Neosho 660) and local matches (25%, 10%, 10%) are on the page. Arithmetic: 1.4/0.75 = $1.867M, or $1,714 per occupant; 1.1/0.9 = $1.222M, or $1,852; 0.925/0.9 = $1.028M, or $1,980. Caveat: the page says recipients 'pay the remaining share of the eligible expenses', and the federal shares are 'approximately'. These totals are therefore approximate eligible project costs, not necessarily the full cost of the multi-use buildings (gym, band space, early-childhood center).

checks.item: Effect/notes: Simmons & Sutter 2008, Weather and Forecasting 23(2):246-258
checks.note: The abstract quote is verbatim; the data cover US tornadoes 1986-2002. It supports 'injuries fell by over 40% at some lead times; results for deaths were mixed'. The 6.6% mobile-home sentence quoted in the storm_shelter notes is verbatim in the full text (results section), not in the abstract. The full text also gives the overall warning effect: injuries down 32% (95% CI 22-41%), and fatalities down about 1%, not significant.

checks.item: Effect: Merrell, Simmons & Sutter 2005, Land Economics 81(1):87-99
checks.note: The quote is verbatim in the abstract on the journal's own page (doi 10.3368/le.81.1.87). The estimate uses Oklahoma data. It supports '$30 million per life saved without discounting' for permanent homes, and the abstract adds that shelters are cost-effective for mobile-home residents.

checks.item: Cost: Texas Water Development Board Flash Flood Warning Siren Guide, Jan 2026
checks.note: PDF returned 200: 28.9 MB, 86 pages, created 26 Jan 2026, cover dated January 2026. The cost, 10%-maintenance and 70 dB quotes are verbatim; extraction drops ligatures but the words match. 'FEMA Hazard Mitigation Grant Program Funding' appears too. The guide says the ranges come from expert and case-study interviews in 2025 and are planning aids. Caveats the research leaves out: these are flash-flood sirens; the costs exclude siting studies, permitting, land or easements, site access, surveys and power installation; and control-software licences of $10,000-$30,000 a year may apply.

checks.item: Cost upkeep: Ann Arbor siren review page
checks.note: Both quotes are verbatim. The page says the City Council appropriated maintenance funds on Sept. 23, 2026. $17,000 / 22 = $773 per siren per year, which matches the research's ~$770. The $60,000 a year in repairs for the first three years comes before that.

checks.item: Cost: Michigan State Police Safe Room Rebate Program FAQ
checks.note: The quote is verbatim. The FAQ says the program uses BRIC funds, the homeowner pays the remaining 25%, and a room costing more than $9,509 needs a benefit-cost analysis. This supports '75% of the cost, up to $7,131.75'. The FAQ has no date or application status and cites P-320 (2014) and P-361 (2015), so it may be old. I could not confirm that this BRIC-funded program is still taking applications.

checks.item: Trigger/notes: FEMA P-361, 4th ed., April 2021 (Texas state mirror PDF)
checks.note: PDF returned 200: 22.7 MB, 214 pages, created 16 Apr 2021. The quotes on funding (Nov 2020, $1.2B, over 40,000 residential and nearly 2,200 community safe rooms), on 5 sq ft per person and on the 1/4-mile and 1/2-mile distances are all verbatim. Wording caveat: the distance text describes an example tornado protection zone (Fig. A4-2) in the operations chapter, and says travel time is the limiting factor (a 5-minute walk is about 1/4 mile). It is guidance, not a siting rule, so the trigger's 'P-361 says to site the shelter within...' overstates it slightly. Confirmed that P-361 (2021) describes cost increases only qualitatively ('relatively minor', 'moderate', 'moderate to significant').

checks.item: Notes: NIBS Natural Hazard Mitigation Saves 2019
checks.note: PDF returned 200, 658 pages. Both quotes (BCR 8.0 and BCR 4.25) are verbatim, in the same paragraph. The next sentence changes how to read the 8.0: 'In these cases, the cost of mitigation is simply the additional cost of hardening the facility.' The wind-grant analysis also uses $9.5M per statistical fatality and 'does not discount human life'. That explains much of the gap with Simmons & Sutter's $30-68M per life saved, which the research leaves as an open question. The 3rd-edition P-361 figure of 5%-7% added building cost is quoted in this report, as the research says.

checks.item: Trigger basis/notes: Clinton County (Ohio) EMA siren post, 3 Apr 2025
checks.note: All three quotes are verbatim. The post is dated Apr 3, 2025 and updated Apr 4. It also says installation costs (pole, equipment, labor) can push the price to $40-50K per unit. It supports the stated basis: about a mile on a calm day, under half a mile upwind in storms. The 1.5 km buffer is the research's own choice.

checks.item: Notes: City of Brighton, CO news item, 2 Aug 2024
checks.note: The link redirects to an archived copy, posted August 02, 2024. The quote is verbatim, and the item announces that the city retired its siren system.

checks.item: Notes: Sedgwick County, KS outdoor warning system page
checks.note: The quote is verbatim: 153 sirens in 21 jurisdictions. I did not check the OSM count of 87 (see not_checked).

checks.item: Notes: NIST Technical Note 1950 (Kuligowski & Wakeman, Feb 2017)
checks.note: PDF returned 200, 147 pages, February 2017. The quote is verbatim, in a summary of surveys in Ford County, KS. The same passage reports that 75.5% of residents rated sirens their main tornado alert and 67.2% thought sirens were meant to be heard indoors.

checks.item: Trigger data: FEMA NRI Census Tracts feature service, layer 0 (tract counts)
checks.note: I queried the service live. Field TRND_RISKR has the alias 'Tornado - Hazard Type Risk Index Rating'. Counts: 85,154 tracts in total; Very High 5,613; Relatively High 15,946 (together 21,559); Relatively Moderate 17,676; Relatively Low 20,041; Very Low 24,691; No Rating 126; Insufficient Data 1,061. These match the research exactly, as does its list of rating values.

checks.item: Trigger data: FEMA NRI item page (version and terms)
checks.note: The HTML item page is only a script shell (200, 1 KB), so I read the same item through ArcGIS REST (sharing/rest/content/items/<id>?f=json). It gives 'National Risk Index Data Version: December 2025 (1.20.0)', modified 2025-12-18 21:25 UTC, owner FEMA_NationalRiskIndex. The terms confirm the required 'not endorsed by FEMA' statement, citing the endpoint or dataset with its version and access date, no reverse engineering, and planning use only.

checks.item: Trigger data: ACS 2020-2024 table-based summary file B25024 (.dat)
checks.note: The research gave no quote for this file, so quote_found does not apply; I recomputed its figures instead. Downloaded 47.9 MB, last-modified 29 Jan 2026. National: 8,042,724 mobile homes of 143,775,355 units = 5.59% (5.6% stated). Block groups (summary level 150) with at least one unit: 239,637, including 2,490 in Puerto Rico. At or above 10% mobile homes: 42,991 (17.94%). At or above 20%: 25,090 (10.47%). All match. Without Puerto Rico the figures would be 237,147, 18.13% and 10.58%. The file names columns B25024_E010 and B25024_E001, the same variables the API calls B25024_010E and B25024_001E.

checks.item: Trigger data: Census API variable list, ACS 2024 5-year group B25024
checks.note: 200. Labels: B25024_001E 'Estimate!!Total:'; B25024_002E 'Estimate!!Total:!!1, detached'; B25024_010E 'Estimate!!Total:!!Mobile home'; concept 'Units in Structure'. I also confirmed in the B25003 group JSON that B25003_002E is 'Owner occupied'.

checks.item: Trigger data: SPC 1950-2025 actual tornadoes CSV
checks.note: Downloaded 9.0 MB. The file has 73,458 rows, all with sg=1 (one row per tornado), covering 1950-2025. Rows with mag 2 or higher: 13,404. Deaths: 6,341 in total, 6,061 in mag 2 or higher. All match the research exactly. 1,546 rows have mag -9 (unknown) and fall outside the F2+ count. The named fields mag, inj, fat, slat, slon, elat, elon, len and wid are all in the header.

checks.item: Trigger data: SPC SVRGIS page
checks.note: The page reads 'SVRGIS (Updated: 23 April 2026)' and covers tornadoes 1950-2025, as stated. I also requested headers for the cited path zip (.../zipped/1950-2025-torn-aspath.zip): HTTP 200, application/zip, 4,968,330 bytes, last-modified 28 Apr 2026. I did not unpack it.

checks.item: Trigger data: taginfo stats for emergency=siren
checks.note: The JSON gives 26,178 objects in total (26,148 nodes, 30 ways) with data_until 2026-11-09T00:59:50Z. Both match.

checks.item: Trigger data: OSM wiki Tag:emergency=siren
checks.note: 200. The page defines the tag and lists optional siren:purpose (for example tornado) and siren:range, as stated.

checks.item: Trigger data: OpenStreetMap copyright and licence page
