checks.note: Data are under ODbL: 'You are free to copy, distribute, transmit and adapt our data, as long as you credit OpenStreetMap and its contributors.' Altered or derived data may be distributed only under the same license. Matches the research's description.

checks.item: Trigger data: NWS disclaimer (public domain)
checks.note: Information on NWS web pages is in the public domain unless noted otherwise. Users must not claim it as their own, imply NOAA/NWS endorsement, or present modified content as official. SPC is an NWS center, so this covers the SPC data, although the SVRGIS page does not repeat it.

checks.item: Trigger data: ACS 2020-2024 table-based summary file B25003 (.dat)
checks.note: The research gave no quote and no number from this file, so quote_found does not apply. The file returns HTTP 200 (26.9 MB, last-modified 29 Jan 2026). A range read shows the header 'GEO_ID|B25003_E001|...|B25003_E002' (owner occupied). The research only claims the file exists and has these columns; I did not parse the whole file.

not_checked: OSM emergency=siren counts from the project's Nov 2026 Geofabrik extracts: 135 in St. Charles County and 87 in Sedgwick County; statewide 2,262 Iowa, 488 Missouri, 369 Oklahoma, 159 Kansas, 74 Alabama. No URL was cited because they come from local extracts. I tried to cross-check with the Overpass API, but the proxy reset the connection. Only the counties' own totals (143 and 153) were verified.

Claims that something does not exist cannot be checked against a page: no study of a community shelter's or of sirens' effect on home values, none linking siren coverage to tornado deaths, and no national inventory of community safe rooms.

fema.gov pages named in open_questions: Safe Room FAQ and Funding pages, P-320 6th edition (Dec 2024), HMGP and 5% Initiative pages, OpenFEMA HMA Projects. These are not cited URLs. One test request from this session also got 403 from fema.gov, so I could not check whether a newer P-320 edition updated the 2019-dollar costs, or whether sirens are HMGP-eligible.

Publisher pages and full texts of the three Simmons & Sutter papers (Springer, Taylor & Francis, Wiley). These were not cited; only the IDEAS/RePEc abstracts were checked, so model details such as the specifications behind the 5-8% rent premium were not reviewed.

The wording of the Census API terms notice, the Clare County (MI) PDF, the GEMA mirror of P-361 3rd edition and the UNT web-archive fact sheet. The research gives no URL for any of these (the last three are mentioned only in open_questions), so I did not attempt them.

The SPC path zip (https://www.spc.noaa.gov/gis/svrgis/zipped/1950-2025-torn-aspath.zip): checked only from response headers (200, 4,968,330 bytes, last-modified 28 Apr 2026). It is not unpacked; the counts were verified against the CSV instead.
verify.summary:
I checked 30 URLs: the 6 effect and cost URLs, plus 24 from the notes and trigger data. WebFetch failed with ENOTFOUND here, as the research reported, so I fetched every page with curl through the session proxy. Scratch copies are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/dl.

All 6 primary citations load, their quotes appear verbatim, and they support the stated effect or cost:
- Natural Hazards 2007: lot rents 5-8% higher.
- Wicker release: $1,657,000 total cost, 90% federal.
- PLOS ONE 2013: sirens aOR 0.50.
- St. Charles County: $30,000-$50,000 per siren.
- Construction Management and Economics 2007: home prices 3.5-4% (about $4,200) higher.
- FEMA P-320 2021: $9,400-$13,100 and $18,900-$25,500.

The parts of each effect or cost that cite other sources were also confirmed verbatim:
- Risk Analysis 2006: $6.0M vs $68M per life saved.
- Land Economics 2005: $30M per life saved.
- Weather and Forecasting 2008: injuries down over 40% at some lead times.
- TWDB 2026: $24k-$70k per siren and 10% a year for maintenance.
- Ann Arbor: $17k a year for 22 sirens.
- Michigan rebate: 75%, up to $7,131.75.
- Missouri SEMA 2019.

Every number I recomputed matched, so no number needs correcting:
- Coahoma: $166 per sq ft and $1,040 per occupant.
- Missouri: $1,714-$1,980 per occupant.
- NRI: 21,559 of 85,154 tracts (15,946 + 5,613).
- ACS: 5.6% mobile homes; 239,637 block groups; 17.9% and 10.5%.
- SPC: 13,404 of 73,458 tracks; 6,061 of 6,341 deaths.
- Taginfo: 26,178 objects.

Caveats to carry into the page:
1. The siren result is an association from a convenience-sample case-control study, and its warning models were not adjusted for distance to the track. 'Had half the odds' is fine; the summary's 'halved the odds' reads as causal.
2. NIBS's BCR of 8.0 for dual-purpose community safe rooms counts only the extra cost of hardening the building, and NIBS does not discount lives ($9.5M per statistical fatality). This explains much of the gap with Simmons & Sutter.
3. The Missouri per-occupant figures are approximate eligible project costs, not the full cost of the buildings.
4. P-361's 1/4-mile walk and 1/2-mile drive describe an example protection zone, with travel time as the limiting factor. They are not a siting rule.
5. TWDB's $24k-$70k excludes siting, permitting, land and power, and control-software licences of $10k-$30k a year may come on top. These are flash-flood sirens.
6. The Michigan FAQ is undated and BRIC-funded, so check that the program is still open.
7. P-320 and P-361 were read on a Texas mirror and fema.gov still returns 403, so a newer P-320 edition with updated costs cannot be ruled out.

types.name: Land bank takes tax-delinquent and nuisance properties
types.trigger: pop2020 < pop2010 (Decennial P1_001N; re-tabulate 2010 block-group counts to 2020 block groups with the Census relationship file) AND other_vacant_share = ACS B25004_008E / B25001_001E >= 0.10 (2020-2024 ACS 5-year; my proposal: the mapping step's 0.05 flags 30.2% of US block groups with 50+ housing units in my own tabulation, while 0.10 flags 14.7%) AND the state is one of the 20 states plus Puerto Rico with a land-bank enabling law, or a land bank or land-banking program already serves the county (Center for Community Progress map). Optional value screen: ACS B25077 median value so low that land is worth less than acquisition plus demolition.
types.trigger_data: (1) U.S. Census Bureau, ACS 2020-2024 5-year, table B25004 Vacancy Status (line 008 'Other vacant') and B25001 Housing Units, by block group. Table-based summary file https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25004.dat (file dated 29 Jan 2026; 242,297 block-group rows) or the Census Data API, which now needs a free key (keyless requests redirect to missing_key.html). Public Census data under census.gov policies and the API Terms of Service. (2) 2010 and 2020 Census P.L. 94-171 counts (P1 population, H1 housing units) by block group, plus the 2020-to-2010 block group relationship file https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel2020/blkgrp/tab20_blkgrp20_blkgrp10_natl.txt (public). (3) Center for Community Progress National Land Bank Map https://communityprogress.org/resources/land-banks/national-land-bank-map/: land bank point locations, 'updated as of May 2026', with 20 states plus Puerto Rico holding enabling laws as of June 2026. The site says '© 2026 All Rights Reserved', so use it as a lookup or link, not as open data. HUD-USPS vacancy data cannot be used for a public map (see notes).
types.effect: Cuyahoga County (Cleveland), OH, home sales 2009-2013. In the six months before the land bank buys it, each distressed property within 500 ft lowers a home's sale price by 5.2%. Once the land bank owns it the discount falls to 4.4%, a gain of 0.8 percentage points per property within 500 ft; this gap is not always statistically significant. After a land-bank demolition the vacant lot's discount is 2.4%. Estimated value preserved: about $3.8M for homes sold during the 39-month study and about $156M for homes that did not sell.
types.effect_quote: In the six months before they are purchased by the land bank, the distressed properties are estimated to lower the sale price of nearby homes (within 500 feet) by 5.2 percent. The preferred model suggests that a land bank acquisition reduces the distressed property’s negative externality by 0.8 percentage points from 5.2 percent to 4.4 percent.
types.effect_source: Whitaker, S. and Fitzpatrick IV, T.J. (2014). Land Bank 2.0: An Empirical Evaluation. Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland Working Paper 12-30R (Sept 2014). Published as Journal of Regional Science 56(1):156-175 (2016), confirmed on IDEAS.
types.cost: About $23,600 per property handled, all-in (acquisition, demolition, renovation, new construction and other work). Derived: Cuyahoga Land Bank spent about $330 million in 2009-2024 and transacted over 14,000 properties. Cuyahoga County, OH, nominal dollars.
types.cost_quote: From 2009 to 2024, Cuyahoga Land Bank spent about $330 million on demolitions, renovations, new constructions, and other activities. ... Fifteen years ago, Frangos spearheaded the establishment of the Cuyahoga Land Bank, Ohio’s first county land bank, which has since transacted over 14,000 properties and played a critical role in Cuyahoga County’s revitalization.
types.notes: Mapping-step type. Cost cross-check from the same Cleveland Fed paper: 'The land bank’s annual contract and administrative costs were $4.45 million in 2010, $12.4 million in 2011, $12.8 million in 2012, and $17.7 million in 2013.' With 3,405 properties acquired by Sept 2013, that is about $14,000 per property (derived). The Cuyahoga 15-year report (the land bank's own evaluation, Oct 2024) claims 'The average increase in value per demolition was $148,000, resulting in a benefit-cost ratio (BCR) of 9.74'. It is not peer reviewed, so treat it as an upper bound. Detroit evidence: Lee, Chung & Park (2025), Cities 165:106112 (abstract at https://scholar.xjtlu.edu.cn/en/publications/from-blight-to-boon-the-impact-of-land-banking-programs-on-adjace/): 'The findings indicate varied post-intervention trends: a gradual rise near Auction properties; an initial surge followed by decline near Partner Sales; and consistently lower values near Demolition sites.' Trigger caveats: ACS defines 'Other vacant' as a residual that 'includes units held for occupancy by a caretaker or janitor, and units held for personal reasons of the owner' (2022 ACS Subject Definitions, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/tech_docs/subject_definitions/2022_ACSSubjectDefinitions.pdf). It therefore overstates abandonment, and block-group margins of error are large. HUD-USPS data cannot back a public layer. HUD says 'Under the current agreement with the USPS, HUD can make the data accessible only to governmental entities and non-profit organizations registered as users.' The sublicense adds 'in no event does “Use” include selling, licensing, or distributing CTL Information' and requires protecting it 'from access by unauthorized third parties or the public' (https://www.huduser.gov/portal/usps/sublicense_agreement.html).

types.name: Side-lot program (vacant lots sold to next-door owners)
types.trigger: pop2020 < pop2010 AND housing units fell 2010-2020 (Decennial H1_001N). A fall in units signals demolitions that left vacant lots; this is my inference. Also require owner-occupied homes nearby (ACS B25003_002E share of occupied units, e.g. >= 30%; my proposal), because side lots go to the occupied home next door. Where a local assessor or land-bank parcel file exists, count publicly held vacant residential lots that share a side or rear line with an owner-occupied parcel.
types.trigger_data: (1) 2010 and 2020 Census P.L. 94-171 P1 and H1 by block group, with the 2020-to-2010 block group relationship file https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel2020/blkgrp/tab20_blkgrp20_blkgrp10_natl.txt (public). (2) ACS 2020-2024 5-year B25003 Tenure by block group (table-based summary file, released Jan 2026; public, API key needed). (3) No national public dataset of vacant residential parcels exists; parcel aggregators are proprietary. HUD notes that 'In distressed areas, a reduction in total AMS addresses from quarter-to-quarter appears to be a strong indicator of where demolition is occurring.' (https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/usps.html). However, those tract-level USPS data are restricted to registered government and nonprofit users and cannot be redistributed.
types.effect: Home values: no gain measured. For Detroit Land Bank Side Lot sales in 2011-2020, values near the lots were lower before the sale, and the abstract reports no significant post-sale effect (Lee, Chung & Park 2025). Safety: under Chicago's Large Lots program ($1 lots sold to same-block owners), block-level crime fell 3.5% one year after sales overall and 6.8% when the buyer lived in the neighborhood (block-level difference-in-differences).
types.effect_quote: Overall, sales reduce block-level crime rates by 3.5%, but sales to neighborhood residents decrease crime rates by 6.8%.
types.effect_source: Stern, M. and Lester, T.W. (2021). Does Local Ownership of Vacant Land Reduce Crime? An Assessment of Chicago's Large Lots Program. Journal of the American Planning Association 87(1):73-84, doi:10.1080/01944363.2020.1792334. Abstract read on IDEAS/RePEc; the publisher page returned 403.
types.cost: $100 per lot paid by the adjacent owner (Detroit Land Bank Authority Side Lots, current price in 2026). Related DLBA prices: Neighborhood Lots within 500 ft $250, oversize lots $200. Chicago Large Lots sold for $1 per lot (2014 onward). The public administrative cost per transfer was not found.
types.cost_quote: Side Lots are vacant lots adjacent to the applicant’s occupied property on the left side, right side, rear or diagonally behind (even across an alley, but not across the street). Side Lots will be sold for $100.
types.notes: Mapping-step type. Chicago price, from the same JAPA abstract: 'To address these problems, the City of Chicago (IL) has sold more than 1,200 vacant city-owned parcels in distressed communities for $1 through its Large Lots Program since 2014.' Detroit home values (Lee, Chung & Park 2025, Cities 165:106112, abstract only): 'In the Side Lot program, a markedly lower housing values in the pre-intervention were observed, and the Own-It-Now program did not yield statistically significant effects.' Mechanism evidence from Allegheny County, PA, 2012-2014 (Tri-COG Collaborative of councils of governments, hedonic model, lots within 500 ft of a sale; https://tricoglandbank.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/11/Effects-of-Vacant-Land.pdf). For lots current on taxes: 'On average across Allegheny County, stable vacant lots are estimated to increase surrounding home values by 1.6%'. For chronically tax-delinquent lots: 'On average across Allegheny County, blighted vacant lots are estimated to decrease surrounding home values by 6.0%.' This suggests the value comes from turning neglected lots into maintained ones. DLBA rule: 'Side Lots will be made available exclusively to adjacent neighbors for 180 days.'

types.name: Strategic demolition of vacant, unsalvageable homes
types.trigger: pop2020 < pop2010 AND other_vacant_share (B25004_008E / B25001_001E) >= 0.10; the strong case is >= 0.20, which covers 3.7% of US block groups (own tabulation, ACS 2020-2024). Also require ACS B25077 median value at the bottom of the metro range, so that land value does not cover acquisition plus demolition. Prefer moderate over extreme blight: in Detroit, value gains appeared only where blight was low before demolition, and firearm-assault reductions were larger with 6-12 demolitions per block group than with 13 or more.
types.trigger_data: (1) ACS 2020-2024 5-year B25004, B25001 and B25077 by block group (www2.census.gov table-based summary files dated Jan 2026; Census API needs a key; public). (2) 2010 and 2020 P.L. 94-171 P1 and H1 by block group, with the relationship file https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel2020/blkgrp/tab20_blkgrp20_blkgrp10_natl.txt. (3) HUD-USPS vacancy durations by tract, quarterly (https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/usps.html). HUD defines vacant addresses as those 'identified as being vacant (not collecting their mail) for 90 days or longer'. These data are restricted to registered governmental and nonprofit users and the sublicense bars distribution, so use them internally at most.
types.effect: Cleveland (Cuyahoga Land Bank, sales 2009-2013): demolishing a distressed house cuts its drag on homes within 500 ft from -5.2% to -2.4%, a gain of 2.8 percentage points. That gap is not statistically significant in the preferred model (p=0.18); other models give 1.4 to 4.1 points. Detroit (Hardest Hit Fund demolition program from 2014, sales 2009-2019): no average effect on prices, and a modest positive effect only where blight was low beforehand (Alvayay Torrejón et al. 2023). Lee et al. (2025) found 'consistently lower values near Demolition sites'. Safety: Detroit block groups with more than 5 demolitions had 11% fewer firearm assaults (95% CI 7-15%) (Jay et al. 2019).
types.effect_quote: By demolishing a distressed property the Land Bank reduces its impact 2.8 percentage points from 5.2 to 2.4. The tract fixed effect model suggests no value is recovered by acquisition and 1.4 percentage points is recovered by demolition.
types.effect_source: Whitaker, S. and Fitzpatrick IV, T.J. (2014). Land Bank 2.0: An Empirical Evaluation. Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland WP 12-30R; Journal of Regional Science 56(1):156-175 (2016).
types.cost: $14,100 to $17,643 per house (Michigan, demolitions funded by the TARP Hardest Hit Fund). The average rose from $9,266 to $17,643 per house in under three years up to mid-2016, then fell to about $14,100 in the first half of FY2017. Detroit averaged $17,622 at the June 2016 audit. Ohio rose from $9,293 to $15,019 per house. Detroit's whole program demolished over 20,800 properties for over $250 million, about $12,000 each (derived).
types.cost_quote: In Michigan, which accounts for nearly half of all committed TARP dollars, the average cost of demolition paid with TARP dollars increased by 90% in less than three years from $9,266 per house to $17,643. In Ohio, the average cost of demolitions charged to TARP increased 62% over 2 ½ years (from $9,293 per house to $15,019).
types.notes: Mapping-step type; overlaps the existing blight_rehab type ('Rehab or replace blighted homes'). Detroit, the program named in the ask: Alvayay Torrejón, Paredes & Skidmore (2023), Journal of Regional Science 63(5):1073-1099 (abstract at https://econpapers.repec.org/article/blajregsc/v_3a63_3ay_3a2023_3ai_3a5_3ap_3a1073-1099.htm): 'On average, blight removal through the demolition program does not appear to have been capitalized into the residential property prices. However, when considering the effect of ex‐ante program property characteristics, we find a modest positive effect of demolitions on property prices in areas with a low level of blight before the demolitions.' The same abstract says the program 'has demolished more than 20,800 properties at the cost of over $250 million'. Paredes & Skidmore (2016 working paper; Regional Science and Urban Economics 66:16-27, 2017), https://ideas.repec.org/p/cat/dtecon/dt201607.html: 'Using efficiency as the criteria for justifying spending public funds on demolition, average property values would have to increase by a factor of five to justify the demolition program.' Safety: Jay et al. (2019), J Behav Med 42(4):626-634, PMID 31367928 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31367928/): 'Receiving over 5 demolitions was associated with a 11% reduction in firearm assaults, relative to comparable control locations, 95% CI [7%, 15%], p = 0.01.' It found no effect on drug crime and no displacement. Cleveland: 'The difference between the coefficients (2.8) does not reach statistical significance (p=0.18).' SIGTARP footnote: post-audit Michigan average '($17,643 less $14,100)' for 1,020 houses in FY2017 Q1-Q2. The Cuyahoga Land Bank's own figure of $148,000 in neighbor value gained per demolition is not peer reviewed. The detroitmi.gov Prop N cost documents could not be reached.

types.name: Urban farm or forest on assembled vacant land
types.trigger: pop2020 < pop2010 AND enough cleared land in the block group or an adjacent one to assemble at least 0.5 acre for a farm or 10,000 sq ft for a forest patch (Baltimore and USDA Forest Service siting criteria). Nationwide proxy: housing units lost 2010-2020 (Decennial H1_001N) in the block group plus its neighbors, treating each lost unit as roughly one cleared lot (my inference; lot sizes vary), AND a high other_vacant_share. Confirm with local parcel or land-bank inventories.
types.trigger_data: (1) 2010 and 2020 Census P.L. 94-171 P1 and H1 by block group, with the relationship file https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel2020/blkgrp/tab20_blkgrp20_blkgrp10_natl.txt (public). (2) ACS 2020-2024 B25004 and B25001 by block group (Jan 2026). (3) There is no national open vacant-land or parcel dataset; local assessor files are needed to confirm that assemblable acreage exists.
types.effect: Home values: none measured for urban farms or planted forests on assembled vacant land; no study was found, and Detroit's Hantz Woodlands is unstudied. Safety, from Youngstown, OH, a shrinking city where 23,831 of 62,569 parcels were vacant in 2010: under the 'Lots of Green' program, vacant lots converted to community reuse (mostly community gardens and orchards) saw significant drops in felony assaults and burglaries compared with matched untreated lots. Motor-vehicle thefts rose. The nearest home-value analog is New York City community gardens, which raised neighboring values 'especially in the poorest neighborhoods' (Voicu & Been 2008); that evidence belongs to the existing community_garden type.
types.effect_quote: Regression models adjusted for spatial autocorrelation found the most consistent significant reductions in burglaries around stabilisation lots, and in assaults around community reuse lots. Spill-over crime reduction effects were found in contiguous areas around newly treated lots.
types.effect_source: Kondo, M., Hohl, B., Han, S., Branas, C. (2016). Effects of greening and community reuse of vacant lots on crime. Urban Studies 53(15):3279-3295 (author copy via USDA Forest Service Treesearch, PDF https://research.fs.usda.gov/download/treesearch/49785.pdf).
types.cost: About $60,000 per acre to set up a commercial urban farm on city-owned vacant land (derived). Strength to Love Farm, Sandtown-Winchester, Baltimore, broke ground June 2013: 1.5 acres, $90,000 in site costs covering site acquisition, preparation and permits, hoop houses and growing media, equipment, and utility hookups. Farming labor and operating costs are excluded.
types.cost_quote: The 1.5-acre site is being leased from HCD as part of “Homegrown Baltimore”, a program to increase healthy food access in the City, especially in neighborhoods lacking grocery stores. ... Site Costs = $90,000 ... Farming labor, insurance, production costs, tools, marketing, etc., not included.
types.notes: Mapping-step type. The cost source is USDA Forest Service NRS-INF-32-15 (Sept 2015), 'Green Pattern Book', written with the City of Baltimore and read from EPA's archived copy. Siting criteria from the same book: 'Sites for urban agriculture should be a minimum 1/2 acre lot (or collection of lots).' and 'Minimum size of 10,000 square feet for forest patches; smaller areas might be used for buffers'. Youngstown magnitudes for all greening treatments combined (GLS, authors' log-point reading): '85% reduction in felony assaults, 24% reduction in burglaries, 69% reduction in robberies, and 7% reduction in thefts, and 53% increase in motor vehicle thefts holding all other values constant.' Voicu & Been (2008), Real Estate Economics 36(2):241-283 (abstract at https://ideas.repec.org/a/bla/reesec/v36y2008i2p241-283.html): 'We find that gardens have significant positive effects, especially in the poorest neighborhoods. Higher‐quality gardens have the greatest positive impact.' I did not verify its magnitudes. Lighter tree and green-infrastructure lot treatments in Detroit (The Greening of Detroit, funded by DWSD, 2013, 10 lots, mostly volunteer labor; nonprofit document https://detroitfuturecity.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/Vacant-Land-Treatment-Program.pdf): 'The cost per lot is $2,500, with a total estimated cost of $25,000.' Tri-COG (Allegheny County) found green-infrastructure lots had 'a more positive effect than blighted vacant lots' but no conclusive estimate by submarket. Tiny forests and community gardens already exist as catalog types.

types.name: Replace lead water service lines
types.trigger: The block group falls inside the service area of a public water system (EPA boundaries, joined on PWSID) whose inventory under the Lead and Copper Rule Revisions reports lead or galvanized-requiring-replacement (GRR) service lines, or many lines of unknown material, in EPA's SDWIS Service Line Inventory. Rank by the system's lead-line count per service connection times the share of homes built before 1980 (ACS B25034). Not limited to shrinking cities, but lead lines cluster in older industrial cities.
types.trigger_data: (1) EPA SDWIS Federal Reporting Services, Service Line Inventory https://sdwis.epa.gov/ords/sfdw_pub/r/sfdw/sdwis_fed_reports_public/service-line-inventory: counts of lead, GRR, non-lead and unknown lines for each public water system, from state submissions; the filter lists quarters 2025Q1 through 2026Q3. Public EPA data. (2) EPA Public Water System Service Area Boundaries v3 (March 2026) https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/public-water-system-service-areas: over 44,000 community water systems covering about 99% of the population they serve, linked by PWSID. Mixes modeled and state-sourced boundaries; EPA 'disclaims responsibility for the spatial accuracy and attribution of these GIS features'. (3) ACS 2020-2024 B25034 Year Structure Built by block group (public).
types.effect: Rhode Island (Providence Water service area): replacing the public-side lead line raised home sale prices 7-8%, about $16,000-$19,000 on the $238,000 average sale. It also cut children's blood lead by about 0.4 µg/dL. Information alone had little effect: after DC Water published its lead-line map in 2016, prices of homes with and without lead lines did not diverge significantly (Jiang 2022).
types.effect_quote: Replacements significantly reduced child blood lead levels by about 0.4 µg/dL, increased property values by 7-8 percent, and increased the probability of moving among renters.
types.effect_source: Marcus, M. (2023). Burying the Lead: Effects of Public Lead Service Line Replacements on Blood Lead Levels and Property Values. Vanderbilt University and NBER working paper, NBER conference version dated July 22, 2023.
types.cost: $6,507 to $8,519 per full service line replacement, the 25th to 75th percentile of project costs in EPA's 7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey (DWINSA), national, 2022 dollars, as used in the final Lead and Copper Rule Improvements (LCRI). The full range across the 33 projects was $1,248 to $15,837. In Providence, the public side alone averaged $4,800 and the owner's side about $3,800 (Providence Water 2021, as cited by Marcus).
types.cost_quote: As described in chapter 4, section 4.2.2.2 of the final LCRI Economic Analysis (USEPA, 2024a), the EPA uses the 25th and 75th percentile values to provide a range of national costs for the final LCRI that reflect the degree of uncertainty in the average service line replacement unit cost ($6,507 and $8,519 for a full service line replacement).
types.notes: Not proposed by the mapping step; included because the group ask lists it (new key). Marcus's valuation: 'Using the average home sales price of $238,000, this suggests a valuation of about $16,000 to $19,000 per public-side LSLR, which is about three to four times as large as the average cost of a public-side replacement, $4,800 (Providence Water, 2021).' Most replacements were partial, since only 1-2 percent of owners also replaced their side. DC information shock, Jiang (2022) job-market paper (https://sites.asit.columbia.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/18/2022/09/JMP-1.pdf): 'neither a difference-in-differences model nor a repeat sales model captures a significant divergence between housing prices of the two types of properties after the release, implying the housing market response to the information was limited.' LCRI: 'Buildings and homes built before 1986 often have LSLs connecting their plumbing system to the main water supply line under the street.' ACS B25034 bins (1980-1989) straddle 1986, so use the pre-1980 share as the proxy. EPA's national estimate (Nov 2025 DWINSA fact sheet, https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2025-11/fact-sheet-2025-7th-dwinsa-update.pdf): 'With the latest data from 2025, EPA estimates that there are 4 million lead service lines across the country.'

types.name: Fix-It-First home repair grants for low-income owners (Philadelphia BSRP model)
types.trigger: Tract or block group with many low-income owner-occupants in old homes: HUD CHAS owner households at or below 50% (or 80%) of HUD area median family income (HAMFI) with at least one housing problem, an ACS B25035 median year built before about 1960, and a high owner share (B25003). Strongest fit in shrinking areas (pop2020 < pop2010) where owners cannot recoup repair costs through resale. Thresholds are my proposals.
types.trigger_data: (1) HUD CHAS (Comprehensive Housing Affordability Strategy) custom ACS tabulations, 2018-2022, released Dec 23, 2025, at tract and other summary levels; public download and query tool at https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/cp.html. (2) ACS 2020-2024 5-year B25035 (median year built), B25034 and B25003 by block group (www2.census.gov summary files, Jan 2026; public).
types.effect: Home values: none measured. Safety (Philadelphia, 2006-2013, 13,632 repaired homes on 6,732 block faces, compared with waitlisted blocks): each additional home on a block face that received a Basic Systems Repair Program (BSRP) repair was associated with 21.9% fewer total crimes, including assault -19.0%, robbery -22.6% and homicide -21.9%. The effect grew with the number of repaired homes on the block.
types.effect_quote: The main regression analysis demonstrated that the addition to a block face of a property that received a BSRP intervention was associated with a 21.9% decrease in the expected count of total crime (incidence rate ratio [IRR], 0.78; 95% CI, 0.76-0.80; P < .001), 19.0% decrease in assault (IRR, 0.81; 95% CI, 0.79-0.84; P < .001), 22.6% decrease in robbery (IRR, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.75-0.80; P < .001), and 21.9% decrease in homicide (IRR, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.71-0.86; P < .001).
types.effect_source: South, E.C., MacDonald, J., Reina, V. (2021). Association Between Structural Housing Repairs for Low-Income Homeowners and Neighborhood Crime. JAMA Network Open 4(7):e2117067.
types.cost: Up to $20,000 per home: the BSRP grant cap during the 2006-2013 study period, Philadelphia. Covers free electrical, plumbing, heating and roofing repairs, done by city contractors and run by the Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation (PHDC).
types.cost_quote: The BSRP intervention includes a grant of up to $20 000 provided to low-income owners for structural repairs to electrical, plumbing, heating, and roofing damage.
types.notes: Not proposed by the mapping step; included because the group ask lists Fix-It-First and BSRP (new key). It differs from the existing blight_rehab type, which rehabs vacant homes. Program facts from the paper: 'Operational since 1995, the BSRP is funded by the City of Philadelphia and run by the Philadelphia Housing Development Corporation'; 'The waiting time from enrollment to receipt of BSRP intervention has been 2 to 3 years.' Dose-response: 'A significant dose-dependent decrease in total crime was found such that the magnitude of association increased with higher numbers of homes participating in the BSRP on a block.' The current PHDC page (https://phdcphila.org/repair/basic-systems-repair-program/) says 'The Basic Systems Repair Program (BSRP) provides free repairs to correct electrical, plumbing, heating, limited structural and carpentry, and roofing emergencies in eligible owner-occupied homes in Philadelphia.' It lists a maximum household income of $122,700 for a family of 4 and states no grant cap. No evaluation was found of code enforcement paired with repair, or of home-repair grants' effect on home values.

types.name: Clean and green vacant lots (shrinking-city trigger for the existing type)
types.trigger: pop2020 < pop2010 AND other_vacant_share >= 0.10 (ACS) or, where parcel data exist, vacant land above about 3% of the area. In Philadelphia, a vacant-land share above 3% deepens the price penalty from vacancy, and greening there 'effectively eliminates this negative impact'; the city average was 5.8%.
types.trigger_data: (1) ACS 2020-2024 5-year B25004 and B25001 by block group (www2.census.gov summary files dated Jan 2026; API key needed; public). (2) 2010 and 2020 P.L. 94-171 P1 and H1 by block group with the 2020-to-2010 relationship file (public). (3) Local assessor parcel land use for vacant-land share; there is no national open dataset.
types.effect: Philadelphia LandCare (Pennsylvania Horticultural Society, PHS): homes within 1,000 ft of a greened lot gain about 4%, rising from 4.3% after year 1 to 13% after 6 years before tapering. The gain is 9% at the city-average 5.8% vacant-land share and peaks at 19% in high-vacancy neighborhoods. Safety, from a randomized trial of 541 Philadelphia lots over 38 months: in neighborhoods below the poverty line, crime fell 13.3%, gun violence 29.1%, burglary 21.9% and nuisances 30.3%.
types.effect_quote: Using data from a longstanding program in Philadelphia, we find that prices for houses within 1,000 feet of a greened vacant lot rise by about 4%, consistent with the literature, with the effect size increasing over time. Using the extensive data available in Philadelphia, we show how these effects vary by the attributes of the neighborhood in which they occur, with larger effects in areas with a high share of vacant land and higher-than-average median household incomes, with peak responses estimated at 19% and 15%, respectively.
types.effect_source: Lin, D., Jensen, S.T., Wachter, S. (2022). The Price Effects of Greening Vacant Lots: How Neighborhood Attributes Matter. Working paper dated June 15, 2022, presented at the 2023 AEA/ASSA meeting.
types.cost: About $5 per square meter (about $0.46 per sq ft) to clean and green a lot, plus about $0.50 per square meter per year to maintain it (Philadelphia, PHS treatment, as reported by Branas et al. 2018).
types.cost_quote: This intervention has been shown to be inexpensive and highly cost-effective (32), with initial costs averaging about $5 per square meter and maintenance averaging $0.50 per square meter thereafter (33).
types.notes: Existing catalog type (vacant_lot_green); added here for the shrinking-city trigger and newer evidence. From the same working paper: 'In our city-wide results, we find a positive and significant impact of vacant land conversion on the value of nearby properties (within 1,000 feet), with a 4.3% rise in value after the first year, and 13% after 6 years (which then attenuates).' And: 'we estimate a 9% greening effect evaluated at the 5.8% city average level of the vacant land share, with the effect peaking at 19% for high-vacancy neighborhoods.' Safety randomized trial, Branas et al. (2018), PNAS 115(12):2946-2951: 'Significant reductions in crime overall (−13.3%, P < 0.01), gun violence (−29.1%, P < 0.001), burglary (−21.9%, P < 0.001), and nuisances (−30.3%, P < 0.05) were also found after the treatment of vacant lots in neighborhoods below the poverty line.' In Youngstown (Kondo et al. 2016), stabilized lots showed the most consistent drop in burglaries. Heckert & Mennis's (2012) 5.6% estimate is cited by Lin et al.; I did not open the original, and the HUD Cityscape PDF link returned 404.

result.summary:
I researched 7 shrinking-city types: the 4 from the mapping step (land_bank, side_lot, blight_demolition, urban_farm), 2 new keys the group ask names (lead_service_line, home_repair_grant), and the existing vacant_lot_green. Every quote below was read in the primary source; derived figures are labeled as derived.

Home-value evidence:
- Strongest: vacant-lot greening in Philadelphia raises values about 4% within 1,000 ft, up to 19% in high-vacancy areas (Lin, Jensen & Wachter 2022). Public-side lead-line replacement in Providence raised values 7-8% (Marcus 2023).
- Land banks (Cleveland Fed WP 12-30R / Journal of Regional Science 2016): a distressed property's 5.2% discount on homes within 500 ft falls to 4.4% once the land bank owns it, and to 2.4% after demolition. The demolition gain of 2.8 points is not statistically significant in the preferred model (p=0.18).
- Detroit demolition: no average price effect, and modest gains only where blight was low (Journal of Regional Science 2023). Lower values near demolition sites (Cities 2025). But 11% fewer firearm assaults in block groups with more than 5 demolitions (J Behav Med 2019).
- Side lots: no home-value gain measured in Detroit. In Chicago, block crime fell 3.5%, and 6.8% when the buyer was local (JAPA 2021).
- Urban farms and forests: no home-value study exists. Youngstown community-reuse lots cut assaults and burglaries.
- Philadelphia BSRP home repair: 21.9% less crime per repaired home on a block; no home-value study.

Unit costs:
- Land bank: about $23,600 per property handled (Cuyahoga, 2009-2024, derived).
- Side lots: $100 per lot (Detroit) and $1 per lot (Chicago).
- Demolition: $14,100-$17,643 per house (Michigan, TARP-funded, SIGTARP 2017); about $12,000 per property for Detroit's whole program (derived).
- Urban farm: about $60,000 per acre (Baltimore, derived from $90,000 for 1.5 acres).
- Lead line: $6,507-$8,519 per full replacement (EPA, 2022 dollars).
- BSRP: up to $20,000 per home.
- Greening: about $5 per square meter, plus $0.50 per square meter per year.

Trigger data:
- ACS 2020-2024 B25004 'Other vacant' and B25001 are published at block group (summary file dated Jan 2026). The Census API now requires a key.
- 2010 and 2020 Decennial P1 and H1, with the 2020-to-2010 block group relationship file.
- EPA SDWIS Service Line Inventory (per water system, quarters through 2026Q3), joined to EPA water-system service areas v3 (March 2026).
- HUD CHAS 2018-2022 (released Dec 2025).
- The Center for Community Progress land bank map (May 2026; 20 states plus Puerto Rico have enabling laws) is marked all rights reserved.

Key caveats:
- HUD-USPS vacancy data go only to registered government and nonprofit users. The sublicense forbids distributing them or letting the public access them, so they cannot be a public map layer.
- A 5% 'other vacant' cut flags 30.2% of US block groups with 50+ homes (my tabulation); 10% flags 14.7% and 20% flags 3.7%. Combine it with population loss.
- 'Other vacant' includes homes held for personal reasons, so it overstates abandonment.
- There is no national open vacant-parcel dataset, so side-lot and urban-farm triggers rely on proxies such as housing-unit loss.

Working files are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/sc/dl. The other-vacant tabulation script is /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/sc/scripts/ov_share.py.
open_questions: detroitmi.gov could not be reached: curl got a Cloudflare 403, and WebFetch says the host is outside this session's allowed network domains. Not verified as a result: the Detroit Demolition Dept FY24 budget response (a search snippet says the average Prop N demolition cost $23,481.29), the 2019 Detroit Auditor General figures ($17,198 per demolition, or $27,750 with soft costs), and the DLBA Vacant Land Policy (2020). The domain must be allowed in the session's network settings to check them.

Publisher pages returned 403 (Taylor & Francis, Wiley, ScienceDirect), so only abstracts were read for Stern & Lester 2021 (JAPA), Alvayay Torrejón et al. 2023 (JRS), Lee, Chung & Park 2025 (Cities) and Paredes & Skidmore 2017 (RSUE). Magnitudes for Detroit side lots and demolitions beyond those abstracts were not extracted.

HUD-USPS vacancy data: whether City Pretty's operator qualifies as a registered government or nonprofit user, and whether derived tract flags with no address detail may be shown publicly, needs HUD's confirmation (USPSVacancydata@hud.gov). As read, the sublicense bars distribution and public access.

No nationwide public dataset of vacant residential parcels was found, so the side_lot and urban_farm triggers rely on proxies (2010-2020 housing-unit loss). Assessor or parcel aggregator data are local or proprietary.

No home-value evaluation was found for urban farms or planted forests (Hantz Woodlands, the Cleveland Botanical Garden/Oberlin 2014 hedonic pilot), for home-repair grants or BSRP, or for code enforcement paired with repair. The 2006 Flint Side Lot Transfer evaluation (University of Michigan Deep Blue) could not be downloaded because the page is JavaScript-only.

Marcus (2023) 'Burying the Lead' publication status is unconfirmed (the NBER conference version was used). The Pitt UCSUR 2018 Pittsburgh lead-laterals study (reported as about 5% lower prices) returned 404 and was not verified.
Voicu & Been (2008) community-garden magnitudes were not checked (abstract only), nor was the Heckert & Mennis (2012) 5.6% estimate (cited secondhand; HUD Cityscape link 404).
The public administrative cost per side-lot transfer (staff, title, recording) was not found for Detroit, Chicago or Cleveland.
Not checked: whether EPA revised the LCRI or its compliance dates after October 2024.
Not computed: how many block groups pass both population loss 2010-2020 and other-vacant at 10% or more. This needs the P.L. 94-171 block-group files and the relationship-file allocation.

checks.item: land_bank effect_url: Whitaker & Fitzpatrick, Land Bank 2.0, Cleveland Fed WP 12-30R (Sept 2014)
checks.corrected: Replace 'home sales 2009-2013' with 'single-family home sales January 2010 - March 2013 (44,375 sales, 39 months)'. Source text: 'Out of the 44,375 sales between January 2010 and March 2013'. In effect_quote, put '...' between the two sentences.
checks.note: PDF read. Every effect number is verbatim. The abstract gives 5.2%, 4.4% once the land bank takes possession, 2.4% for a land-bank demolition lot, $3.8 million for sold homes and about $156 million for homes that did not sell. p.3 says 'While the differences are not always statistically significant' and gives the '39-month study period'. The only wrong detail is the sales window: the data run from January 2010 to March 2013, and 2009 is the year the land bank was created. The quote joins an abstract sentence and a p.19 sentence without an ellipsis; both sentences are verbatim. The notes' cost line ('$4.45 million in 2010 ... $17.7 million in 2013') is verbatim, and $47.35M / 3,405 = $13,906 checks out. Side note: IDEAS lists the JRS 2016 article (56(1):156-175), but the abstract shown there is 'borrowed from another version', the Nov 2012 WP 12-30. That version reported a 3-5% discount, +5% near land-bank-owned homes and +9% near demolitions, none significant. The journal version's own numbers are therefore unconfirmed.

checks.item: land_bank cost_url: Cuyahoga Land Bank 15-Year Economic Impact Analysis (Oct 2024)
checks.corrected: Wording only: the report says the $330 million went to 'demolitions, renovations, new constructions, and other activities' and does not name acquisition. Use '(demolition, renovation, new construction and other activities)' instead of '(acquisition, demolition, ...)'.
checks.note: PDF read. Dated October 2024; 'All report information is accurate through May 31, 2024'. The land bank published it, with co-authors Ryan Sutter and Steve Weitzner. Both quoted passages are verbatim: '$330 million' (p.12) and 'transacted over 14,000 properties' (tribute, p.3). Derived: $330M / 14,000 = $23,571, so 'about $23,600' is correct arithmetic, and it is an upper bound because the count is 'over' 14,000. The notes quote '$148,000 ... BCR 9.74' (p.8) is verbatim. The report also gives 'nearly 10,000' demolitions, 2,600+ renovations and about 250 new homes.

checks.item: side_lot effect_url: Stern & Lester 2021, JAPA 87(1):73-84, IDEAS abstract
checks.corrected: Home values: no post-sale gain reported. For Detroit Land Bank Side Lot sales in 2011-2020, values near the lots were markedly lower before the sale; the abstract gives no post-sale result for Side Lots, and its 'did not yield statistically significant effects' is about Own-It-Now (Lee, Chung & Park 2025). Safety: under Chicago's Large Lots program ($1 lots sold to same-block owners), block-level crime fell 3.5% after sales overall and 6.8% when the buyer lived in the neighborhood (block-level difference-in-differences).
checks.note: Abstract read on IDEAS; the quote is verbatim. These details are all there: $1, 'more than 1,200' parcels, 'since 2014', 'Program buyers must be same-block landowners', 'block-level difference-in-differences', and same-neighborhood buyers bought 69% of parcels. Not in the abstract: any 'one year after sales' timing. The Detroit half of the stated effect misreads the Lee et al. abstract (see the XJTLU item).

checks.item: side_lot cost_url: Detroit Land Bank Authority Side Lots page
checks.note: Page read (footer © 2026). 'Side Lots will be sold for $100.' and the adjacency definition are verbatim. The menu says 'Find available vacant lots within 500 feet of your home for $250' (Neighborhood Lots). The page also says 'Oversize Lots are priced at $200 and Accessory Structures are priced at $250', and the 180-day exclusivity sentence is verbatim. The program has been 'offered by the DLBA since 2014'. The Chicago $1 price is from the JAPA abstract (checked). No administrative cost per transfer is given, which matches the claim.

checks.item: blight_demolition effect_url: Cleveland Fed WP 12-30R (Cleveland part of the effect)
checks.corrected: Replace 'Cleveland (Cuyahoga Land Bank, sales 2009-2013)' with 'Cleveland (Cuyahoga Land Bank, single-family sales January 2010 - March 2013)'. Source text: 'Out of the 44,375 sales between January 2010 and March 2013'.
checks.note: The quote is verbatim and contiguous (pp.18-19). Also verbatim: 'The difference between the coefficients (2.8) does not reach statistical significance (p=0.18)', and 'The difference between soon-to-be treated properties and land bank demolitions ranges from 1.4 to 4.1 percentage points', which supports the 1.4-4.1 range. Only the sales window is wrong. The Detroit parts of the effect come from other pages: Alvayay Torrejon 2023 (EconPapers), Lee et al. 2025 (XJTLU) and Jay et al. 2019 (PubMed record). All three are checked below and supported.

checks.item: blight_demolition cost_url: SIGTARP Quarterly Report to Congress, Apr 26 2017, Section 3 (blight demolition costs)
checks.note: PDF read. The quote is verbatim except for the footnote marker '4' after $17,643. Footnote ii: 'average cost per house savings of $3,543 ($17,643 less $14,100) for each of 1,020 houses demolished in the first and second quarter of fiscal year 2017'. The text says 'The average cost of TARP-funded demolition in Detroit at the time of SIGTARP's June 2016 audit was $17,622'. Detroit's quarterly chart rises from $11,515 to a $18,118 peak and falls to $13,516. The rises check out: 9,266 x 1.90 is about 17,643, and Ohio 15,019 / 9,293 = +62%. The derived Detroit whole-program figure, $250M / 20,800 = $12,019, uses the EconPapers abstract (checked).

checks.item: urban_farm effect_url: Kondo et al. 2016, Urban Studies, USDA Treesearch 49785 landing page
checks.note: The landing page has the full abstract (quote verbatim), marks the paper 'Formally Refereed' (Urban Studies 53(15):3279-3295), and links the PDF. The abstract supports these points: Lots of Green began in 2010; a difference-in-differences design against 'randomly selected and matched, untreated vacant lot controls'; community reuse 'mostly involving community gardens'; fewer assaults around community-reuse lots; and 'Significant increases in motor vehicle thefts around both types of lots'. The community-reuse burglary drop and '23,831 of 62,569 parcels' are in the linked PDF, checked as a separate item. The safety evidence comes from community-reuse lots (mostly gardens) used as an analog for farms, and the effect text says so.

checks.item: urban_farm cost_url: USDA Forest Service Green Pattern Book NRS-INF-32-15 (EPA archived copy)
checks.note: PDF read (NRS-INF-32-15, September 2015). Strength to Love Farm is on the 1800 block of Lorman Street, Sandtown-Winchester, and broke ground in June 2013. It is a 1.5-acre site leased from HCD under Homegrown Baltimore. 'Site Costs = $90,000' covers site acquisition, prep and permits; hoop house construction and growing media; equipment and supplies; and electric, water and other connections. 'Farming labor, insurance, production costs, tools, marketing, etc., not included.' All three quoted parts are verbatim. Derived $90,000 / 1.5 acres = $60,000 per acre is correct. The siting quotes ('minimum 1/2 acre lot', '10,000 square feet for forest patches') are verbatim. Caveat: the farm 'will eventually consist of several crop squares', so $90,000 may cover only the first build-out.

checks.item: lead_service_line effect_url: Marcus, Burying the Lead (NBER conference version, July 22 2023)
checks.note: PDF read (dated July 22, 2023). The abstract quote is verbatim; the data are from Rhode Island and Providence Water. The paper says 'Using the average home sales price of $238,000 ... about $16,000 to $19,000 per public-side LSLR', with a public-side cost of $4,800. Owners' side 'about $3,800 on average'; 'only 1-2 percent' of owners replaced their private line. The DC information-shock sentence in the effect is from Jiang 2022 (checked separately, supported).

checks.item: lead_service_line cost_url: Federal Register, final LCRI, 89 FR 86418 (Oct 30 2024)
checks.note: Page read (FR Doc 2024-23549); the quote is verbatim on page 86570. Also there: the source is the '7th Drinking Water Infrastructure Needs Survey and Assessment', 'the full range of service line replacement unit costs considered in the DWINSA data set is $1,248 to $15,837', and EPA declined to use 'the minimum and maximum values, from the 33 DWINSA reported projects'. No dollar year is printed next to $6,507/$8,519, though the rule's cost tables are in 2022 USD. The Providence $4,800 and $3,800 figures come from Marcus (checked). The notes' pre-1986 LSL sentence is verbatim in this rule.

checks.item: home_repair_grant effect_url: South, MacDonald & Reina 2021, JAMA Netw Open 4(7):e2117067 (PMC)
checks.note: Page read; the quote is verbatim. The data run from January 1, 2006 to April 30, 2013, with '13 632 houses on 6732 block faces'. The dose-dependent decrease is stated verbatim (IRR 0.53 for 1 home, down to 0.34 for 4). Nuance: 21.9% comes from the main model across all city block faces. Restricting to blocks that ever received BSRP (after receipt vs. blocks still waiting) gave 25.4% (IRR 0.75). The paper's own design summary does describe the comparison as treated blocks vs. waiting-list blocks. The notes quotes (operational since 1995, PHDC, 2-3 year wait) are verbatim. No home-value outcome is reported, which matches the claim.

checks.item: home_repair_grant cost_url: same JAMA Netw Open article (PMC)
checks.note: The quote is verbatim (Key Points). Methods: 'The BSRP provides grants of up to $20 000 to low-income owners to fix structural emergencies', and 'A city contractor team completes the needed structural work'. The program is run by PHDC. The article states the $20,000 cap for the program as studied but does not date it. The paper cites a 2020 income limit of under $48,300 for a family of 4; the current PHDC page lists $122,700 and gives no cap.

checks.item: vacant_lot_green effect_url: Lin, Jensen & Wachter, Price Effects of Greening Vacant Lots (AEA 2023 paper link)
checks.note: The AEA link serves the PDF directly (dated June 15, 2022); the abstract quote is verbatim. Introduction p.3: '4.3% rise in value after the first year, and 13% after 6 years (which then attenuates)', and '9% greening effect evaluated at the 5.8% city average level of the vacant land share, with the effect peaking at 19% for high-vacancy neighborhoods'. The trigger's 'above 3%' and 'effectively eliminates this negative impact' are verbatim, and the program is Philadelphia LandCare run by PHS. The Heckert & Mennis 5.6% figure is cited here. The safety figures in this effect come from Branas et al. 2018 (the cost_url page) and match it exactly: 541 lots, 38 months, -13.3% crime, -29.1% gun violence, -21.9% burglary and -30.3% nuisances below the poverty line.

checks.item: vacant_lot_green cost_url: Branas et al. 2018, PNAS 115(12), eScholarship copy
checks.corrected: About $5 per square meter (about $0.46 per sq ft) to clean and green a lot, with maintenance 'averaging $0.50 per square meter thereafter' (Philadelphia; Branas et al. 2018, citing Bonham & Smith 2008). The paper gives no time unit for the maintenance figure, so drop 'per year' unless another source supports it.
checks.note: PDF read (CC BY-NC-ND copy); the quote is verbatim (it spans line breaks). The initial $5/m2 and the $0.46/ft2 conversion are correct. Nothing in the paper says the $0.50/m2 maintenance cost is per year, so 'per year' is unsupported. In the trial the treatment was done 'by teams of local landscape contractors'; the cost figures cite ref 33, Bonham & Smith 2008.

checks.item: side_lot effect (Detroit part): Lee, Chung & Park 2025, Cities 165:106112, XJTLU abstract
checks.corrected: For Detroit Land Bank Side Lot sales in 2011-2020: 'In the Side Lot program, a markedly lower housing values in the pre-intervention were observed' (Lee, Chung & Park 2025). The abstract reports no post-sale estimate for Side Lots.
checks.note: Abstract read (published 1 Oct 2025; adjusted interrupted time series difference-in-differences; Detroit 2011-2020; five programs). In the abstract, 'did not yield statistically significant effects' refers to the Own-It-Now program, not Side Lots. The claim that 'the abstract reports no significant post-sale effect' for Side Lots is a misreading. 'No gain measured' still holds only in the sense that no Side Lot gain is reported.

checks.item: blight_demolition effect (Detroit part): Lee, Chung & Park 2025, XJTLU abstract
checks.note: 'consistently lower values near Demolition sites' is verbatim and is described as a post-intervention trend in Detroit, 2011-2020.

checks.item: blight_demolition effect and cost (Detroit): Alvayay Torrejon, Paredes & Skidmore 2023, JRS 63(5):1073-1099, EconPapers abstract
checks.note: Abstract read. The Detroit Demolition Program, funded by the Hardest Hit Fund, 'began in 2014 and has demolished more than 20,800 properties at the cost of over $250 million'. The study uses 'housing sales price information from 2009 through 2019' and a repeat-sales design. The no-average-effect and low-blight sentences are verbatim. Derived $250M / 20,800 is about $12,000 per property, correct arithmetic (both inputs are stated as 'more than' and 'over').

checks.item: blight_demolition effect (safety): Jay et al. 2019, J Behav Med 42(4):626-634, PubMed 31367928
checks.note: The PubMed web page could not be read directly. curl got a 'Cookies must be enabled' interstitial (HTTP 203), and WebFetch cannot resolve the host in this session. I read the same record (PMID 31367928) through NCBI's E-utilities efetch API. The quote is verbatim: 11% fewer firearm assaults, 95% CI [7%, 15%], p = 0.01. Reductions were larger for 6-12 demolitions than for 13 or more, and 'No effects were observed for illegal drug violations and no evidence of spatial crime displacement was detected.' The program 'demolished over 10,000 buildings in its first 3 years'.

checks.item: urban_farm effect details: Kondo et al. 2016 full text (Treesearch PDF)
checks.note: PDF read. The 2010 Vacant Property Survey 'found that 23,831 of 62,569 parcels were vacant'. 'Community reuse treatment resulted in statistically significant reductions according to GLS models in felony assaults and burglaries (P < 0.01)'. For community reuse, 'motor vehicle thefts had statistically significant and positive direct and indirect effects'. Of the 77 reuse lots, 'most are community gardens, urban farms or orchards (47)'. Controls were caliper-matched. The notes' GLS magnitudes quote (85% / 24% / 69% / 7% / +53%) is verbatim and covers both treatments combined.

checks.item: urban_farm effect analog: Voicu & Been 2008, Real Estate Economics 36(2):241-283, IDEAS abstract
checks.note: Abstract read (New York City, difference-in-differences hedonic model); the quote is verbatim, including 'especially in the poorest neighborhoods'. The abstract gives no magnitude; Lin et al. 2022 cite a 3.6% price effect for this study.

checks.item: lead_service_line effect (DC information): Jiang 2022 job-market paper
checks.note: PDF read (October 2022). DC Water launched its online lead-line map on June 6, 2016, and the abstract quote ('neither a difference-in-differences model nor a repeat sales model ...') is verbatim. The paper also reports a marked rise in requests for lead tests after the release.

checks.item: land_bank notes / trigger: HUD-USPS sublicense agreement
checks.note: Both clauses are verbatim. The sublicense also cites 39 U.S.C. § 412, which 'prohibits the public disclosure of address lists'. This supports the claim that the data cannot back a public layer.

checks.item: side_lot and blight_demolition trigger_data: HUD USPS vacancy data page
checks.note: Three passages are verbatim: the '90 days or longer' vacancy definition, the sentence saying a quarter-to-quarter drop in AMS addresses indicates demolition, and the sentence limiting access to registered government and nonprofit users.

checks.item: land_bank trigger_data: Center for Community Progress National Land Bank Map
checks.note: Verbatim: 'The data in this map has been updated as of May 2026', and 'As of June 2026, the following 20 states and Puerto Rico have passed state-enabling land bank legislation' (Washington 2026 is the latest). The footer reads '© 2026 All Rights Reserved'.

checks.item: land_bank notes: 2022 ACS Subject Definitions ('Other vacant')
checks.note: The definition 'Other Vacant - If a vacant unit does not fall into any of the categories specified above, it is classified as Other vacant' is followed by the quoted text, verbatim. It confirms that 'Other vacant' is a residual category.

checks.item: side_lot notes: Tri-COG Collaborative, vacant lots and green infrastructure, Allegheny County 2012-2014
checks.note: PDF read. Hedonic model counting lots within 500 feet of a sale. 'Vacant Lot' means current on taxes and 'Delinquent Vacant Lot' means chronically tax delinquent, as the notes say. Pooled effects are +1.6% and -6.0% (verbatim). Green infrastructure has 'more positive effect than blighted vacant lots' (verbatim), with a 'lack of a conclusive trend' within submarkets.

checks.item: home_repair_grant notes: PHDC Basic Systems Repair Program page
checks.note: The quote is verbatim. The income table gives $122,700 for a family of 4, and no grant cap is stated, as the notes say.

checks.item: blight_demolition notes: Paredes & Skidmore working paper, IDEAS
checks.note: The 'factor of five' quote is verbatim (WP revised Nov 2016). IDEAS lists the other version: Regional Science and Urban Economics 66(C):16-27 (2017).

checks.item: urban_farm notes: Detroit Future City, Vacant Land Treatment Program sheet
checks.note: Ten vacant lots in Cody Rouge treated by The Greening of Detroit, funded by DWSD, starting January 2013. '$2,500' per lot and '$25,000' total are verbatim, and the sheet says 'much of the labor undertaken by citizen volunteers'.

checks.item: lead_service_line notes: EPA 2025 Update to the 7th DWINSA fact sheet
checks.note: Fact sheet dated November 2025; the '4 million lead service lines' sentence is verbatim.

not_checked: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-b25004.dat - trigger_data, left out by the 30-item cap. HEAD request only: HTTP 200, 35.3 MB, Last-Modified 29 Jan 2026, which matches 'file dated 29 Jan 2026'. The 242,297-row count was not checked.

https://www2.census.gov/geo/docs/maps-data/data/rel2020/blkgrp/tab20_blkgrp20_blkgrp10_natl.txt - trigger_data, left out by the 30-item cap. HEAD request only: HTTP 200, text/plain, 46.0 MB. Contents not checked.

https://sdwis.epa.gov/ords/sfdw_pub/r/sfdw/sdwis_fed_reports_public/service-line-inventory - trigger_data, left out by the 30-item cap. Quick read only: the page loads and its filter lists quarters 2025Q1 to 2026Q3. Counts not checked.

https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/public-water-system-service-areas - trigger_data, left out by the 30-item cap. Quick read: 'version 3' released March 2026, 'over 44,000 community water systems' covering 'roughly 99%' of the population they serve, and the disclaimer quote is verbatim.

The researcher's own block-group tabulations (other-vacant share of 5%/10%/20% flags 30.2%/14.7%/3.7% of block groups) are not from a cited page and were not recomputed.
