verify.summary:
I checked 30 items: all 14 effect_url and cost_url citations, plus 16 note URLs that back parts of the effect, cost and notes text. Every page was freshly downloaded and read. PubMed was the one exception: the page returned a cookie wall, so I read the same record through NCBI's E-utilities API. Every quote was found. 25 items support the claim as written and 5 do not.

The 5 that need fixing:
1. **land_bank effect and blight_demolition effect** (Cleveland Fed WP 12-30R): the sales window is wrong. The paper uses sales from January 2010 to March 2013 (44,375 sales, 39 months), not 2009-2013. All the effect numbers are verbatim: 5.2%, 4.4%, 2.4%, p=0.18, the 1.4-4.1 point range, $3.8M and $156M. The land_bank effect_quote also joins an abstract sentence and a p.19 sentence without an ellipsis.
2. **side_lot effect (Chicago abstract and Detroit abstract):**
   - Detroit: the Lee, Chung & Park abstract's 'did not yield statistically significant effects' is about the Own-It-Now program, not Side Lots. It reports only markedly lower values before Side Lot sales, so 'the abstract reports no significant post-sale effect' is a misreading.
   - Chicago: 'one year after sales' is not in the Stern & Lester abstract. The 3.5% and 6.8% figures are verbatim.
3. **vacant_lot_green cost** (Branas 2018): maintenance is given as '$0.50 per square meter thereafter' with no time unit, so 'per year' is unsupported. The initial $5 per square meter is correct.

Minor points:
- **land_bank cost:** it lists 'acquisition', but the report names 'demolitions, renovations, new constructions, and other activities'.
- **BSRP:** the 21.9% is from the main model over all city block faces. The comparison restricted to blocks still waiting for repairs gave 25.4%.
- **LCRI:** no dollar year is printed next to the unit costs, although the rule's tables are in 2022 USD.
- **Cleveland Fed paper:** IDEAS lists the 2016 Journal of Regional Science article, but the abstract shown there is borrowed from the 2012 working paper, which reported different estimates, none significant. The journal version's own numbers are unconfirmed.

Derived figures recomputed, all correct:
- $330M / 14,000 = $23,571
- $47.35M / 3,405 = $13,906
- $90,000 / 1.5 acres = $60,000 per acre
- $250M / 20,800 = $12,019
- $5 per square meter = $0.46 per square foot

Five trigger-data URLs fell outside the 30-item cap and are listed under not_checked with the results of a quick read or header check.

Working files: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/vshrink_1794287657. The dl/ folder has each page plus its extracted text; scripts/findq.py and the quotes*.json files hold the quote matcher and the quote lists.

types.name: Keep the rural hospital or emergency room open (operating support)
types.trigger: Block group in a nonmetro county (USDA ERS 2023 Rural-Urban Continuum Code 4-9) whose nearest hospital with an emergency department is the only one within a 30-minute drive. The hospital is a CMS Hospital General Information row with Emergency Services = Yes and type Critical Access, Acute Care or Rural Emergency Hospital. Drive time is computed on OpenStreetMap roads from the block group's population-weighted center. The case is strongest when it is the county's only hospital: the measured income and job losses happen only when the sole hospital closes.
types.trigger_data: CMS Provider Data Catalog, Hospital General Information (dataset xubh-q36u), https://data.cms.gov/provider-data/dataset/xubh-q36u. Covers every Medicare-registered hospital nationally, with address, county, hospital type and an Emergency Services yes/no field. Metadata modified 2026-07-22, released 2026-08-13. The current CSV has 5,419 rows: 1,382 Critical Access Hospitals, 43 Rural Emergency Hospitals, and 4,495 rows with emergency services. U.S. government data with access level 'public'; no license is named. There are no coordinates, so addresses must be geocoded. Nonmetro test: USDA ERS 2023 Rural-Urban Continuum Codes, https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/rural-urban-continuum-codes (county level; page updated 12/30/2025; based on the 2023 OMB metro delineation; free download).
types.effect: Home values: no price effect measured. Across 100+ rural hospital closures in 2005-2017, county housing markets did not change: HMDA mortgage originations, denials, purchases and average loan amounts all held steady. Health-care employment fell sharply and stayed down (Alexander & Richards 2023). Other measured effects: closing a county's only hospital cut per-capita income by $703 (1990 dollars), or 4%, and raised unemployment 1.6 percentage points. Closures where another hospital stayed open had no long-run effect (Holmes et al. 2006, 1990-2000 closures). In California, rural closures raised inpatient mortality for time-sensitive conditions by 0.78 points (8.7%); urban closures had no measurable effect (Gujral & Basu, NBER working paper 2019).
types.effect_quote: We find sharp and persistent reductions in employment, but these localize to health care occupations and are more impactful in areas experiencing complete closures. Aggregate consumer financial health and housing markets appear unaffected by the shuttering of a rural hospital.
types.effect_source: Diane Alexander and Michael R. Richards, 'Economic consequences of hospital closures,' Journal of Public Economics vol. 221 (2023). The same abstract was read on NBER Working Paper 29110 (July 2021, revised January 2023) and on the RePEc/IDEAS record of the journal article.
types.cost: $295,051.54 per month per Rural Emergency Hospital in calendar 2026, paid in 12 monthly installments: about $3.54 million a year (my multiplication). Every REH gets the same amount regardless of size. This is Medicare's extra facility payment when a struggling rural hospital becomes a 24/7 emergency-and-outpatient Rural Emergency Hospital, on top of payments for outpatient services. National, 2026; the CY 2025 amount was $285,625.90.
types.cost_quote: You get additional facility payments in 12 monthly installments. [...] The CY 2026 REH facility monthly payment amount is $295,051.54 with the sequestration amount deducted.
types.notes: Cost source: CMS MLN Fact Sheet MLN2259384 (December 2025), which also says 'The additional monthly facility payment for every REH is the same.' The REH payment prices a 24-hour ER without inpatient beds. Keeping full inpatient service relies on Critical Access Hospital cost-based Medicare payment plus local support, which this research did not price. Holmes, Slifkin, Randolph & Poley, Health Services Research 41(2):467-485 (2006), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1702512/: 'Results indicate that the closure of the sole hospital in the community reduces per-capita income by $703 (p<0.05) or 4 percent (p<0.05) and increases the unemployment rate by 1.6 percentage points (p<0.01).' Gujral & Basu, NBER Working Paper 26182, https://www.nber.org/papers/w26182: 'However, estimating differential impacts shows that rural closures increase inpatient mortality by 0.78% points (an increase of 8.7%), whereas urban closures have no measurable impact.' Alexander & Richards measure housing-market activity (HMDA loan counts and loan sizes), not sale prices. Pharmacy closures were not researched. Grocery is split out as rural_grocery.

types.name: New or upgraded fire and EMS station (incl. volunteer department support)
types.trigger: Homes more than 5 road miles from the nearest fire station, the ISO Public Protection Classification line beyond which property is rated Class 10. Distance is measured over OpenStreetMap roads from station points. Also flag block groups whose nearest department is all-volunteer (USFA Dept Type = Volunteer). The USFA registry has no service-area boundaries, so coverage has to be approximated from station or headquarters locations.
types.trigger_data: U.S. Fire Administration National Fire Department Registry, https://apps.usfa.fema.gov/registry/download. Two CSVs: (1) a national list, which per the page includes all 50 states and U.S. territories; the file downloaded 10 Nov 2026 has 27,117 departments with headquarters address, county, number of stations and Dept Type (18,952 Volunteer, 4,166 Mostly volunteer, 2,606 Career, 1,393 Mostly career); (2) a station list with station addresses for departments that supplied them. Registration is voluntary and the lists are continuously updated. Federal public data; no license is stated. Addresses must be geocoded. Station points can be filled in from OpenStreetMap amenity=fire_station (ODbL 1.0, https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright).
types.effect: Home values: house values fell at least 6.7% in the year after a community voted to cut fire protection funding. The study is a regression discontinuity comparing fire districts that barely passed or barely failed a fire levy renewal. Cuts larger than the median 18.8% funding drop brought bigger price drops, and the drop did not persist (Brasington & Parent 2024). Insurance: the Texas Department of Insurance says any building more than five road miles from a fire station gets a PPC score of 10, and that premiums generally fall when a community's PPC score improves. It gives no dollar amount.
types.effect_quote: House values drop at least 6.7 % the year after a community votes to cut fire protection funding, which is a quarter of a standard deviation of sale price and larger than the capitalization of crime, school quality, or environmental quality. Tax levies representing more than the median 18.8 % funding drop elicit a larger drop in house prices.
types.effect_source: David M. Brasington and Olivier Parent, 'Fire protection services and house prices: A regression discontinuity investigation,' Regional Science and Urban Economics vol. 105 (2024), article 103984. Abstract read on its RePEc/IDEAS record.
types.cost: About $1.74 million per fire station project (my division). FEMA's 2009 Recovery Act fire station construction grants paid to modify, upgrade or build non-federal stations, with no local cost share. As of 1 Oct 2010 they totaled $207.461 million across 119 awards. National figure in 2009-2010 dollars, not inflation-adjusted, and it mixes new stations with upgrades.
types.cost_quote: As of October 1, 2010, 119 SCG grants were awarded, totaling $207.461 million to fire departments within the United States.
types.notes: Cost source: Congressional Research Service report RL32341, 'Assistance to Firefighters Program: Distribution of Fire Grant Funding' (3 Jan 2011), read on the EveryCRSReport copy. It also says 'There is no cost share requirement for SCG grants' and that the Recovery Act 'provided an additional $210 million in firefighter assistance grants for modifying, upgrading, or constructing state and local non-federal fire stations', with a $15 million cap per grant. The figure is old. A current local bid or a USDA Rural Development Community Facilities award would be better, but rd.usda.gov refused automated access. Trigger rule source: Texas Department of Insurance PPC FAQ, https://tdi.texas.gov/Fire/fmppcfaq.html: 'Any building more than five road miles from a fire station or outside the boundary of a city or volunteer fire department service area has a PPC score of 10.' and 'If a community’s PPC score improves, insurance premiums will generally decrease.' The Brasington & Parent abstract does not name the state and does not say the districts are rural. It measures the price effect of losing fire funding, not of building a new station.

types.name: Trailheads, river access and campgrounds
types.trigger: Rural block group (outside 2020 Census urban areas) within 10 miles of open-access public land (PAD-US Public Access = Open Access) or a river or lake (OpenStreetMap waterway=river or natural=water), with no trailhead (highway=trailhead), boat launch (leisure=slipway) or campground (tourism=camp_site) mapped within that distance.
types.trigger_data: USGS Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US) 4.1, https://doi.org/10.5066/P96WBCHS. Released March 2025, the most recent version per the USGS PAD-US data-history page. National, with public-access, manager and designation fields. The service metadata carries a liability disclaimer and advises using agency data for single-agency questions. Rural/urban split: 2020 Census urban areas, https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/guidance/geo-areas/urban-rural.html (TIGER/Line, public). An urban area needs at least 2,000 housing units or 5,000 people; everything else is rural. Rivers, lakes and existing facilities: OpenStreetMap, ODbL 1.0 (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright).
types.effect: Home values: a review of 20 hedonic studies found that homes near trails typically sold for 3% to 5% more than comparable homes. The rural premium is probably smaller: in opinion surveys, only 16% of 1,212 residents along 10 rural trails thought the trail raised their property's value, against 47% along 22 urban trails; 6% overall thought it lowered values (Crompton & Nicholls 2019). County level: in 2000, rural recreation counties had median rents of $474, 23% above the $384 in other nonmetro counties, and median household income 10% higher (USDA ERS 2005).
types.effect_quote: Twenty hedonic analyses were identified and their results showed that proximity to a trail resulted in home prices that typically were between 3% and 5% higher than those of comparable homes in the area.
types.effect_source: John L. Crompton and Sarah Nicholls, 'The Impact of Greenways and Trails on Proximate Property Values: An Updated Review,' Journal of Park and Recreation Administration 37(3): 89-109 (2019). Abstract read on the journal page.
types.cost: Rural trailhead: a $406,822.79 federal Recreational Trails Program (RTP) award for the Town of Haysi, VA Riverfront Trailhead, a motorized trailhead with parking, ADA work, amenities and signage (grant started 9/15/2020, completed 1/29/2025). Smaller 2025 awards in the same report: $160,000 for a James River Water Trail boat ramp (Botetourt County, VA) and $96,000 for trailhead improvements (Town of Narrows, VA). RTP pays at most 80% of eligible costs, so total project cost is at least 25% above the award. Virginia, 2020-2025 dollars.
types.cost_quote: 331M190 Town of Haysi Riverfront Trailhead $406,822.79 9/15/2020 1/29/2025 [...] Scope: Construction of motorized trailhead including parking, ADA enhancements, trail amenities, and signage.
types.notes: Cost source: Virginia DCR, Recreational Trails Program FY25 Annual Report. Table 3 lists completed projects. Table 4 lists 2025 awards, including 'Botetourt County James River Water Trail Last Lock Boat M^ $160,000.00 $160,000.00' (Ramp is on the next line). The report also states: 'The program reimburses up to 80% of eligible project costs up the award amount.' Rural survey sentence from the same abstract: 'However, while 47% of the 2,647 respondents living close to one of the 22 urban trails believed it increased their property’s value, this was believed by only 16% of the 1,212 who resided proximate to one of 10 rural trails.' USDA ERS, Reeder & Brown, 'Recreation, Tourism, and Rural Well-Being,' ERR-7 (August 2005), https://ageconsearch.umn.edu/record/7220/files/er050007.pdf: 'According to Census data in 2000, median monthly rents for housing averaged $474 in recreation counties, 23 percent higher than the $384 median rent in other nonmetro counties (fig. 4).' These county results describe whole recreation economies, not the effect of one trailhead. No rural-specific hedonic estimate was found, and no primary-source cost per campsite.

types.name: Pave gravel roads
types.trigger: Public roads that front homes, tagged in OpenStreetMap as highway=residential, unclassified, tertiary or service (access not private) with surface=unpaved, gravel, dirt, ground or compacted, and with buildings or addresses alongside. Prioritize segments carrying about 200 or more vehicles a day (state or county traffic counts): Minnesota data show gravel upkeep costs jump at that level.
types.trigger_data: OpenStreetMap road network and surface tags (planet file or Geofabrik state extracts), https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright. National, continuously updated, ODbL 1.0 (share-alike, attribution required). Surface is missing on many rural roads, so untagged county and township roads should show as 'surface unknown', not paved.
types.effect: Home values: no U.S. estimate found. In Acayucan, Mexico, first-time paving of residential streets in outlying neighborhoods was assigned at random. Within two years, property values rose 17% by professional appraisal (land value +72%) and 28% by homeowners' own valuations. The gain built into property values was about as large as the construction cost (Gonzalez-Navarro & Quintana-Domeque 2016). Costs: in Minnesota county data, gravel road maintenance costs rise significantly at about 200 vehicles a day, which the state DOT summary offers as a possible paving threshold (MnDOT/LRRB 2006).
types.effect_quote: Using professional appraisals, we find that plots increased in value by 0.54 log points (or 72%), representing a 17% increase in property values (the sum of land and structure). According to homeowner valuations, we estimate an effect of street pavement on property values of 28%.
types.effect_source: Marco Gonzalez-Navarro and Climent Quintana-Domeque, 'Paving Streets for the Poor: Experimental Analysis of Infrastructure Effects,' Review of Economics and Statistics 98(2): 254-267 (2016). Quote taken from the authors' Oxford Department of Economics Discussion Paper 757 (September 2015).
types.cost: $600,000-$800,000 per mile to grade and pave a road, depending on terrain and the number of drainage structures, versus about $2,000 a year to maintain a well-traveled gravel road (Washington County, Iowa road department; undated county web page, read November 2026).
types.cost_quote: It costs between $600,000 and $800,000 per mile to properly grade and pave a new road, depending upon the lay of the land and the number of drainage structures. Paving is an expensive alternative when a well traveled gravel road can be maintained for $ 2,000 per year.
types.notes: The effect quote drops a footnote marker after '(or 72%)'. The Mexico study covers streets in outlying urban neighborhoods, not U.S. rural roads. Its journal abstract adds: 'A cost-benefit analysis indicates that the valuation of street asphalting as capitalized into property values is about as large as construction costs.' Threshold source: MnDOT/Minnesota LRRB technical summary 'Making informed decisions on when to upgrade a gravel road' (October 2006), https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/17871: 'Note that at a traffic volume of 200 ADT, gravel road maintenance costs increase significantly.' Cheaper alternative, re-graveling: Washtenaw County (MI) Road Commission, https://www.wcroads.org/faq/unpaved-roads/: 'Applying gravel or limestone to help “lift” a road can cost between $55,000- $65,000 per mile.' The full 2005 LRRB report on mdl.mndot.gov refused automated access.

types.name: Extend public water and sewer to homes on wells and septic
types.trigger: Block groups where many households use private wells or septic, from USGS estimates of domestic-well households (2010 block groups) or from homes outside both EPA public water service areas and EPA sewersheds. Limit to homes within about a mile of an existing service-area boundary, where a line extension is plausible.
types.trigger_data: USGS, Johnson & Belitz (2019), 'Domestic well locations and populations served in the contiguous U.S.: datasets for decadal years 2000 and 2010,' https://doi.org/10.5066/P9FSLU3B (ScienceBase item 5b9fffe6e4b08583a5c2779e). Estimates are based on block groups, by block-group and road-enhanced methods; contiguous U.S. only; published 2019-06-12; USGS public data. USGS built them because 'The 1990 census was the last nationally consistent survey of a home’s source of water'. EPA Public Water System Service Areas, version 3 (March 2026), https://www.epa.gov/ground-water-and-drinking-water/public-water-system-service-areas: over 44,000 community water systems covering about 99% of the population they serve. Many boundaries are modeled, and EPA disclaims their spatial accuracy. EPA National Sewershed Dataset, https://www.epa.gov/cwns/sewersheds: nearly 17,000 publicly owned treatment works covering about 78% of the 2020 population. Built on H3 hexagons and not authoritative for individual properties.
types.effect: Home values: no study measures a water or sewer line extension itself. Closest: in Washington County, PA, across the public-water service boundary, groundwater risk from nearby shale-gas wells cut values of well-dependent homes by up to 24% relative to homes on piped water. This is from the NBER working paper (Muehlenbachs, Spiller & Timmins); the published AER 2015 version reports 'large negative impacts' for groundwater-dependent homes. For sewer the sign can flip: in Miami-Dade, 2002-2022, homes on septic sold at a 3.1% premium, credited to lower operating costs (Hardin, Lin & Thibodeau, 2024 draft). Health: North Carolina children in homes on private wells had 25% higher odds of elevated blood lead than children on regulated community water (Gibson et al. 2020). Connecting 10% of North Carolina's well users to community water would prevent an estimated 2,920 emergency visits a year for acute stomach and intestinal illness (DeFelice et al. 2016).
types.effect_quote: We find that proximity to wells increases housing values, though risks to groundwater fully offset those gains. By itself, groundwater risk reduces property values by up to 24 percent.
types.effect_source: Lucija Muehlenbachs, Elisheba Spiller and Christopher Timmins, 'Shale Gas Development and Property Values: Differences across Drinking Water Sources,' NBER Working Paper 18390 (2012). Later published as 'The Housing Market Impacts of Shale Gas Development,' American Economic Review 105(12): 3633-3659 (2015).
types.cost: Water: $36,467 average long-term cost per connection to tie a domestic-well home into a public water system ('physical consolidation'), versus $103,411 per connection for state small water systems (California State Water Resources Control Board, 2024 Cost Assessment, June 2024; statewide model). Sewer: about $15,000 per home for the homeowner's septic-to-sewer conversion where a public sewer is available (Miami-Dade Water and Sewer, current page). That figure does not include extending the main.
types.cost_quote: Table 18: Average Estimated Long-Term Solution Cost per Service Connection for State Small Water Systems & Domestic Wells [...] Physical Consolidation $103,411 $36,467 $40,794
types.notes: Table 18 columns are State Small Water Systems, Domestic Well, Average. Sewer cost, https://www.miamidade.gov/global/water/septic-to-sewer-assistance.page: 'The septic-to-sewer conversion would cost a homeowner approximately $15,000.' That is an urban county; rural main extensions cost more per home. Gibson et al., PNAS 117(29) (2020), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7382258/: 'The analysis shows that children in homes relying on private wells have 25% increased odds (95% CI 6.2 to 48%, P < 0.01) of elevated blood Pb, compared with children in houses served by a community water system that is regulated under the Safe Drinking Water Act.' DeFelice, Johnston & Gibson, Environmental Health Perspectives 124 (2016), https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5047767/: 'An estimated 2,920 (95% CI: 2,650, 3,190) annual emergency department visits could be prevented by extending community water service to 10% of the population currently relying on private wells.' Septic premium: Hardin, Lin & Thibodeau, 'House Prices and Septic Tanks: An Examination of Miami-Dade County' (FIU draft, 20 Aug 2024), https://environment.fiu.edu/programs/environmental-finance-risk-management/environmental-finance-publications/efrm-working-paper-series-2023/2024_08_20_miami_septic_tanks_draft.pdf: 'Instead, the value of an installed septic system and the corresponding reduction in operating and maintenance costs are associated with a premium of 3.1%.' Present the water benefit mainly as health and contamination risk. The shale-gas price discount applies only where groundwater is threatened.

types.name: Bring fiber (100/20 Mbps or better) broadband to unserved homes
types.trigger: Block groups where many broadband serviceable locations lack fixed service of at least 100/20 Mbps (BEAD 'underserved') or 25/3 Mbps ('unserved') in the FCC National Broadband Map availability data. Rural block groups first.
types.trigger_data: FCC National Broadband Map / Broadband Data Collection, data download at https://broadbandmap.fcc.gov/data-download/nationwide-data. National, provider-reported fixed availability by location, published twice a year. The FCC's 29 Apr 2026 fact sheet (https://docs.fcc.gov/public/attachments/DOC-421212A1.txt) cites the 'Availability Data As Of' Jun 30, 2025 release. Terms are not confirmed: broadbandmap.fcc.gov and the FCC help center refused automated access. Location coordinates (the Fabric) are understood to need a CostQuest license, so plan to map at census block or H3 hexagon level.
types.effect: Home values: homes with access to 25 Mbps broadband sold for about $5,977 (3%) more than similar homes in neighborhoods with 1 Mbps; the rural premium was lower, at $5,099 (Molnar, Savage & Sicker 2019, national sample). Fiber specifically: about 1% in a standard hedonic model, and 2% (Minnesota) to 9% (Texas) with instrumental variables, using 1.7 million sales in Iowa, Minnesota and Texas, 2015-2021 (Whitacre 2024). Remote rural counties: a 10% increase in coverage raised the median house value by $661 at 0.2 Mbps and $232 at 25 Mbps, with no significant effect above 100 Mbps (Deller & Whitacre 2019).
types.effect_quote: Results show that single-family homes with access to a 25 Mbps broadband connection have a price that is about $5,977, or 3%, more than similar homes in neighborhoods with 1 Mbps. The rural premium is lower at $5,099.
types.effect_source: Gabor Molnar, Scott J. Savage and Douglas C. Sicker, 'High-speed Internet access and housing values,' Applied Economics 51(55): 5923-5936 (2019). Abstract read on its RePEc/IDEAS record.
types.cost: About $10,744 per location in West Virginia's approved BEAD plan, which is 93.6% fiber-to-the-premises across 73,091 locations: a $7,466 average BEAD subsidy plus a $3,278 average provider match (NTIA overview updated 11/20/2025; my sum). Across the 33 state BEAD overviews checked, the average subsidy per location ranged from $2,019 (South Carolina) to $21,986 (North Dakota). These averages mix fiber with satellite and fixed wireless.
types.cost_quote: Avg. BEAD Cost per Location: $7,466 Avg. Match per Location: $3,278
types.notes: In the group brief but not in the mapping step's list. Whitacre, 'The fibre broadband housing premium across three US States,' Regional Studies, Regional Science 11(1): 38-62 (2024), abstract at https://ideas.repec.org/a/taf/rsrsxx/v11y2024i1p38-62.html: 'A more rigorous instrumental variable approach estimates the fibre premium at 2% in Minnesota and 9% in Texas.' Deller & Whitacre, Papers in Regional Science 98(5) (2019); working paper https://api.aae.wisc.edu/pubs/pdf/sps/stpap591.pdf: 'Focusing on the preferred W2SLS specification, a ten percent increase in coverage of at least 0.2MBPS results in the median house value increasing by $661.' NTIA says its overview figures are 'subject to change pending NTIA curing and NIST final review and award.' Full texts on tandfonline.com could not be opened; only the abstracts were read.

types.name: Main Street downtown revitalization program for a small town
types.trigger: Small town (roughly 2,000-50,000 people, a design choice) in a nonmetro county or small urban area, with a cluster of storefronts along a main street (OpenStreetMap shop and amenity points) and no local Main Street program.
types.trigger_data: Census Bureau 2020 urban areas and TIGER/Line places (https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/guidance/geo-areas/urban-rural.html; public), plus USDA ERS 2023 Rural-Urban Continuum Codes for nonmetro counties (https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/rural-urban-continuum-codes). Storefront clusters from OpenStreetMap (ODbL). No national file of designated Main Street programs was found; state coordinating programs post their own lists (for example https://www.commerce.nc.gov/main-street-program/designated-communities).
types.effect: Home values: none measured. Jobs and businesses: pooled across four Midwest states, adopting the Main Street Program had no significant effect on downtown retail jobs or establishments (difference-in-differences). Iowa was the exception, showing the hoped-for gains (Van Leuven 2022). Self-reported network figures (trade source): Main Street America programs reported $5.68 billion of local reinvestment, 6,630 net new businesses, 35,162 net new jobs and 10,556 rehabilitated historic buildings in 2023, or $18.03 of new investment per $1 of program operating spending. These are not causal estimates.
types.effect_quote: Using a pooled sample of four Midwest states, the author found no significant effect of Main Street Program adoption on downtown jobs or establishments. [...] Iowa emerges as a state where the Main Street Program appears to yield its hypothesized economic benefits to the downtown business districts of participating communities.
types.effect_source: Andrew J. Van Leuven, 'The Impact of Main Street Revitalization on the Economic Vitality of Small-Town Business Districts,' Economic Development Quarterly 36(3): 193-207 (2022). Abstract read on its RePEc/IDEAS record.
types.cost: Program operations: $45,000 to $150,000 a year depending on district size, with Georgia's average at $338,000 a year (staff salaries, benefits, training). Source: Georgia Main Street resource library, undated page. The stated average is above the stated range.
types.cost_quote: Depending on the district’s size, the program’s budget can range from $45,000 to $150,000 annually. The average budget in Georgia for a Main Street program’s operations is $338,000 annually.
types.notes: In the group brief but not in the mapping step's list. National Main Street Center / Main Street America statistics (trade, self-reported by programs), 24 Apr 2024, https://es.mainstreet.org/the-latest/news/main-spotlight-announcing-the-2024-main-street-america-designated-communities-and-collective-impact-of-local-programs-in-2023: 'In 2023, Main Street America programs generated $5.68 billion in local reinvestment, helped open 6,630 net new businesses, facilitated the creation of 35,162 net new jobs, catalyzed the rehabilitation of 10,556 historic buildings, and leveraged 1,664,763 volunteer hours.' and 'On average, for every dollar that a Main Street program spent to support their operations, $18.03 of new investment was generated back into their downtown and commercial corridor communities.' The www.mainstreet.org domain did not resolve from this session, so the cumulative since-1980 totals were not read. Whether georgiamainstreet.org is run by a state agency was not confirmed.

types.name: Keep or open a grocery store in a rural food desert
types.trigger: Rural census tract (tract center outside 2020 urban areas) flagged low-income and low-access at the 10- or 20-mile demarcation in the USDA ERS Food Access Research Atlas. Or a block group whose only grocery store (OpenStreetMap shop=supermarket or grocery) is at risk of closing.
types.trigger_data: USDA ERS Food Access Research Atlas, https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-access-research-atlas. Census tracts; page updated 10/15/2026. Two maps: the SNAP-authorized Retailer Access Map (new in July 2026; straight-line and driving distance) and the Large Retailer Access Map (last updated 2021; next update expected Winter 2026-27). Tract data can be downloaded; USDA public data. The documentation (https://www.ers.usda.gov/data-products/food-access-research-atlas/documentation) gives 10- and 20-mile demarcations for rural areas.
types.effect: Home values: no rural grocery-closure study found. Closest: using over one million sales near 159 Walmarts that opened in 2000-2006, prices of nearby houses rose 2-3% within 0.5 mile and 1-2% at 0.5-1 mile (Pope & Pope 2015).
types.effect_quote: Using a difference-in-differences specification, our estimates suggest that a new Walmart store actually increases housing prices by between 2% and 3% for houses located within 0.5 miles of the store and by 1–2% for houses located between 0.5 and 1 mile.
types.effect_source: Devin G. Pope and Jaren C. Pope, 'When Walmart comes to town: Always low housing prices? Always?' Journal of Urban Economics 87: 1-13 (2015). Abstract read on its RePEc/IDEAS record.
types.cost: Opening or renovating a store: about $2.4 million of state grant per store under the Illinois Grocery Initiative's New Stores in Food Deserts program (15 May 2025 awards; e.g., $2,398,989 for a store renovation in Roodhouse, IL). The grant covers construction or renovation plus first-year wages, utilities and initial inventory. Keeping a store open: North Dakota's 2025 Rural Grocery Store Sustainability Grants gave 11 rural communities a combined $1 million, about $91,000 each (my division), with a 20% local match.
types.cost_quote: This funding will support construction and renovation costs for new stores, as well as many first-year operations costs, such as employee wages, utility costs, and initial inventory of food. [...] MR MARKET LLC Roodhouse $2,398,989 Renovation project in Roodhouse
types.notes: Named in the group brief (grocery closures, USDA food access atlas). The mapping step folded it into rural_hospital; it is split out here because the trigger and cost differ. result.summary:
No saved rural-group progress from the interrupted run was found in the scratchpad, so this research was redone from scratch. It covers the 5 types from the mapping step plus 3 types named in the group brief (broadband, Main Street, grocery). I downloaded every cited page or PDF and checked all 64 quotes word for word against the saved copies; all matched.

Home-value effects measured:
- Fire protection: house values fell at least 6.7% the year after a fire levy was voted down (Brasington & Parent 2024).
- Trails: about 3-5% higher near trails in urban and suburban hedonic studies, and probably less near rural trails (Crompton & Nicholls 2019).
- Broadband: about 3% ($5,977) for 25 Mbps access, with a rural premium of $5,099 (Molnar et al. 2019); 1-9% for fiber (Whitacre 2024).
- Paving: 17-28% from first-time street paving, but only in a Mexico randomized trial (no U.S. study found).
- New Walmart: 2-3% within half a mile (Pope & Pope 2015), the closest evidence for grocery stores.

Null or non-price results:
- Rural hospital closures: no measurable change in housing markets, but health jobs fell. Closing the sole hospital cut per-capita income 4% and raised unemployment 1.6 points; rural closures raised inpatient mortality 8.7%.
- Water and sewer: no study measures a line extension itself. Near shale-gas wells, groundwater risk cut values of well-dependent homes by up to 24% (working paper). Miami-Dade septic homes sold at a 3.1% premium. Children on private wells had 25% higher odds of elevated blood lead.
- Main Street: no significant effect on downtown jobs pooled across four Midwest states, with Iowa the exception.

Unit costs found:
- Rural Emergency Hospital: $295,051.54 a month in 2026, about $3.54M a year.
- Fire station: about $1.74M per 2009-10 Recovery Act grant (old).
- Rural trailhead: $406,823 federal grant (Haysi, VA).
- Paving: $600k-$800k per mile (Washington County, IA).
- Water: $36,467 per domestic-well connection (California 2024).
- Sewer: about $15,000 per home for the homeowner's conversion (Miami-Dade).
- Broadband: about $10,744 per location in West Virginia's BEAD plan.
- Main Street program: $45k-$338k a year (Georgia).
- Grocery: about $2.4M per new or renovated store (Illinois); about $91k per store to keep one open (North Dakota).

Trigger datasets checked: CMS Hospital General Information, ERS 2023 Rural-Urban Continuum Codes, USFA fire department registry, PAD-US 4.1, 2020 Census urban areas, OpenStreetMap, USGS domestic-well estimates, EPA water service areas (v3) and sewersheds, FCC National Broadband Map (via an FCC document only), and the ERS Food Access Research Atlas.

Scratch files: notes at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/rural/notes.md; quote check at /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/rural/check/quotes.json and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/rural/check/verify.py; downloaded sources under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/rural/dl/.
open_questions: FCC sites (broadbandmap.fcc.gov, help.bdc.fcc.gov, www.fcc.gov) refused automated access. The current National Broadband Map data vintage (December 2025 or later) and the redistribution terms for public availability files versus the licensed CostQuest location Fabric are not confirmed; this needs a manual check.

rd.usda.gov (USDA Rural Development) refused automated access, so recent rural fire-station project costs from the Community Facilities program were not read. The fire_station unit cost rests on 2009-10 Recovery Act grant averages (CRS RL32341). The DHS OIG report OIG-12-23 on those grants also could not be opened (403 error and a certificate error on the UNT archive copy).

No U.S. study measures how paving a gravel road changes home values; the only causal estimate is a Mexico randomized trial. The full 2005 MnDOT/LRRB 'Economics of Upgrading an Aggregate Road' report (mdl.mndot.gov) was refused; only the 2006 technical summary was read.

No study measures the home-value effect of extending public water or sewer lines. The evidence conflicts: groundwater risk cut values of well-dependent homes by up to 24% near shale gas (NBER working paper; the AER version's exact figure was not read), while Miami-Dade septic homes sold at a 3.1% premium (unpublished draft).

USGS domestic-well estimates are for 2000 and 2010 block groups only, with no 2020 release found. EPA water service areas and sewersheds are partly modeled, and EPA disclaims their accuracy for individual properties.

No rural-specific hedonic estimate for trailheads, river access or campgrounds was found. No primary-source campground cost per campsite was found. The Crompton & Nicholls full text (author copy) was refused (403); only the abstract was read.

tandfonline.com was blocked, so the full texts of Molnar et al. 2019 and Whitacre 2024 were not read; only the abstracts on RePEc/IDEAS. BEAD per-location costs mix fiber with satellite and fixed wireless; a fiber-only national per-location cost was not found.

Main Street: www.mainstreet.org did not resolve, so the cumulative since-1980 reinvestment statistics were not read (only the April 2024 Main Street America release). No national file of designated programs was found for the trigger. The Georgia budget page states an average ($338,000) above its own range, and who runs it was not confirmed.

Alexander & Richards measure rural hospital-closure effects on housing through HMDA mortgage counts and loan sizes, not sale prices. A direct home-price study of rural hospital closures (beyond a small Illinois repeat-sales pilot, not read) remains open.
The Rural Emergency Hospital payment prices an emergency-only hospital. The annual cost of keeping a full-service Critical Access Hospital open (the local operating subsidy) was not priced.
Rural pharmacy-closure effects (for example on medication adherence) and the health effects of rural grocery closures were not researched.

The Brasington & Parent abstract does not say which state the fire districts are in or whether they are rural, and it measures funding cuts, not new stations. A study of new rural fire or EMS stations and home values was not found.
Hospital, fire-station and grocery triggers need geocoding (the CMS and USFA files have addresses only) and drive-time routing on OpenStreetMap; those steps were not tested here.

checks.item: rural_hospital effect_url (Alexander & Richards, NBER w29110)
checks.note: HTTP 200. The quote is word for word in the abstract. The abstract also says 'We examine over 100 rural hospital closures spanning 2005-2017'. The page shows Issue Date July 2021, Revision Date January 2023, and the published version in Journal of Public Economics vol 221 (2023). The HMDA details are not in the abstract, so I checked the working-paper PDF (nber.org/system/files/working_papers/w29110/w29110.pdf, section 5.3). It says loans originated, denied and purchased 'are stable during the three-year window before and after a rural hospital closure' and 'there is no effect of hospital closures on the average loan amounts either'. The authors call these estimates 'somewhat imprecise'. The paper measures loan activity, not sale prices, so 'no price effect measured' is accurate. The Holmes and Gujral & Basu sentences in this effect text depend on their own URLs, checked below.

verify.summary:
I checked 30 URLs myself: all 16 effect and cost URLs, plus the 14 sources quoted in the notes. Each page was downloaded fresh with curl and every quote was matched ignoring whitespace and punctuation. There was no saved progress from an earlier verification run, so this was done from scratch.

Effect and cost URLs (16):
- All 16 could be read (HTTP 200).
- All 16 quotes were found. The Oxford paving paper has a footnote marker '4' after '(or 72%)', which the notes already disclose.
- All 16 support the stated effect or cost. No number differs from its source, and the derived figures are correct: $3.54M a year (REH), $1.74M per fire grant, $10,744 per broadband location, about $2.4M per Illinois store, about $91k per North Dakota store.
- Extra details were confirmed in the full texts. The NBER w29110 PDF (section 5.3) shows HMDA originations, denials and purchases stable and no effect on average loan amounts. The AER abstract says 'large negative impacts on nearby groundwater-dependent homes'. The NTIA overviews for South Carolina ($2,019) and North Dakota ($21,986, only 279 locations) match the stated range.

Three wording fixes:
- West Virginia BEAD: the PDF is a 'Final Proposal' overview whose figures are 'subject to change pending NTIA curing and NIST final review and award'. It does not say the plan is approved.
- California $36,467: this is a modeled average for high-risk domestic wells.
- Molnar et al.: 'national sample' is not stated in the abstract.

Minor caveats are in the notes (paving study timing, the AER corrigendum, North Dakota awards ranging from $35,525 to $150,000).

Quoted note sources (14):
- 9 could be read and verified word for word: Gujral & Basu, Texas PPC FAQ, Washtenaw, Miami-Dade, the FIU draft, Whitacre, Deller & Whitacre, Main Street America, North Dakota Commerce.
- 5 could not be read, so these claims stay unverified:
  - Holmes et al. (PMC): $703 / 4% / 1.6 points.
  - Gibson et al. (PMC): 25% higher odds of elevated blood lead.
  - DeFelice et al. (PMC): 2,920 emergency visits.
  - USDA ERS ERR-7 on AgEcon Search: $474 vs $384 rents and income 10% higher.
  - MnDOT/LRRB summary on ROSA P: the 200 ADT threshold.

Why those 5 failed: the PMC pages return a reCAPTCHA page to curl, AgEcon returns an empty HTTP 202, and ROSA P returns 403. WebFetch could not resolve any of these hosts in this session. I then tried NCBI's E-utilities and Europe PMC APIs and one more AgEcon retry. The auto-mode classifier blocked that as bot-check circumvention, so I stopped and did not try other workarounds. To close these 5, open them in a browser, add the hosts to the session's network settings for WebFetch, or approve another route such as the NCBI E-utilities.

The 14 trigger-dataset URLs were not checked: they are outside the effect/cost scope and over the 30-URL cap.

Working files are in /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/vrural_1794288241: downloads under dl/, and scripts/qcheck.py with scripts/items.json for the quote check.

types.name: Retrofit a dead mall or strip center into a town center
types.trigger: A big retail site that is mostly parking and partly empty. In data terms: an OpenStreetMap shop=mall or landuse=retail polygon of about 10 acres or more, where surface parking (amenity=parking with parking=surface) covers about half the site or more. It must also meet one of two vacancy tests: (a) the census tract's USPS business-address vacancy rate (vacant business addresses ÷ all business addresses, from the HUD-USPS data) is in the top fifth for its county or metro; or (b) at least a quarter of the Overture places inside the polygon are marked operating_status = permanently_closed or temporarily_closed. The acreage, parking-share and vacancy cut-offs are City Pretty's own choices; no source sets them.
types.trigger_data: (1) OpenStreetMap, via Geofabrik's state extracts. It is updated all the time. License: 'OpenStreetMap is open data, licensed under the Open Data Commons Open Database License (ODbL) by the OpenStreetMap Foundation (OSMF).' (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright). US counts as of 2026-11-09 from Geofabrik taginfo (https://taginfo.geofabrik.de/north-america:us/, API /api/4/tag/stats): shop=mall 5,147 features; parking=surface 733,993; shop=vacant 14,718; disused:shop 12,848. The vacancy tags are too sparse to use on their own. (2) HUD Aggregated USPS Administrative Data on Address Vacancies (https://www.huduser.gov/portal/datasets/usps.html). Census tracts, released quarterly, with vacant and no-stat counts for both residential and business addresses. Terms: 'Under the current agreement with the USPS, HUD can make the data accessible only to governmental entities and non-profit organizations registered as users.' Use is limited to the 'stated purpose' in the sublicense, so raw tract values may not be publishable on an open map. (3) Openly licensed fallback: Overture Maps Places, field operating_status, defined as 'An indication of whether a place is: in continued operation, in a temporary operating hiatus, or closed permanently.' (https://docs.overturemaps.org/schema/reference/places/place/). Licenses vary by source (https://docs.overturemaps.org/attribution/): Meta and Microsoft data are CDLA Permissive 2.0, Foursquare data Apache 2.0, AllThePlaces data CC0 1.0.
types.effect: +1.43% on average for a home next to a shopping center just after the center is redeveloped. The gain fades quickly with distance and over time. This is from the Netherlands (inner-city shopping centers, difference-in-differences); the abstract does not define 'next to' as a distance. Related US evidence: around an open-air mixed-use shopping center, prices fell within a 'critical radius' and rose beyond it (Kholdy, Muhtaseb & Yu 2014; the radius is not in the abstract). New Walmart stores raised prices 2–3% within 0.5 mile and 1–2% at 0.5–1 mile (Pope & Pope 2015). Among the sources I could open, none measures nearby home values after a US dead mall was converted into a town center.
types.effect_quote: We find the price of a property located next to a redeveloped shopping center increases by 1.43% on average just after redevelopment. Our results indicate that these positive external effects wear off rather rapidly across space and over time.
types.effect_source: Zhang, Song; van Duijn, Mark; van der Vlist, Arno J. (2020). 'The external effects of inner-city shopping centers: Evidence from the Netherlands.' Journal of Regional Science 60(4): 583–611. doi:10.1111/jors.12473. Abstract read on IDEAS/RePEc and confirmed in the publisher's Crossref record (https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1111/jors.12473).
types.cost: Public cost on a 52-acre regional mall site in Alexandria, Virginia (approved July 6, 2021): $86 million in city bonds for site preparation and infrastructure, about $1.65 million per acre. On top of that came $54 million in bonds to buy land for a hospital and lease it out. Total planned investment is more than $2 billion, about $38 million per acre, hospital included. Land bought by a public redevelopment agency in Gwinnett County, Georgia: $16.5 million for 23 acres with 293,059 sq ft of retail buildings, about $0.72 million per acre (Sept. 2024); and $11.5 million for the 11.5-acre former Sears site, about $1.0 million per acre (Sept. 2025). All in nominal dollars. I worked out the per-acre figures myself.
types.cost_quote: City Council also approved the use of $54 million in public bond financing to allow the City to acquire the land for the hospital and lease it to Inova, as well as $86 million in public bond financing for site preparation and infrastructure at the Landmark site and adjacent Duke Street and Van Dorn Street corridors.
types.notes:
Site size and total investment, from the same Alexandria release: 'The 52-acre Landmark site is one of the most desirable large-scale underdeveloped locations remaining inside the Capital Beltway. The project will transform the currently unoccupied mall into a mixed-use, walkable urban village and will propel the revitalization of the West End of the City of Alexandria.' And: 'The plan will result in more than $2 billion in investment in the community, including the new Inova hospital, medical office buildings, for-rent and for-sale multifamily residential units, retail, commercial, and entertainment offerings.'

Gwinnett County, Macy's site (https://www.gwinnettcounty.com/-/news-events/news-releases/news-details/gwinnett-county-acquires-23-acre-macy-s-site-at-gwinnett-place-mall-1): 'The Gwinnett County Board of Commissioners today approved the Urban Redevelopment Agency of Gwinnett County’s purchase of the Macy’s sites at Gwinnett Place Mall, totaling 23 acres, for $16.5 million.'

Gwinnett County, Sears site (https://www.gwinnettcounty.com/-/news-events/news-releases/news-details/urban-redevelopment-agency-of-gwinnett-county-to-purchase-former-sears-property-at-gwinnett-place-mall-1): 'The Urban Redevelopment Agency of Gwinnett County today approved the $11.5 million purchase of the 11.5-acre former Sears site at Gwinnett Place Mall.'

Supporting effects, all peer-reviewed abstracts:
- Kholdy, Muhtaseb & Yu (2014), Journal of Real Estate Practice and Education 17(1): 1–18 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/taf/rjrpxx/v17y2014i1p1-18.html): 'we find that the open-air shopping center has a negative impact on the price of residential properties within a critical radius to the center, and a positive impact on the price of residential properties beyond the critical radius.' So homes right at the edge of a busy new center may lose value.
- Pope & Pope (2015), Journal of Urban Economics 87: 1–13 (https://ideas.repec.org/a/eee/juecon/v87y2015icp1-13.html): 'Using a difference-in-differences specification, our estimates suggest that a new Walmart store actually increases housing prices by between 2% and 3% for houses located within 0.5 miles of the store and by 1–2% for houses located between 0.5 and 1 mile.'
- Pivo & Fisher (2011), Real Estate Economics 39(2): 185–219 (Crossref abstract: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.1111/j.1540-6229.2010.00296.x): 'On a 100‐point scale, a 10‐point increase in walkability increased values by 1–9%, depending on property type.' This covers office, retail and apartment values in NCREIF data, not single-family homes.

Not peer-reviewed:
- Cortright (2009), Impresa for CEOs for Cities (https://nacto.org/wp-content/uploads/walking_the_walk_cortright.pdf): 'In the typical market, an additional one point increase in Walk Score was associated with between a $500 and $3,000 increase in home values.' Walk Score is proprietary, so the map cannot use it as a trigger.
- Eppli & Tu, a report hosted on EPA's site (https://archive.epa.gov/epa/sites/production/files/2014-01/documents/eppli_tu.pdf), found a 16% premium in Kentlands and 6.5% in Lakelands, Maryland. These are planned new-urbanist neighborhoods, not mall retrofits.

Caveats: The headline effect is Dutch and is about renovating inner-city centers, so the size of the effect near a US suburban dead mall is unknown. The Alexandria total includes a hospital. Strip centers are much smaller than regional malls, so per-acre costs are more useful than project totals.

types.name: Walking paths between cul-de-sacs
types.trigger: A block group in the bottom quarter of US block groups for EPA street intersection density (Walkability Index field D3B_Ranked ≤ 5 on its 1–20 national scale) that also has many dead-end streets in OpenStreetMap (ends of residential, living_street or unclassified ways that join no other street; service roads and driveways excluded). A school (NCES EDGE point), park (OSM leisure=park/playground) or shops (OSM shop=*) must be within 0.5 mile in a straight line of a cul-de-sac end, while the shortest OSM walking route there is at least about twice as long. There must also be a short gap of roughly 300 ft or less to the destination or the next street, across public land or an existing easement; checking this needs parcel data. All distances and cut-offs are City Pretty's own choices.
types.trigger_data: (1) EPA Smart Location Database v3.0 and EPA National Walkability Index, covering every 2019 Census block group nationwide. The SLD guide describes D3b as 'Street intersection density (weighted, auto-oriented intersections eliminated)', with extra fields D3bao, D3bmm3/4 and D3bpo3/4 counting intersections by type and number of legs. The intersection measures come from 2018 Q4 HERE NAVSTREETS. EPA page (last updated Sept. 8, 2026): https://www.epa.gov/smartgrowth/smart-location-mapping. Downloads: https://edg.epa.gov/EPADataCommons/public/OA/SLD/SmartLocationDatabaseV3.zip and https://edg.epa.gov/EPADataCommons/public/OA/WalkabilityIndex.zip (both last modified June 8, 2021). License: CC0 1.0 (https://creativecommons.org/publicdomain/zero/1.0/) on the data.gov records https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/smart-location-database and https://catalog.data.gov/dataset/walkability-index; the Walkability Index was issued 2021-05-13. Ranked fields come from 20 national quantiles: 'To score block groups, the block groups were placed into 20 quantiles by variable value (quantiles are groupings with equal numbers of records), each containing 5 percent of the total block groups.' (2) Dead ends and walking-route length: OpenStreetMap, ODbL 1.0 (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright). (3) Schools: NCES EDGE public and private school geocodes for school years 2023–24 to 2025–26, based on TIGER 2025 (https://nces.ed.gov/programs/edge/Geographic/SchoolLocations). Federal data; the page states no license terms.
types.effect: Home values: I found no measurement for adding a path to an existing cul-de-sac. Related home-price evidence points both ways. Portland-area buyers paid more for more connected street networks and shorter dead-end streets, but preferred being 'less connected to the outside' (Song 2002 dissertation; no size given in the abstract). Homes on cul-de-sacs in Savannah, Georgia sold for more than 9% more (Cebula 2009). Safety (the measured effect): more street permeability goes with higher burglary risk, and cul-de-sacs, especially winding ones, have lower risk (Johnson & Bowers 2010, street-segment analysis; the abstract does not name the place). A UK Home Office-funded study of 12 developments (2,193 homes; police-recorded crime 2007–2009) found that cul-de-sacs linked by footpaths ('leaky') had 110% more crime than true cul-de-sacs, and through roads had 93% more (Armitage 2011, unpublished briefing).
types.effect_quote: The findings demonstrate that increased permeability is associated with elevated burglary risk, that burglary risk is lower on cul-de-sacs (particularly those that are sinuous in nature), and that the risk of burglary is higher on more major roads and those street segments that are connected to them.
types.effect_source: Johnson, Shane D.; Bowers, Kate J. (2010). 'Permeability and Burglary Risk: Are Cul-de-Sacs Safer?' Journal of Quantitative Criminology 26(1): 89–111 (March 2010). Published abstract read in the U.S. Justice Department's NCJRS Virtual Library (NCJ 230224); the Springer page blocked automated access.
types.cost: Paved multi-use trail: median $261,000 per mile, average $481,140, range $64,710 to $4,288,520 (42 observations from 11 sources). National data in 2012 dollars, from the UNC Highway Safety Research Center, prepared for FHWA, 2013. By my arithmetic, a 300-ft connector costs about $15,000 (median) to $27,000 (average), and a 500-ft one about $25,000 to $46,000. These figures leave out buying a strip of land or an easement, design, and lighting (a streetlight has a median cost of $3,600 each in the same table).
types.notes:
The cost quote is one table row. Columns in order: Median, Average, Minimum, Maximum, Cost Unit, Number of Sources (Observations). From the same document: 'Costs are updated to 2012 US Dollar equivalents, and include labor, materials, mobilization costs and contractor profits.' and 'These resources were prepared for the Federal Highway Administration and supported by the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation through its Active Living Research program.' Streetlight row: 'Streetlight $3,600 $4,880 $310 $13,900 Each 12 (17)'.

Crime numbers: Armitage, R. (2011), 'The Impact of Connectivity and Through-Movement within Residential Developments on Levels of Crime and Anti-Social Behaviour', University of Huddersfield briefing note. It is unpublished, from a Home Office-funded project managed by CABE (https://eprints.hud.ac.uk/id/eprint/13592/1/Briefing_Notes_-_The_Impact_of_Connectivity.pdf): 'The results found that, compared to the true cul-de-sac (the safest), through roads experienced 93% more crime and leaky culs-de-sac 110% more crime.' Sample: 'Micro Level – 12 developments (2193 properties) from the three police forces Greater Manchester, West Midlands and Kent.' Design advice from the same note: 'Footpaths should be located at the front of properties and be wide, well-lit and direct.'

Home-value evidence:
- Song, Yan (2002), PhD dissertation, University of Illinois. Abstract public; full text restricted (https://www.ideals.illinois.edu/items/80811): 'The findings of the regression model reveal that consumers are willing to pay more for some new urbanist features such as being located within ¾-mile of light rail line; more park, light industrial uses, and transit services being provided in the neighborhood; being located not by cul-de-sacs but instead by more connective street network; more streets, shorter dead-end streets, more and smaller blocks being provided in the neighborhood, and enhanced pedestrian walkability to commercial uses.' Also: 'Counter to what new urbanists have promoted, consumers prefer being less connected to the outside...'
- Cebula (2009), Review of Regional Studies 39(1): 9–22 (https://rrs.scholasticahq.com/article/8197.pdf): 'On the other hand, location on a cul-de-sac results in a housing price premium in excess of 9 percent, while location on a lake or river yields a price premium of roughly 14 percent.'
- Yencha (2019), Transportation Research Part A 130: 689–709 (abstract: https://econpapers.repec.org/article/eeetransa/v_3a130_3ay_3a2019_3ai_3ac_3ap_3a689-709.htm), about 60,000 Ohio sales: 'nearby establishments are an amenity capitalized into home prices only when there also exists access to adequate pedestrian pathing'. This is the main argument that a connector can unlock value from nearby shops.

Data caveat: the SLD does not count dead ends, so they must come from OSM. The SLD's intersection data date from 2018.

types.name: Build missing sidewalks
types.trigger: Street segments in OpenStreetMap (highway=residential, unclassified, tertiary, secondary or primary) tagged sidewalk=no, sidewalk:both=no or sidewalk:left/right=no. They count if they lie within 0.5 mile of a school (NCES EDGE point), within 0.25 mile of a transit stop (OSM highway=bus_stop or public_transport=platform, or agency GTFS stops), or within 0.25 mile of shops (OSM shop=*). Streets with no sidewalk tag and no footway=sidewalk way drawn alongside should be shown as 'unknown', not 'missing'. Optionally, rank segments higher in block groups with an EPA National Walkability Index of 10.51 or more ('Above average walkable'), where Li et al. (2015) found larger price gains. The distance cut-offs are City Pretty's choices. FHWA and the City of Tampa both prioritize school zones and transit but give no distances.
types.trigger_data: OpenStreetMap, ODbL 1.0 (https://www.openstreetmap.org/copyright), updated all the time and downloadable as daily Geofabrik state extracts. Tags are defined on the wiki (https://wiki.openstreetmap.org/wiki/Key:sidewalk): sidewalk=no means 'There is no sidewalk at all.'; sidewalk:both/left/right give each side; sidewalk=separate means the sidewalk is drawn as its own highway=footway + footway=sidewalk way. US tag counts as of 2026-11-09 (Geofabrik taginfo, https://taginfo.geofabrik.de/north-america:us/): sidewalk=no 362,528 ways; sidewalk:left=no 339,534; sidewalk:both=no 75,133; any sidewalk=* tag 761,239 ways; footway=sidewalk 4,429,429 ways. For comparison there are 9,232,894 highway=residential ways, so coverage is partial and patchy. Schools: NCES EDGE school geocodes, 2023–24 to 2025–26 (https://nces.ed.gov/programs/edge/Geographic/SchoolLocations; federal, no license stated). Walkability ranking: EPA National Walkability Index, CC0 1.0 (https://edg.epa.gov/EPADataCommons/public/OA/WalkabilityIndex.zip).
types.effect: Home values: small where streets are car-dependent. Austin, Texas, 2010–2012 single-family sales, spatial hedonic model: adding sidewalks in car-dependent neighborhoods gave only a minimal price increase, and sidewalks and amenities raise prices more in neighborhoods that are already walkable (Li et al. 2015). The abstract gives no dollar or percent figure. Safety: sidewalks cut crashes involving pedestrians walking along roadways by 65–89% (FHWA Proven Safety Countermeasures, from a 2005 Florida DOT study).
types.effect_quote: Results show that improving walkability through increased access to amenities in car-dependent neighborhoods does not appear to increase property values; adding sidewalks in these neighborhoods leads to a minimal increase in property values. Investments in neighborhood amenities and sidewalks will yield a greater home price increase in a walkable neighborhood than in a car-dependent neighborhood.
types.effect_source: Li, Wei; Joh, Kenneth; Lee, Chanam; Kim, Jun-Hyun; Park, Han; Woo, Ayoung (2015). 'Assessing Benefits of Neighborhood Walkability to Single-Family Property Values: A Spatial Hedonic Study in Austin, Texas.' Journal of Planning Education and Research 35(4): 471–488. doi:10.1177/0739456X15591055. Abstract read in the publisher's Crossref record; the SAGE page blocked automated access.
types.cost: About $750,000 per mile of new sidewalk, including engineering design, survey and construction (City of Tampa, Florida). The page was updated April 13, 2026, but the same passage cites 2022 budget conditions, so the dollar year is unclear. Tampa says its roughly 1,300 miles of gaps would cost $975 million. National construction-only bid data, 2012 dollars: concrete sidewalk median $27 per linear foot (average $32; 164 observations from 46 sources). By my arithmetic that is about $143,000 to $169,000 per mile for one side of the street (UNC Highway Safety Research Center for FHWA, 2013).
types.cost_quote: The average cost to construct new sidewalks is about $750,000 per mile which includes engineering design, survey, and construction.
types.notes:
Safety source: FHWA, Proven Safety Countermeasures: Walkways, FHWA-SA-21-047, 2021 (https://rosap.ntl.bts.gov/view/dot/66694). Quote: 'Sidewalks 65-89% reduction in crashes involving pedestrians walking along roadways.' The sheet cites 'Gan et al. Update of Florida Crash Reduction Factors and Countermeasures to Improve the Development of District Safety Improvement Projects. Florida DOT, (2005).' Where to build, same sheet: 'It is important to provide and maintain accessible walkways along both sides of the road in urban areas, particularly near school zones and transit locations, and where there is a large amount of pedestrian activity.'

Tampa's ranking criteria (same page as the cost): 'All new sidewalk construction projects, also known as capital improvements, are prioritized and selected for inclusion in the long-term work program based on criteria such as documented safety needs, ADA issues, and proximity to schools and transit facilities.' Its list also includes 'Proximity to daily needs (e.g. grocery)'.

National bid data (https://www.pedbikeinfo.org/downloads/Countermeasure_Costs_Summary_Oct2013.pdf), table row 'Concrete Sidewalk $27 $32 $2.09 $410 Linear Foot 46 (164)'. Columns: Median, Average, Min, Max, Unit, Sources (Observations). These bid costs leave out right-of-way, drainage and design, which is why Tampa's all-in figure (about $142 per foot) is much higher.

Other home-value evidence:
- Sohn, Moudon & Lee (2012), URBAN DESIGN International 17: 115–128, King County, WA assessed values (copy on floridadep.gov: https://floridadep.gov/sites/default/files/Economic%20Value%20of%20walkable%20neighborhoods%2C%20Sohn%2C%20Moudon%20and%20Lee%2C%202012_0.pdf): 'Second, better sidewalk coverage in their neighborhood was positively related to increasing property values of rental multi-family residential and retail service uses.' and 'In contrast, few measures of the correlates of walking were significantly associated with single-family residential and office property values.'
- Yencha (2019), about 60,000 Ohio sales: nearby shops add to home prices 'only when there also exists access to adequate pedestrian pathing'.
- Cortright (2009), not peer-reviewed, Walk Score: 'It should be stressed that our measure of walkability captures not just the benefits associated with walking but with greater accessibility generally.' So Walk Score premiums should not be credited to sidewalks.

Suggestion: for a home-value map, Li et al. imply ranking missing sidewalks higher where destinations already exist (higher Walkability Index). Safety-led ranking would favor school and transit areas instead.

result.summary:
Researched the three suburban project types. Every quote below was checked word for word against a page or PDF I downloaded (saved under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-city-pretty/763724d0-bb10-5922-8d31-bd70781887d0/scratchpad/sub/dl/, checked with sub/scripts/checkq.py).

(1) Dead mall or strip center retrofit. Best measured effect: +1.43% for homes next to a redeveloped shopping center, fading quickly with distance and time (Zhang, van Duijn & van der Vlist 2020, Journal of Regional Science; Netherlands). US support: an open-air mixed-use center lowered prices inside a 'critical radius' and raised them beyond it; new Walmarts raised prices 2–3% within 0.5 mile. Costs: Alexandria, VA put $86M in bonds into site prep and infrastructure on the 52-acre Landmark Mall site (about $1.65M per acre), against more than $2B of total investment. Gwinnett County, GA paid $16.5M for 23 acres and $11.5M for 11.5 acres of Gwinnett Place Mall. Trigger data: OpenStreetMap for malls and surface parking. Vacancy data has a catch: HUD-USPS business vacancy is open only to governments and registered non-profits. Overture Places' operating_status field is the openly licensed fallback.

(2) Cul-de-sac connectors. No study measures what adding a path does to home values. Related home-price evidence points both ways: connectivity premium in Portland (Song 2002) versus a 9%+ cul-de-sac premium in Savannah (Cebula 2009). The measured effect is on safety: more street permeability goes with higher burglary risk (Johnson & Bowers 2010). A UK Home Office-funded study found cul-de-sacs linked by footpaths had 110% more crime than closed ones (Armitage 2011). Cost: paved trail median $261,000 per mile (2012 dollars, UNC Highway Safety Research Center for FHWA), about $15,000–$27,000 for a 300-ft connector. Trigger data: EPA Smart Location Database and National Walkability Index (block groups, CC0), plus OpenStreetMap dead ends and NCES school locations.

(3) Missing sidewalks. Home values: only a minimal gain in car-dependent Austin neighborhoods, with bigger gains where the area is already walkable (Li et al. 2015). Safety: 65–89% fewer crashes involving pedestrians walking along roadways (FHWA). Cost: $750,000 per mile including design, survey and construction (City of Tampa). National bid-item cost is $27–$32 per linear foot in 2012 dollars. Trigger data: OpenStreetMap sidewalk tags. US counts as of 2026-11-09 show coverage is partial (362,528 ways tagged sidewalk=no, against 9.2M residential ways), so streets with no tag must be shown as unknown, not missing.

Limits: the WebFetch tool could not resolve hosts in this session, so I fetched pages with curl through the proxy. ScienceDirect, Springer, SAGE, SSRN, Wiley, ResearchGate and some PDFs blocked automated access with bot checks, which I did not try to get around. The shared web-search budget ran out before I found a US city's actual cost for a cul-de-sac connector project. A follow-up message can resume the searches.
open_questions: Song & Knaap (2003), 'New urbanism and housing values', Journal of Urban Economics 54(2), and Matthews & Turnbull (2007), 'Neighborhood street layout and property value', JREFE 35(2). These are the main US hedonic studies of street connectivity and home values. ScienceDirect, Springer, SSRN, EconBiz and CiteSeerX all blocked or failed automated access, so neither is cited.

Li et al. (2015), full text. A CNU news summary says a 1% rise in sidewalk density was worth $785 in the most walkable Austin areas, but I could not open the paper (SAGE blocked access), so no dollar figure for sidewalks is cited.
Kholdy, Muhtaseb & Yu (2014), full text. The size of the 'critical radius' and the percent effects are not in the abstract, and the Taylor & Francis paper is paywalled.

Zhang, van Duijn & van der Vlist (2020), full text. The distance meant by 'next to' and the sample size (said elsewhere to be 273 centers) could not be checked. The Wiley and Groningen PDFs returned 403 bot-check pages.

No opened study measures nearby US home values after a dead mall was converted into a mixed-use town center. Candidates to look for: Belmar (Lakewood, CO), Downtown Westminster (CO), WestEnd Alexandria (VA).

A US city or county cost for a cul-de-sac-to-cul-de-sac or cul-de-sac-to-school path, including easement purchase, lighting and design. Not found before the web-search budget ran out; the cost given is a national per-mile trail figure.
Asabere (1990), 'The Value of a Neighborhood Street with Reference to the Cul-de-Sac', JREFE 3(2). No abstract was available on IDEAS or Crossref, so it is not cited.

Redfin's Walk Score study, and buyer surveys such as NAR's or NAHB's. These include the '89% of buyers say sidewalks are important' claim from the mapping step. They are trade sources I did not open, so the claim is unverified.

FHWA's 65–89% sidewalk crash reduction comes from Gan et al. (2005) for the Florida DOT, which I did not open. Whether the same reduction holds on low-speed suburban residential streets is untested here.

HUD-USPS vacancy data: City Pretty would need to confirm whether it qualifies as a governmental or non-profit user and whether tract-level business vacancy rates derived from the data may be shown publicly under the sublicense.

OpenStreetMap sidewalk coverage varies by county. Before triggering, measure for each county the share of residential streets that carry any sidewalk tag or a separately drawn footway=sidewalk way, and suppress the trigger where coverage is low.
The paper on department store closures and housing markets (ResearchGate, reportedly about a 1–3% drop in nearby prices) was not opened; its location and authors are unknown.

checks.item: mall_retrofit effect_url: Zhang, van Duijn & van der Vlist (2020), +1.43% next to a redeveloped shopping center
checks.note: HTTP 200 (curl through the session proxy). Both quoted sentences appear word for word in the abstract. The page confirms Journal of Regional Science 60(4): 583-611 (September 2020), DOI 10.1111/jors.12473, a difference-in-difference design and 'nearby residential property prices'. As the result says, the abstract gives no distance for 'next to'. Caveat: the study covers redevelopment of existing Dutch inner-city centers, not conversion of dead US malls. The result already says this.

checks.item: mall_retrofit cost_url: Alexandria Landmark Mall ($86M bonds for site prep/infrastructure, $54M for hospital land, 52 acres, >$2B, July 6, 2021)
checks.corrected: Exact page wording: '$86 million in public bond financing for site preparation and infrastructure at the Landmark site and adjacent Duke Street and Van Dorn Street corridors.' Part of the $86M pays for off-site corridor work, so $86M / 52 acres (about $1.65M per acre) overstates the on-site cost per acre.
checks.note: City release, 'For Immediate Release: July 6, 2021' (page marked [Archived]). Council 'unanimously approved' the agreements at its July 6 meeting. The cost quote and both notes quotes (the 52-acre sentence and the 'more than $2 billion in investment ... including the new Inova hospital' sentence) appear word for word. The $54M is to 'acquire the land for the hospital and lease it to Inova'. Arithmetic checks: 86/52 = 1.65 and 2,000/52 = 38.5. The page says 'former Landmark Mall' and 'currently unoccupied mall', not 'regional mall'. The $2B figure is a projection (the release carries a forward-looking safe-harbor statement).

checks.item: cul_de_sac_connector effect_url: Johnson & Bowers (2010), permeability and burglary risk
checks.note: NCJRS record NCJ 230224: Journal of Quantitative Criminology, Volume 26, Issue 1, dated March 2010, pages 89-111, authors Shane D. Johnson and Kate J. Bowers. The abstract is labelled '(Published Abstract)' and the quote is word for word. The abstract describes 'original analyses conducted at the street segment level' and names no study area, as the result says. It measures the permeability of the road network, not footpath links as such. The footpath ('leaky cul-de-sac') figures come from Armitage (2011), checked separately.

checks.item: cul_de_sac_connector cost_url (also cited in new_sidewalks notes): UNC HSRC/FHWA cost summary, rows for paved trail, streetlight and concrete sidewalk
checks.note: PDF read with pdftotext. These rows appear word for word: 'Multi-Use Trail - Paved $261,000 $481,140 $64,710 $4,288,520 Mile 11 (42)', 'Streetlight $3,600 $4,880 $310 $13,900 Each 12 (17)' and 'Concrete Sidewalk $27 $32 $2.09 $410 Linear Foot 46 (164)'. The column order (Median, Average, Minimum, Maximum, Cost Unit, Number of Sources (Observations)) is as stated. The '2012 US Dollar equivalents' sentence and the FHWA/Robert Wood Johnson Foundation sentence are word for word. The work was created by UNC's Highway Safety Research Center; the source paper is Bushell, Poole, Rodriguez & Zegeer (July 2013). Arithmetic checks: 300 ft costs $14,830 at the median and $27,337 at the average; 500 ft costs $24,716 and $45,562; sidewalk is $27 x 5,280 = $142,560 and $32 x 5,280 = $168,960 per mile. The PDF says costs include 'labor, materials, mobilization costs and contractor profits'. It lists no exclusions, so the claim that land, easement, design, drainage and lighting are left out is the researcher's reasonable inference.

checks.item: new_sidewalks effect_url: Li et al. (2015), Austin, minimal gain from sidewalks in car-dependent areas
checks.note: The Crossref JSON (publisher SAGE) contains the abstract, and the quote is word for word. It confirms JPER 35(4): 471-488, the subtitle 'A Spatial Hedonic Study in Austin, Texas', 2010-2012 single-family sales and a Cliff-Ord spatial hedonic model. The abstract gives no dollar or percent figure, as the result says. Note: the paper measures walkability with Street Smart Walk Score and sidewalk density, not EPA's National Walkability Index. Treating NWI >= 10.51 as 'walkable' in the trigger is therefore the researcher's proxy, not the paper's definition.
